#22071. Latest Update: Inside Sullivan Middaugh’s Balancing Act Between Off-Road Dominance and LA 2028

📅 03 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1759 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Triathlete ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Inside Sullivan Middaugh’s Balancing Act Between Off-Road Dominance and LA 2028

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1759 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Triathlete

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that there are few races Sullivan Middaugh would like to target more than next year’s XTERRA World Championship in Fresh Mexico.
  • That’s because Middaugh is part of an exciting crop of American men trying to help the Project Podium program live up to its name at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.
  • It has been revealed that the challenge is that the 2027 XTERRA World Championship weekend in Ruidoso falls between the World Triathlon Championship Finals in Hamburg, Germany, and another top-level race in Weihai, China.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that there are few races Sullivan Middaugh would like to target more than next year’s XTERRA World Championship in Fresh Mexico. However, if everything goes to plan, there’s only a slim chance he’ll be on the start line to defend his title.

That’s because Middaugh is part of an exciting crop of American men trying to help the Project Podium program live up to its name at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics. And with an increasingly crowded triathlon calendar, the timing doesn’t quite work.

It has been revealed that the challenge is that the 2027 XTERRA World Championship weekend in Ruidoso falls between the World Triathlon Championship Finals in Hamburg, Germany, and another top-level race in Weihai, China. Both are part of the rebranded T50 Championship series.

Not only could these events prove critical in helping the U.S. secure three men’s spots for Los Angeles – the host nation is already guaranteed two – but Hamburg could also present an opportunity for Middaugh to stake his claim to one of those places.

He can’t afford to let up. It’s still early in the Olympic qualification cycle, but the U.S. currently has eight men in the top 50 of the Olympic rankings, more than any other nation, with Middaugh the fourth-ranked American at 31st overall.

But while the focus will understandably shift toward the work of coach Parker Spencer’s Project Podium squad, which splits its time between Tempe, Arizona, in the winter and Park City, Utah, in the summer, XTERRA will never be entirely out of mind.

After all, it’s the discipline that put the Middaugh family on the triathlon map, and never more so than earlier this month, when Sullivan claimed his first full-distance XTERRA world title, younger brother Porter finished seventh, and father Josiah, at 48 years young, placed sixth.

Three members of the same family, spanning two generations, finishing in the top seven of a World Championship race is a remarkable feat, with few obvious parallels across elite sport.

According to recent reports, the achievement was even more special because it had been 11 years since an American man last won the event. That was Josiah, in 2015. Before him, you have to go back another 15 years to Michael Tobin’s victory in 2000.

“No, I haven’t heard anything quite like that,” Sullivan confirms. “And especially having my dad in the race is pretty incredible!”.

More than the result itself, it’s the opportunity to continue racing alongside his father that Sullivan appreciates.

“Following in his footsteps is pretty awesome,” he continues. “Every year he says he’s gonna retire, but I don’t know. It’s been pretty awesome to be able to continue to train and race with him. I grew up just following him on the XTERRA circuit and going to races and watching him. I never really thought we’d be racing together.”.

Industry observers note that sullivan’s success also made up for his defeat by Reed Legg at the North American Championship earlier this year. Legg’s victory interrupted a Middaugh dynasty that has seen Josiah win 15 U.S. elite national titles and Sullivan dominate the more recent championship era.

And it was made all the sweeter by the XTERRA World Championship’s return to the U.S. after four years in Italy.

“I put it on my calendar and kept it in mind all year,” Sullivan notes. “It was a race at altitude, which I grew up at, and so I felt like it was a good opportunity. Grindstone Lake, where we swam, is at 7,000 feet and the course got up to maybe a little bit over 8,000 feet. But at home in Colorado, my house is at like 7,500 feet, and you can only really go up from there. So, the six or seven weeks leading in, I went home and trained with dad because I knew it would be a massive advantage if I could be fully acclimatized.”.

While Porter, who also trains with Project Podium, finished seventh, Sullivan believes his younger brother might have mounted a stronger challenge had he not been racing at the Under-23 World Championship in Spain.

Sullivan skipped that race to sharpen his mountain biking skills, although it didn’t prevent an early spill on the bike.

“Yeah, I overcooked the corners a little bit on the first couple of turns in the single track section,” he explains. “It wasn’t a bad spill out, but I kinda had to slam on the brake, go off the trail, tip over and get up quick. My bike computer fell off, which wasn’t a big deal, and maybe a blessing in disguise to not worry about power and just focus on effort.”.

Sullivan had an almost four-minute lead heading onto the run and extended his advantage with the day’s fastest 10K split, but at no point did he feel comfortable.

Sources indicate that “I didn’t really get any splits and thought that no lead was safe on the run. I just tried to give it full gas, focusing on pushing the climbs and rolling the downhills because I knew they’d be coming.”.

Among the athletes trying to hunt him down were two very familiar faces – Porter and Josiah – and there was a brief moment of family camaraderie as their paths crossed on the course.

In a recent development, “I just focus on myself for the most part, but it reminds you that they’re also out there battling. I saw them running together, so that was pretty cool because I knew they’d be pushing each other. We were all pumped, gave each other a high five, and that was pretty much it.”.

There were plenty more high fives and hugs at the finish, where Sullivan’s mom, sister, and grandparents were also in attendance.

While this was Sullivan’s first full-distance XTERRA world title, he had previously won the Short Track World Championship in Molveno, Italy, in 2024.

In recent years, short-track racing has typically taken place a couple of days before or the day after the main event, although it wasn’t on the schedule in Ruidoso.

“It’s like a three or four-minute swim, maybe a 15-minute bike and a seven-minute run,” Sullivan indicates, with distances depending on the course layout. “It’s all under 30 minutes for the most part, so more intense and a little bit different, and you can’t make as many mistakes. I think it suits me because I’ve spent a lot of time training for sprint distance draft-legal triathlons. I really enjoy it.”.

While XTERRA might be seen as a distraction from road triathlon, Sullivan believes it complements his efforts elsewhere.

It has been revealed that “It helps me with my skills for the draft-legal stuff as well. I look to people like Flora Duffy and Hayden Wilde who were able to do well at both, and think they’re an example for me.”.

For the next 18 months, the priority will be collecting Olympic qualification points, with the window having opened in May.

Sullivan has already recorded top-10 finishes at World Triathlon Cups in Huatulco, Mexico; Edmonton, Canada; Rio de Janeiro, Brazil; and Asunción, Paraguay. He also competed at the Americas Triathlon Championships in Antofagasta, Chile, finishing 11th. He now heads to Chile for two more World Cup races, in San Pedro de la Paz and Iquique.

It has been revealed that while USA Triathlon hasn’t officially released its selection policy for Los Angeles, Sullivan expects the Olympic test event in July 2027 and the World Championship Finals in Hamburg to be key races. He anticipates that a top-eight finish, combined with being the leading American, could be enough to meet the automatic selection criteria.

But first, he needs to secure starts at the biggest races. “Spots keep flipping, so it’s gonna be pretty tough,” he adds. “I’ve been mostly focusing on the World Cup level, which is the step below the World Championship Series, but as my swim develops, I’ll try and focus more on the World Championship Series because that’s the level you need to be at in the Olympics.”.

The higher the level, the more critical the swim becomes. “If you’re the best swimmer, you can be in the race up until the run, but if you don’t have a good swim, you may never even be in the race,” he explains. “The swim sets you up for a good day to get in the right bike group, but you also need to be able to run well off a hard bike. That’s something XTERRA helps me with.”.

Sullivan admits that bridging the gap in the swim is his biggest immediate challenge, but he also knows he’ll need a blistering run to compete at the very top.

Industry observers note that “Especially with Alex Yee and Hayden Wilde, it is just getting faster and faster,” he says. “You need to be an elite runner if you want to be on the podium, and that means hitting sub-14 minutes sometimes in the 5K and sub-29 minutes occasionally on the 10K. Right now, I’m in the low 14s and around 30, maybe a little under depending on the course.”.

In a recent development, if he can get there, it will be with the help of Project Podium. Established in 2018, Project Podium is funded by USA Triathlon, corporate sponsors, and private donors, including longtime benefactors Dr. Bill Warren and his wife Lynne. Based at Arizona State University, the program provides promising American male triathletes with coaching, scholarships, and financial support as they pursue Olympic ambitions.

Sullivan, who graduated with a degree in biomedical sciences in August, has enormous respect for coach Spencer, who he states also understands his passion for the trails and why XTERRA should remain part of his program.

“I love mountain biking, and so it’s good for me to be able to kinda go in and out, but I think that as the Olympics get closer I’ll have to take a slight step away from XTERRA, but we’ll see.”.

Finally, if Sullivan’s Olympic dream does come to fruition, could there be more than one Middaugh on the U.S. team?

Industry observers note that “That’s definitely a big ask, but would be amazing. I don’t know if it’s on the cards for ’28, but maybe for ’32 it could be more plausible. I think we both have the ability to get to that level if we stick with it, and when I see Porter in the race, we don’t really need to say anything. We just understand what we need to do.”.

#22070. What Yoga Can Teach You About Overcoming Common Obstacles in Life

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1521 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Yogajournal ↗ Open Full Page

What Yoga Can Teach You About Overcoming Common Obstacles in Life

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1521 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Yogajournal

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, in Yoga Journal’s Archives series, we share a curated collection of articles originally published in past challenges beginning in 1975.
  • According to recent reports, as we practice asanas (yoga postures) with awareness, we not only feel better, we are also better able to feel.
  • According to recent reports, in the Yoga Sutra, Patanjali explains the five main kleshas (obstacles) on the yogic path.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, in Yoga Journal’s Archives series, we share a curated collection of articles originally published in past challenges beginning in 1975. This article about overcoming obstacles in life first appeared in the May-June 2003 concern of Yoga Journal. You can find more of our Archives here.

According to recent reports, as we practice asanas (yoga postures) with awareness, we not only feel better, we are also better able to feel. That is, we become more sensitive to everything in our lives. As our sensitivity deepens and widens, we begin to practice asanas in such a way that we are practicing the larger yoga, which is the discovery of our Self and our dharma (our true purpose) and the overcoming of the obstacles that impede this journey.

According to recent reports, in the Yoga Sutra, Patanjali explains the five main kleshas (obstacles) on the yogic path. They are avidya (ignorance); asmita, (ego); raga (attachment to pleasure); dvesha (aversion to pain); and abhinivesha (the fear of death). Though there are many yogic methods for dealing with the kleshas, asana practice—both the poses we explore and the manner in which we work in them—can be one of the most powerful of yoga’s tools for helping us overcome these afflictions.

For all these obstacles, hatha yoga has a powerful remedy: backbends. Let us then take a look at the ways in which backbends—and specifically one of the most common backbends, Urdhva Mukha Svanasana (Upward-Facing Dog Pose)—can help us face the kleshas and overcome them.

How can we work on the kleshas while practicing backbends?

In the epic poem Savitri, the Indian sage Sri Aurobindo writes, “Where ignorance is, there suffering too must come.” Patanjali indicates that avidya, or ignorance, is the father of all the kleshas, so let us begin there.

Industry observers note that because backbends demand such focus, they are extremely powerful tools for overcoming ignorance. In an asana, any part of the body in which awareness is not present when it should be can be called ignorant. And any ignorant part of the body prevents the free flow of energy, causing stagnation. So our work is to bring awareness to the parts that are ignorant, replacing avidya (ignorance) with vidya (knowledge).

Among the asanas, backbends are especially useful in this process, since they require strong concentration and open the chest and heart center. There are many manifestations of bodily ignorance that show up regularly in prone backbending poses. The most common mistake is to do these poses with the shoulder blades up near the ears. Another common site of ignorance, especially in Urdhva Mukha Svanasana, is the neck. If you are not aware of your neck while doing this pose, you compress your cervical vertebrae and demonstrate once again that “where ignorance is, there suffering too must come.”.

Avidya in our physical body also manifests in the mind, which becomes unable to pay attention or retain and recall information. If we are to dispel our ignorance, we must cultivate the ability to focus our attention as well as the ability to calm our minds. Indeed, an unfocused brain cannot be calm. Thus, the ability to focus is a precursor to learning how to make the brain quiet.

As we practice and discover the ignorant parts of our body, our more refined awareness lets us see that these parts are being sacrificed to fulfill the ego. The ego’s desire to gratify itself makes us oblivious to restraint. We plow into poses just so that we can appear to be doing the posture. When we abuse the lumbar spine in Urdhva Mukha Svanasana to get a deeper-looking backbend, rather than slowly strengthening the lift of the pit of the abdomen, that too is ego.

The ego doesn’t care about balance or integrity, because it is more concerned with performance and getting as far as possible as fast as possible. The ego is competitive, yet it feeds itself both on achievement and on self-pity. Whether the ego states, “I am the greatest” or “I am the weakest,” it is all the same: It is all about the “I.”.

Backbends also help us overcome the obstacle of asmita, the ego, because they open the heart center, the seat of our connection with our higher Self. Asmita is the mistaken identification of the small, individual self with the universal, supreme Self. The ego believes it knows everything and thinks that the universe revolves around it. As the ego grows, consciousness moves away from the heart and into the brain. Over time, the connection between the mind and the heart—the smaller self and the larger Self—is lost. Backbends help bring us back to this connection.

The ego also blocks our progress in asana, for it assumes we have knowledge where we are ignorant. When we puff out the chest to appear powerful, denying the very weakness in our core, that is ego. The ego makes us believe that we have achieved a certain level of practice when actually we haven’t. It encourages us to practice for self-glory and pride rather than for the discovery of the spirit-self.

To work on the ego is to face the shadow self. The shadow self is that part of us which does not want to go to the light. It is the part we hide so that we can appear to be good. We do not want to face it, because it runs contrary to our self-image and is out-of-sync with our conscience. Yet unless we are willing to uncover and work on our shadow in both our asanas and our lives, unless we are observing our ego’s urge to repress our darker parts, we are not truly progressing on our path.

Sources indicate that backbends not only help us uncover the shadow but also create space for the heart chakra to open. As this happens, we release our egoistic viewpoints and see the basis of others’ thoughts, even when they are opposed to our own. Isn’t this the foundation for creating world peace, one yogi at a time?

Recent findings suggest that in asana practice, as elsewhere in life, we are attached to pleasure (raga) and averse to pain (dvesha). But the true practitioner of yoga understands that temporary discomfort often leads to more stable and permanent pleasure. In fact, our aversion and attachment often stem from confusion. Looking only at the immediate effects of actions, we mistakenly label as pleasurable that which feels good in the moment even if, in truth, its real long-term effect will be painful.

In the practice of Urdhva Mukha Svanasana, for example, relaxing the shoulders and arms may momentarily feel pleasurable, but this attachment to pleasure will, in the long run, cause tension and compression in the neck and collapsing in the chest. On the other hand, pushing down strongly with the arms, contracting the triceps, and using the side chest muscles can initially be painful—it certainly requires strong effort—yet these actions lead to freedom in the neck and expansion in the chest.

Be conscious throughout your practice of Urdhva Mukha Svanasana—indeed, in all backbends—that you do not just fold the spine at a single point or area. Much as folding a paper clip many times at one point eventually breaks the metal, such acute folding of your spine can create compression and damage. The lower back and the neck are especially susceptible to such collapse.

The chest and heart openings provided by backbends also counteract the last three of the five kleshas: raga, dvesha, and abhinivesha. Raga, our attachment to pleasure, is a futile grasping of the ephemeral—we clutch what is only transient. In doing so we close our chest and shut down the heart center. Dvesha, aversion to pain, also closes the door to our hearts. When we cover up pain, we cover up our shadows, the parts of ourselves that we repress because they do not please the ego. As with raga, our aversion is not expressed with open, wide arms but with a clutching, defensive posture.

Abhinivesha, the fear of death, is the father of all fear, the primal cause for all shrinking of the chest, hunching of the spine, and withdrawing back into our small selves.

In a recent development, as we practice Urdhva Mukha Svanasana, how can we work on the final klesha, abhinivesha, the fear of death? By approaching and practicing the pose as though it were new to us every time we come into it. The fear of death is the fear of change; only as we accept change can we turn this fear away and grow. Doing the pose today as we did it yesterday is reenacting a dead pose. Doing the pose according to the inspirations of today gives birth to a pose that is alive.

Yet upcoming life doesn’t exist without the old life dying; we must let go of yesterday’s accomplishments in order to keep growing. Each time we practice asanas in a new way, we work on overcoming our personal fears of death and rebirth, taking another step into a truer and more luminous life.

#22069. Are seed oils bad for you? Vegetable oil vs. olive oil vs. butter

Are seed oils bad for you? Vegetable oil vs. olive oil vs. butter

📅 22 Jan 2025 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2984 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Precisionnutrition

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, from TikTok to bestseller lists, vegetable oils—a.k.a.
  • To be fair, folks have debated the merits of vegetable oils dating back to when they first entered the marketplace.
  • According to recent reports, more recently, however, with the advent of the carnivore diet, vegetable oil hate has roared back into the socials.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, from TikTok to bestseller lists, vegetable oils—a.k.a. “seed oils”—are a big topic right now.

To be fair, folks have debated the merits of vegetable oils dating back to when they first entered the marketplace.

According to recent reports, more recently, however, with the advent of the carnivore diet, vegetable oil hate has roared back into the socials. Maybe you’ve come across posts that refer to these cooking oils as “toxic sludge,” “motor oil,” “the hateful eight,” and “the biggest cause of chronic disease that nobody knows about.”.

The anti-vegetable oil logic goes something like this….

Animal fats have been with humans for thousands of years. Vegetable fats, on the other hand, were invented during the last century when profit-seeking companies wanted to find a way to sell cheap-to-grow foods to unsuspecting consumers.

Another argument: Like margarine, vegetable oils were marketed as healthier alternatives for butter, and yet, people argue, these oils are worse than butter, raising your risk for obesity, anxiety, depression, ulcerative colitis, and more.

In contrast to the above line of thought, other experts will tell you that vegetable oils are harmless, potentially even health-promoting—and absolutely better than butter.

Like so many nutrition topics, the truth is too nuanced to fit on a meme.

In this story, we’ll help you sort the science from the pseudoscience so you can make informed decisions about the oils you choose to include in your diet.

Recent findings suggest that sometimes called “seed oils,” vegetable oils start, as you might suspect, from the seed of a plant. The most common ones you’ll find in a typical grocery aisle include:.

By the way, if you feel like there’s a bunch of oils missing from that list, it’s probably because those oils come from non-seed plants (such as olive, avocado, palm, or coconut oil, which all come from fruits, and aren’t considered vegetable or seed oils).

Sources indicate that non-vegetable oils—such as olive and avocado oil—are derived from naturally fatty foods. In fact, olives are so oily that you could theoretically make your own olive oil at home. (Just Google “how to make olive oil from scratch,” and you’ll find a number of videos walking you through the steps.).

The same can’t be noted of most vegetable oils, which mostly come from foods with a relatively tiny fat content to begin with.

Case in point: A cup of green olives contains about 20 grams of fat,1 whereas a cup of corn has 2 grams.2.

As a result, manufacturers must use an extensive multi-step process to extract this small amount of oil from these non-oily foods. These steps include:.

During this process, health-promoting polyphenols and other stabilizing nutrients are lost, and small amounts of unsaturated fats are transformed into trans fatty acids (also called partially hydrogenated fat).

(Interesting fact: This also happens during deep frying. When vegetable oils sizzle in a restaurant’s deep fryer for hours, the trans fat content of the oil increases.).

To call these processed oils “toxic” might be an exaggeration. However, nutrition scientists generally agree that people should avoid trans fats in the diet, and in 2018, the Food and Drug Administration banned manufacturers from adding trans fats to processed foods.3 4.

At PN, we’ve created several visual guides people can use to make informed decisions about what to eat.

(We’ve also created a shopping list, which you or your clients can print out and take to the grocery store. Check it out: Healthy Fats Shopping List).

In these guides, we’ve placed a few vegetable oils—expeller-pressed canola oil, high-oleic sunflower, and safflower oils—in the “Eat Some” section. For us, “eat some” is another way of saying that these foods will neither improve health nor harm health—when consumed in reasonable amounts. In some cases, like in the example of dark chocolate, when consumed in small amounts, they might even improve health.

The rest of the vegetable oils, along with butter and other saturated fats, fall into the “Eat Less” category, as the image below reveals. You’ll find vegetable oils in bold.

Industry observers note that we’ve gotten hate mail from folks who say certain vegetable oils—especially cold-pressed canola oil—should appear alongside olive oil in the “eat more” category. Plenty of others say all vegetable oils belong in the “eat less” column, and that butter belongs in “eat some” or even “eat more.”.

To understand the scientific reasoning behind our recommendations, let’s explore some head-to-head matchups.

These oils are the least refined of their kind.

Sources indicate that to make extra virgin olive oil (EVOO), manufacturers grind and mechanically press olives, without using any heat. Similarly, expeller-pressed canola oil is made by mechanically pressing rapeseed, without the use of heat or chemical solvents.

Olive oil is richer in heart-healthy monounsaturated fatty acids (MUFAs) than almost any other cooking oil.

Recent findings suggest that in addition, unlike the more refined “light” olive oil, EVOO maintains most of the olive fruit’s original polyphenols. These plant-based substances help to combat inflammation and protect cells from damage.

More studies vouch for EVOO’s health-promoting qualities than for any other cooking fat.

Sources indicate that for example, researchers asked 22,892 adults from Southern Italy to self-report their olive oil consumption. People who consumed the most olive oil (more than two tablespoons a day) were 20 percent less likely to die over the 13-year study than people who consumed the least olive oil (less than one tablespoon a day).5.

Other research has linked the consumption of olive oil with a reduced risk of:.

Consumption of olive oil is also associated with reductions in LDL cholesterol, especially when used to replace saturated fats like butter and coconut oil.10.

Years ago, culinary experts recommended using EVOO only on salads and other uncooked foods. Back then, they assumed EVOO’s relatively low smoke point (350 to 410F) meant the oil would break down when heated, losing some of its distinctive flavor and health benefits.

We now know that smoke point isn’t as significant a deal as previously thought.

That’s especially true in the case of EVOO, whose polyphenols and high concentrations of monounsaturated fats help keep the oil stable when heated.

In research that heated a variety of cooking oils to 464 F (240C) and then held them at 356 F (180C) for several hours, EVOO remained more stable than any other oil tested, including canola oil.11.

One of the more affordable cooking oils on the shelf, canola oil, is made from a Canadian-made hybrid of the rapeseed plant.

(The word “canola” refers to the first three letters of “Canada” with a fun “ola” added to the end for marketing purposes.)12.

Among vegetable oils, canola is the richest in heart-healthy monounsaturated fats (though several non-vegetable oils have it beat) as well as alpha-linolenic acid, a plant-based omega-3 fatty acid.

In addition, canola oil contains plant substances called phytosterols that help influence blood cholesterol for the better, especially when used as a substitute for butter, research has found.13 14 15.

Extra virgin olive oil is the clear winner.

The body of research in support of EVOO dwarfs the body of research in support of expeller-pressed canola.

Sources indicate that in addition, EVOO has a more favorable fatty acid profile. By the way, so does avocado oil, which is why you’ll also find it in the “eat more” column.

Sources indicate that however, you can buy roughly twice as much expeller-pressed canola oil for half as much money as EVOO. Because of this, expeller-pressed canola can be a good budget-friendly choice. In addition, because of expeller-pressed canola’s more neutral flavor, many people prefer it over EVOO for baking.

When used in moderation, expeller-pressed canola can be part of a healthy diet. It is likely to be at least health neutral, if not somewhat health beneficial.

This match-up comes down to how processing methods affect the end product.

An expeller press is a machine that squeezes oil out of seeds.

It’s able to do this without the use of solvents or heat, which helps preserve beneficial compounds such as alpha-linolenic acid and phytosterols.

Refining removes some protective alpha-linoleic acid while adding small amounts of unhealthy trans fatty acids. This results in a product that is proportionally lower in omega-3 fatty acids and higher in omega-6 fatty acids.

Expeller-pressed canola oil wins, but only by a small margin.

It has been revealed that that’s because canola oil starts with a less controversial fatty acid profile than many other vegetable oils, as the chart below indicates. Soybean oil, for example, has less heart-healthy monounsaturated fat and much more theoretically inflammation-contributing omega-6 fat.

The typical American consumes around 16 to 20 times more omega-6 fats than omega-3s.

This imbalance could theoretically increase inflammation in your body, potentially raising your risk for diabetes, obesity, and other health problems, argue some experts.16.

Years ago, the recommendation to balance your omega 6s with omega 3s was widespread. (The suggested “ideal” ratio: Anywhere from 1:1 to 4:1, in favor of omega 6s.).

These days, there’s more debate among nutritional scientists as to whether this imbalance contributes to chronic inflammation, especially when those omega 6s are consumed in whole foods that contain many other beneficial compounds.

For example, nuts and seeds—both naturally rich in omega-6 fats—have been associated with a range of health benefits, including reductions in blood cholesterol and inflammation.17 18.

In 2019, Harvard Health ran the headline “No need to avoid healthy omega-6 fats.” In support of their argument, a 2019 study from the American Heart Association journal Circulation determined that, if anything, the consumption of omega-6 fats reduced the risk for stroke, heart disease, and early death.19.

Recent findings suggest that however, while nuts and refined canola oil may share a somewhat similar fatty acid profile, the two foods differ in one important way. As we mentioned earlier, refined canola oil is basically pure oil. Meanwhile, nuts and seeds come packaged with health-protective fiber, polyphenols, protein, vitamins, and minerals.

Minimally-processed foods, like nuts or extra virgin oils, include a complex matrix of health-promoting nutrients. Highly-processed oils, on the other hand, have lost the vast majority of those healthful compounds, leaving mostly just the fatty acids which are more prone to oxidation (we’ll cover that next).

This is the match-up that triggers the most arguing on the interwebs.

Let’s cover the major claims from both sides—plus what the research states.

It has been revealed that butter proponents argue that saturated fats have been unnecessarily vilified. They point to nutrition recommendations during the 1980s and 1990s that recommended people replace butter with trans-fat rich margarine.

Margarine aside, others claim the research in support of reducing saturated fats is thin at best.20.

However, excessive saturated fat consumption (beyond 10 percent of total calories) does seem to boost cholesterol levels and may increase your risk of heart disease.21.

It has been revealed that some research has found that replacing 5 percent of the saturated fats in your diet with monounsaturated fats could reduce the risk of heart disease by 15 percent. Similarly, replacing 5 percent of the saturated fats in your diet with polyunsaturated fats (with most of that coming from refined vegetable oils) reduces the risk of a future heart attack by 10 percent, according to an analysis of eight studies involving 13,614 people.22 Many other studies support this finding.23.

But not all saturated fats affect blood cholesterol equally. In some dairy foods, a membrane—called a milk fat globule membrane—surrounds the saturated fats and seems to limit their cholesterol-raising properties.

However, butter is low in this protective membrane, and consequently raises blood cholesterol more than other high-fat dairy products, like full-fat milk, cream, yogurt, or cheese.24 25 26.

Sources indicate that the U.S. Dietary Guidelines recommend capping saturated fat at less than 10 percent of your calorie intake. A tablespoon of butter contains 7 grams of saturated fat—a third of the recommended daily limit in a 2000 Calorie diet.

So, while you don’t necessarily need to eliminate butter, it’s worth moderating your intake.

It has been revealed that (Interested in learning about all the nuances of saturated fat consumption? Read: Is saturated fat good or bad for you?).

Due to their chemical structure, polyunsaturated fats are inherently less stable and more prone to oxidation than saturated or monounsaturated fats.

Sources indicate that during the refining process, protective phytochemicals and antioxidants are stripped, making these oils more prone to oxidation. The theory is that this oxidation increases inflammation in the body and elevates the risk of various health conditions.

There’s some evidence to suggest that diets rich in polyunsaturated fats, especially from refined vegetable oils, are associated with increased levels of oxidized blood lipids, lipid peroxidation, and other markers of inflammation.27 28.

If you only use refined corn or safflower oils to lightly coat veggies before roasting them, you likely don’t have much to worry about.

However, for the vast majority of people, the biggest source of refined vegetable oils isn’t home-cooked meals—it’s ultra-processed foods.

It has been revealed that the extra processing and repeated heat exposure used to create ultra-processed foods further oxidize these oils. Additionally, these foods are often loaded with potentially harmful ingredients like added sodium and sugars, and low in beneficial nutrients like fiber, vitamins, minerals, and phytonutrients.

According to recent reports, plus, they’re incredibly calorie-dense and difficult to stop eating, which can raise your risk for obesity. (Find out exactly why highly-processed foods are so “addictive”: Why you can’t stop eating ultra-processed foods.).

In a large review involving nearly 10 million people, the consumption of ultra-processed foods was associated with a higher risk of premature death.29 In addition, studies have linked high consumption of ultra-processed foods with the following health problems:30 31 32 33.

You don’t have to abolish ultra-processed foods.

But your health will benefit from capping your consumption to about 20 percent or so of your intake, with the other 80 percent or so from mostly minimally-processed whole foods.

It has been revealed that this alone will naturally lower your refined vegetable oil intake to a safer level, without much fuss. Plus, consuming refined vegetable oils in the context of a diet that’s rich in colorful plants, fiber, phytochemicals, and antioxidants may help offset the concern of oxidation. (For example, by putting a reasonable amount of commercial salad dressing on a large, colorful salad.).

Ultimately, both should be limited in the diet, and neither are health-promoting.

Most refined vegetable oils are lopsidedly rich in polyunsaturated fatty acids compared to monounsaturated fats, and are stripped of many protective compounds. As mentioned earlier, some experts argue that these omega-6-rich fats may contribute to inflammation (but the evidence here is mixed). Because of how they’re processed, seed oils also contain some of those trans fats that everyone agrees we should all minimize.

According to recent reports, in contrast, butter is low in omega 6s but high in saturated fat, which can be problematic in higher amounts. Especially since it’s so low in the protective milk fat globule membrane. However, compared to refined vegetable oil, butter is less processed. Like olive oil, it’s one of those fats you could theoretically make at home.

This might be obvious from the head-to-head matchups, but we’ll say it anyway.

If you like it and can afford it, EVOO is a great choice.

Sources indicate that cold-pressed avocado oil and walnut oil are also great options, as both are rich in antioxidant compounds. Like EVOO, avocado oil is a rich source of MUFAs. Walnut oil’s fat primarily comes from polyunsaturated fats, so it’s best used as a dressing rather than used for cooking (as it’s less heat stable).

Recent findings suggest that however, like EVOO, avocado and walnut oil tend to be expensive. If you or your client are budget-conscious, expeller-pressed canola oil is a solid runner-up.

Similarly, high-oleic sunflower and safflower oils are richer sources of monounsaturated fats than their high-linoleic cousins. When substituted for saturated fats like butter, high-oleic oils have been associated with cardiovascular benefits.34 35.

Regardless of what cooking fats you or your client choose, you’ll also want to do the following:.

Whole and minimally-processed foods—such as nuts, seeds, avocados, olives, and salmon—are more likely to feature health-promoting monounsaturated (MUFAs) and omega-3 fats. They also come packaged with a wide array of other good-for-you nutrients such as fiber, protein, minerals, and antioxidants.

In contrast, ultra-professed foods are generally devoid of everything you keep hearing you should consume more of. These foods also tend to be calorie-dense, highly rewarding, and hard to stop eating.

If you’re not sure whether packaged food is minimally processed or highly processed, take a close look and consider:.

If you answer “no” to most of the above, the food is likely highly processed.

It doesn’t matter what source of fat is used to fry them.

Sort all fried foods into the “eat less” category.

Sources indicate that EVOO is associated with longer, healthier lives. However, that doesn’t mean you should be doing shots of it.

As a general rule, you’re better off getting most of your fat from foods like avocados, olives, nuts and seeds than from any cooking oil.

Sources indicate that whole food fats are rich in fiber, phytochemicals, vitamins, and minerals, and are generally less calorie-dense than oils. (But having one to three servings of oils or butter per day is reasonable.).

And if you want personalized advice to suit your body, your eating preferences, and your goals, check out our Nutrition Calculator to figure out how fats fit into your overall diet.

#22068. What Happens When Grief Derails Your Triathlon Training

📅 03 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1686 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Triathlete ↗ Open Full Page

What Happens When Grief Derails Your Triathlon Training

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1686 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Triathlete

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Rachel Olson wins 2026 Ironman 70.3 São Paulo after struggling to train through the grief of losing her mother in November 2024.
  • In late September, Rachel Olson crossed the finish line first at Ironman 70.3 São Paulo, nearly 10 minutes ahead of her nearest competitor.
  • It has been revealed that because in the months after her mother Janis died in November 2024 of liver disease, Olson could barely bring herself to work out.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rachel Olson wins 2026 Ironman 70.3 São Paulo after struggling to train through the grief of losing her mother in November 2024. (Photo: Romulo Cruz/Ironman).

In late September, Rachel Olson crossed the finish line first at Ironman 70.3 São Paulo, nearly 10 minutes ahead of her nearest competitor. The race, by her own admission, was “not spectacular” for the longtime pro triathlete. But the support that followed was. The crowd embraced her, and athletes and fans who had followed her story cheered a little louder, as though they knew what it took just to get her to the start line.

It has been revealed that because in the months after her mother Janis died in November 2024 of liver disease, Olson could barely bring herself to work out. She did not want to disappear from triathlon. But she’d go to the pool and just sit on the edge and cry. She’d hop on her bike and feel a sudden urge to turn around. Running, always an easy way to manage significant emotions, became a chore.

Then her body began to rebel: digestive complications, mysterious inflammation, bone-deep exhaustion, muscles that wouldn’t recover.

In a recent development, “My body was basically screaming at me that something was wrong, like it was constantly fighting something,” remarked Olson, 35, who lives in Boulder with her fiancé, fellow pro triathlete Andre Lopes. “Your mind is telling you to process, and your body is telling you to slow down.”.

Recent findings suggest that for endurance athletes, the instinct after a loss is often to train through the emotional pain. The adage goes that exercise helps with grief: Get outside, move your body, clear your head. Sometimes it does. But for Olson and many others, the very thing that once gave life structure can become one more demand on a body and mind already stretched thin.

“Grief doesn’t just live in the mind. It’s in the chest, in the restlessness, in this low-grade energy that has nowhere obvious to go,” remarked Kenza Haddock, president and co-founder of Oceanic Counseling Group in Murrells Inlet, South Carolina. “Endurance sport can tip from processing grief into outrunning it, using exhaustion to stay ahead of the feeling rather than move through it. It can just leave you more numb.”.

Plenty of endurance athletes have turned grief into a mission. In August 2026, Matthew Hollingham, a 25-year-old doctoral student at Penn State, created an “Arctic Circle to Africa” triathlon in memory of his late fiancée Lovisa Arnesson-Cronhamre, who was killed in a hit-and-run while jogging on campus. Over 61 days and 3,545 miles, he swam in a lake above the Arctic Circle, ran a marathon a day for 37 days, and cycled just over 110 miles a day for 23. He raised more than $40,000 for two charities and kept her memory present.

Others have taken similar routes; at the 2026 London Marathon, Laura Coleman-Day, a 33-year-old mother from Lincolnshire in the U.K., went viral for changing into her wedding dress and running the final miles in it as a dedication to her late husband, Xander.

This kind of public mission can be cathartic, says Hilary Bucell, a psychotherapist and lecturer at Columbia University.

“Engaging in something like triathlon can become a ritualized space where the recognition of the loss is welcomed and at the same time, the sport’s necessity for present moment awareness also helps athletes acknowledge fresh life experiences continuing now beyond the loss,” she remarked.

Of course, racing to honor a loved one doesn’t erase grief — it just gives you a place to put it. It can also offer a healthy distraction from the deep ache of a devastating loss.

Recent findings suggest that some aren’t able to navigate their grief in such a public and profound way. There are those like Olson whose grief hits the body hard enough to derail training. In 2023, Gustav Iden, the 2022 Ironman World Champion, ended his season early to heal and regroup after the death of his mother, revealing “it was very emotional, and it was hard to find joy in training after that.” (He returned to racing about a year later.).

Industry observers note that as one of her mother’s main caretakers, Olson spent two years before her death flying to her hometown in Texas for doctor’s appointments. Triathlon took a backseat: She parted ways with her coach and scaled back her training. Even when she did have time to work out, anxiety followed.

“I would think, ‘Am I going to be out on a bike ride and get a phone call saying she’s in the hospital? Are things going to go downhill?’”.

It has been revealed that after Janis died, that anxiety turned physical. Olson was never diagnosed with one specific glitch, but testing showed elevated inflammation markers and low ferritin, requiring an iron infusion.

Industry observers note that “Ultimately, I think my body was responding to trauma. It felt like I had an illness,” she said. “Trying to perform in a body that felt completely foreign to me was incredibly difficult. I didn’t understand why my body wasn’t doing what it had done before.”.

Research suggests that grief can affect the body as well as the mind. The National Institutes of Health (NIH) lists impaired immune response and increased mortality from heart disease, especially in older, widowed patients, among the physical complications. The effects may vary, as not everyone experiences the same physical response.

Part of the explanation may lie in how the brain processes the loss of a loved one through interconnected systems involved in emotion, threat detection, and the regulation of stress hormones. Grief can flood the body with inflammatory signals. and increase cortisol, the steroid hormone produced by the adrenal glands that regulates the body’s response to stress.

In a recent development, “Grief is a neurological event that impacts your ability to learn and remember things, attend to things, and impacts your mood,” remarked Wilfred van Gorp, a Manhattan-based board-certified neuropsychologist. “Losing someone keeps your amygdala on high alert and elevates cortisol. It impacts you in your body as well as your mind.”.

Grief and stress can also disrupt communication between the brain and the gut, which may contribute to everything from irritable bowel syndrome to acid reflux to ulcers, according to research.

For Olson, whose stomach swelled within days of her mother’s death, that brain-gut link was obvious.

“Only two days after [she passed], I woke up, and my stomach was distended about five inches. And then I kind of exploded in inflammation weight,” she shared. “Trying to get that down is not an easy process.”.

Still, Olson pushed on. She’d qualified for her first Ironman World Championship slated for about 10 months after Janis died. She wanted to race there to honor her mom. She also didn’t want to lose her identity as a triathlete. Her training “wasn’t even close” to peak levels. In Kona, her stomach rebelled on the bike. After vomiting for three hours, she pulled out soon after starting the run.

“I held onto triathlon so tightly even though my body wasn’t ready. My mind wasn’t ready,” Olson stated. “I kept pushing because I wanted it so badly. I attached too much weight to needing training [and racing] to go well and needing something in my life to be OK. Looking back, I realize I didn’t have to be OK.”.

After Kona, Olson took a break. She focused on her other jobs as a triathlon coach and as a sales rep, and on envisioning what her wedding to Lopes could look like without her mom.

In a recent development, “I decided I wasn’t going to think about triathlon for a couple of weeks,” she shared. “If I still wanted it afterward, great. If I didn’t, that was OK, too.”.

Spoiler: She still loved it. With the fog lifted, Olson saw a different future in the sport, starting with a new coach, Kasper Pedersen, who could build a sustainable load and understand her fragile state.

Recent findings suggest that “I looked for a coach who understands that life happens,” noted Olson. “Kasper is great at helping me push my boundaries, but he also knows that I may need to go at my own pace.”.

They’re keeping her training volume relatively low as she re-establishes a baseline and repairs her frayed central nervous system.

Industry observers note that “I really wanted to make my body and mind think, ‘This is fun. This is helping us,’ rather than setting off alarm bells every time I went out,” Olson shared. “There are still days where I have to take some time off. … Grief really is a roller coaster. But overall, we’ve done a really good job of figuring out what is working.”.

Sources indicate that talking about it helps, too, though it doesn’t come easily. Olson describes her grief as a “cloud over her personal life,” and opening up about it has cost her: One friend drifted away, unable to understand what she was going through. Olson wonders if she was simply too much to handle. Still, she finds solace in speaking out, and in being a voice for others who may be grieving alone.

In a recent development, “As athletes, we want to put difficult things in the back of our minds and keep going,” she stated. “But I’m glad I can be a voice for other people who are going through the same so they feel less alone than they think they are.”.

If her recent win in Brazil is any sign, Olson is rounding a bend toward healing, with an approach to triathlon (and life) that’s less about control and more about leaning into the process, however unpredictable and messy it may be.

“I feel like I’m a different person than I was before [my mom died]. It will always feel like a part of me has been ripped away. But I also know that there’s literally no pain that hurts as bad as what I went through,” she said. “So I’ll keep telling myself, ‘Yes, I can do this thing.’”.

#22067. This Underrated Yoga Twist Helps Unlock Tight Shoulders

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 17m • 📚 Deep Dive (3438 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Yogajournal ↗ Open Full Page

This Underrated Yoga Twist Helps Unlock Tight Shoulders

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3438 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Yogajournal

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In Yoga Journal’s Archives series, we share a curated collection of articles originally published in past issues beginning in 1975.
  • Pasasana is the first pose in the Second Series of Ashtanga Yoga.
  • It’s essential to recognize that the learning process is a process, a gradual evolution.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In Yoga Journal’s Archives series, we share a curated collection of articles originally published in past issues beginning in 1975. This article about Pasasana first appeared in the September-October 2002 glitch of Yoga Journal. Find more of our Archives here.

Pasasana is the first pose in the Second Series of Ashtanga Yoga. To start this series, you need not only the physical ability to learn the poses but, more importantly, the correct attitude. If you take away anxiety about having to do challenging poses, take away “I-have-to-do-Second-Series” ambition, and release the fear of never achieving Pasasana, you create space for the willingness to persist, an attitude that helps you continue to try even in the face of difficulty.

It’s essential to recognize that the learning process is a process, a gradual evolution. Given that we live in an age of instant gratification, the idea of slowing down and relishing gradual progress can frighten our results-oriented minds. But the desire to be somewhere other than where we are only hinders progress toward the goals to which we aspire.

This interference of the ego is one of the ways in which perception becomes clouded. The clouding of our perception is known as avidya, or the lack of knowledge. Indian yoga teacher T. K.V. Desikachar describes the four “children” of avidya in his book Religiousness in Yoga (University Press of America, 1980). The first child, asmita (ego), always states “I know” or “I am right.” Raga (greed), the second child, wants everything immediately, whether or not the time is right. Under raga’s influence, if you want to move on to a difficult pose, you do, whether you are ready for it or not. The third child, dvesa (aversion), avoids or discards anything that seems difficult. The fourth child is abhinivesa (“clinging to life”). In our experience, this appears as fear not just of death but also of the death of a habit, a mind-set, a sense of achievement—of anything to which we’re attached. Fear has an infinite number of faces: fear of looking inadequate, fear of exploring the unknown, and fear of failing, to name only a few.

Avidya often rears up in the practice of yoga. All its forms feed our misinterpretation of reality, which is usually the source of our discomfort. The first step in finding release from avidya is recognizing the moments when we become entrapped in it. Then we build a sustaining, satisfying practice by learning to work through asmita, raga, dvesa, and abhinivesa. As we do this and begin to live in the truth, we become quiet inside. Like a child who knows they are loved, we walk through life with confidence.

For 99 percent of us, Pasasana is one of those poses best learned with the consistent hands-on help of a teacher and with the aid of props. It is not a pose that most of us will inhabit easily. Many students practice for years before they can do Pasasana with their heels on the floor and their wrists clasped. Because of the often slow progress and the help required in working on this pose, it provides an ideal landscape for avidya to take root and flourish. Suddenly we feel we are a less accomplished student because we need a prop or a hand to help us into the pose. For many students, the reaction to this feeling comes in the guise of avidya’s aforementioned children: stubborn insistence that we already know how to approach the pose; over-eagerness to leap blindly into an advanced expression of the pose that we’re not ready for; aversion to working with a prop, or deliberate resistance that maintains ignorance because we are scared to find out what we don’t know.

According to recent reports, in my efforts to empower students, I give them all the tools I think are appropriate, including props. Props can be a crutch, but if they are used with intelligence, they can lessen the frustration in a pose, and this facilitates learning. To me, developing confidence in a pose through the use of a prop is learning. Sitting on a block while the body learns to open and strengthen is not a crime; dislocating a shoulder or tearing apart a knee is.

In a recent development, pasasana is a perfect pose to illustrate the value of props. What is the point in trying to wrap the arms in Pasasana if your roots, your feet, are not planted firmly on the ground? Without a solid foundation, belief that you understand the pose is illusory, and your practice of Pasasana will feed into the cycle of avidya rather than serving as an opportunity for the experience of Truth.

Sources indicate that for students beginning Pasasana, I often suggest a preparatory version in which we eliminate the wrap of the arms. We remove this difficult element of the pose in order to develop strength in the legs, challenge the Achilles tendon, and set the stage for proper twisting. To come into this Pasasana prep, stand at the front edge of your mat in Samastitihi (Equal Standing). Join the inner edges of your feet together. Spread the toes apart and feel the four corners of each foot making even contact with your mat. From the arches of your feet, lift through the core of the body. Gently draw the sides of the hips in toward the midline. This creates stability and steadiness.

Without a firm foundation, your poses can feed a cycle of ignorance, not an experience of truth.

Now begin to bend your knees. As you squat, keep both knees pointing straight ahead, and keep both the heels firmly rooting into the ground. Do not press the knees together, as this will cause the groins to tighten. With the groins soft, allow the inner thighs to descend toward the ground. Attempt to lower the thighs to a 90-degree angle. Breathe smoothly and evenly. Keeping your heels on the ground, take the left hand to the outside of the left thigh. Using the left hand as leverage, bend your right arm and bring your right elbow to the outside of your left leg. Pause for a moment and make sure that your breath has not become forceful. Stay calm on the inside; let go of struggling and forcing. To safeguard the knees and keep the hips properly level, do not let your elbow push the knees to the right. Also, keep the knees in line with each other: Do not let the right knee move in front of the left one. Use the left hand to help you move the right elbow more deeply down the leg, so that the right armpit and thigh come together like pieces of a puzzle.

To deepen the twist, move it into the upper back by leveraging the elbow and thigh against each other. Draw your right kidney area into your body and drop your shoulders way down away from your ears. Reach the top of the sternum away from your navel and spread across the collarbones. Again use the left hand to bring the right elbow farther down the leg. If the armpit and thigh make contact with each other, straighten your right arm and place the hand on the ground. (If not, continue to work with a bent arm, elbow at the side of the leg.) Line your fingertips up with your toes. Press down through whatever is on the floor. These are your roots. Begin with the feet: Press them deeply down, as though you could dig holes in the floor. Let the arches of your feet act as suction cups that draw energy up the legs. Move the shinbones in the direction of the calves and use the calves to deepen the rooting of the heels into the floor. This will stabilize the pose and help protect the knees.

Industry observers note that now press the palm of the right hand into the floor and drop both shoulders away from the ears. Reach your left arm high and straight up toward the ceiling. Spread tremendously through the arms.

According to recent reports, as you work in the twist, begin low in the spine and continue into the upper back. Move the bottom tips of the shoulder blades deep into the body as the shoulders release down the back. As the shoulder blades draw in, resist the temptation to round and collapse the chest. Instead, let the action of the shoulder blades fuel the opening of the chest. The right arm and left leg act as leverage for the chest to make its ascent up out of the belly. From the twisting of the upper back, reach back with the left hand and attempt to clasp the right inner thigh. Do this by rotating the left shoulder back and moving the left elbow away from the body. Turn the head and gaze straight over the shoulder.

Breathe smoothly. Be mindful of the hips: Keep the side hips firm and do not let the left hip pop out to the side. The hips and knees should still be facing straight forward (Figure 1). After a few breaths, release and repeat the pose on the other side.

In a recent development, if it’s hard for you to sink to a right angle with the heels on the ground, your Achilles tendons will need to lengthen. I strongly discourage the use of a prop under the heels. In this case, a prop is a crutch, not a learning tool: It hinders the lengthening of the Achilles, which is an essential component of Pasasana.

It has been revealed that now let’s go to a wall to work with another preparation for Pasasana. The wall allows us to twist into the pose with the heels on the floor even if the Achilles tendons have not lengthened enough to permit a grounded balance in the middle of the room.

Stand sideways to the wall. Be sure the outside edge of the left foot and thigh are an inch or two away from it. Begin to squat, lowering your buttocks as close as possible to the floor. Again, keep the heels on the ground and the knees in line with each other. On an exhalation, hook the right elbow on the outside of the left thigh as far down the leg as possible. Place both hands on the wall for balance. Perhaps you can now lower the hips a little closer to the floor (knees in line, of course).

Using the hands on the wall, begin to twist from the lowest part of the spine. Press the hands into the wall and isometrically pretend to drag them down. This action will aid you in lengthening the spine, which is always the first rule of twisting. Work to bring the right side of your rib cage into the body and forward toward the wall. Let the spine move up toward the top of the head and create maximum extension from the navel to the sternum. Release the shoulders by letting the trapezius muscles cascade down the back. Slide the shoulder blades down and into the body. Move the top of the sternum farther up toward the ceiling (Figure 2). As you work to open the chest, use the grounding of the feet into the earth like a springboard. The energy of the feet, the lift of the arches, and the corresponding vitality in the legs give the pose a feeling of lightness. Hold the pose for a few breaths, then release and do the other side.

Use the grounding of the feet like a springboard: The corresponding lift of the arches and vitality in the legs will give the pose a feeling of lightness.

Industry observers note that A third Pasasana variation teaches the wrap of the arm by using the aid of the wall for balance. For this variation, stand with the buttocks either against the wall or slightly away from the wall, and squat deeply. (Experiment to find exactly the right place for your feet.) As in the first preparation, begin by bringing the right elbow to the outside of the left leg. Move the elbow deeply down the leg to initiate this action from the back rather than just from the arm. Take the left hand behind you to the wall for balance. Use the left hand at the wall to move the left shoulder blade down the back. Drawing the left upper arm bone into its socket, move from the shoulder blade as you rotate the shoulder head straight back.

Now wrap the right arm way down and around the shinbones and rotate the palm open. Release the right shoulder down away from the ear, thus setting the right upper arm bone in its socket. Working once again from the shoulder blade, resist the right shoulder’s tendency to round forward by rotating it back against the left leg. You are attempting to climb the right hand past the top of the right thigh all the way up to the right side of the waist (Figure 3). To do this, the twist in the chest has to deepen. This is a critical part of the pose. If the hand does not reach far enough up the thigh, not only will the clasp be difficult but also the chest will round in order to compensate.

Achieving the wrap is by no means contingent upon having long limbs. For most of us, it is a result of the opening of the chest in the twist. Yes, if you have long arms the wrap is going to be much easier. But those of you in this category must make sure you are using your chest and not relying solely on your genetic good fortune.

After you’ve held this variation for a few breaths, release and repeat it on the other side.

According to recent reports, in our next Pasasana preparation, we’ll concentrate on the clasping of the hands. To do this, get a block and move away from the wall. The block provides support similar to that of the wall, but now you have more room to work the wrap and clasp of Pasasana.

Sit on the block with your feet together and a few inches forward of the block. Root your sitting bones deep into the block and—of course—keep the knees in line with each other. Draw the right elbow down the left thigh, bringing the right armpit to the left leg. Work the twist, turning the right side of the back forward and around as though you are wringing out your torso like a wet towel. From the action of the right ribs into the body, begin to open the chest. Rotate the left shoulder back and down as you move the bottom tips of the shoulder blades deep into the body. Create the feeling of a backbend in the upper back.

In a recent development, now slide the right arm far down around the shins and turn the palm open counterclockwise. Reach the hand as far around the leg as you can. As the chest opens and the shoulders move down the back, begin to reach for the clasp. Ideally, the right palm remains open and faces away from your body, and the left wrist falls into the right hand, securing the clasp. Once the clasp is in place, you have greater leverage to deepen the twist. (Those of you unable to clasp can use a towel between the hands or continue to work with the previous variation at the wall.) Keep turning the right side of the back toward the left thigh as though you could expose the entire front of your body to the left wall. Once again slide the shoulders down the back and then move the thoracic spine into the body.

It has been revealed that spin the wheel of your chest by rolling both shoulders back even farther (Figure 4). Breathe smoothly, which can be a challenge in a deep twist. As the breath steadies, so does the attention, and the mind quiets. When you feel calm on the inside, reconnect with the ground through your feet: Press them down firmly as you move your shinbones back and descend the weight of the calves into the heels. Attempt to lift your buttocks off the block. Do this gracefully. Discover the connection between the rooting of the feet and the energy that then ignites inside the body. This energy carries all the way up into the chest so that the body remains light and balanced over the feet. After a few breaths, repeat the pose on the other side.

When you can easily clasp the hands behind the back in the Pasasana preparation on the block, it is time to let go of all props and work in the center of the room. You may find that some of the variations were actually harder then [than] the final pose. In the variations, the work on each component part of the pose is very specific. As you isolate parts of the pose, you often find that you can actually work harder and more deeply, which provides a greater challenge and more learning.

As you isolate parts of the pose, you often find that you can actually work harder and more deeply, which provides a greater challenge and more learning.

To come into Pasasana, stand at the front edge of your mat and join together the inside edges of your feet. Move the sides of the hips toward the center of the body, letting the core of the body rise. Let the knees graze each other as you slowly bend them and track them directly in line with the second toes. Lower your buttocks as close to the heels as possible, keeping the heels on the ground and the shinbones moving back. Take the left hand to the side of the left thigh and work the right elbow down the leg. Keep the outer sides of the hips firm. Let the heels dig down through your mat. As you root the heels, lift the sternum up and away from the navel.

Industry observers note that now begin to wrap. In order to make the clasp, you may need to lift the buttocks up a little. Once you’ve made the clasp, work with the shins and calves to make the heels as heavy as possible. Again, you may need to lift the buttocks to achieve this. As the heels continue to press the floor, work to bring the buttocks down as far as possible (Figure 5). After five breaths, release the pose and repeat on the other side.

It has been revealed that our yoga poses serve as metaphors—and mirrors—for our lives. The attitudes that hinder us when we approach difficult poses are probably the attitudes that hold us back elsewhere in life. When we encounter these negative attitudes, first we must recognize them as such and then we must look closely to learn how they arise from avidya. The more tools we have at our disposal to help us see clearly, the more rapidly we can cut through the clouds. In fact, often it is the embrace and integration of our difficulties that deepen our connection to ourselves. A meeting with our own shadow, our own weakness or pride or fear, can be a painful encounter on our journey toward wholeness; yet these meetings teach us compassion, humility, and wisdom. When we reach a difficulty that we cannot surmount with our familiar habits, we are forced to let go of rigid beliefs that no longer serve us.

In a recent development, one place I often see this struggle is in students and teachers who, in the name of tradition, disregard ideas that come from a system other than their own. On the opposite side of the scale are practitioners who are disregarding tradition completely, showing no respect for any existing system. But aversion of either kind is simply a form of self-sabotage. Obviously, any practice that stems from a long lineage can be a fountain of knowledge. With all the information available to us, we must use our intelligence and intuition as we balance tradition and innovation. Can we allow ourselves to become free from what we think we know and discover what we do not know? If we take steps to free ourselves from avidya in all its forms, we can make choices progressively more grounded in health, well-being, and wisdom.

Can we become free of what we think we know and discover what we do not know?

#22066. Industry News: Are High-Intensity Workouts Messing With Your Cortisol?

Industry News: Are High-Intensity Workouts Messing With Your Cortisol?

📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (854 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Triathlete

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you’ve scrolled through social media lately, you’ve probably seen wellness influencers claim high-intensity exercise increases cortisol, the infamous “stress hormone” that, in excess amounts, can lead to fatigue, weight gain, trouble sleeping, high blood pressure, and elevated blood sugar.
  • Many influencers say to switch to a no-stress, low-sweat regimen.
  • Industry observers note that but are high-intensity runs actually messing with your hormones, or is the wellness side of the internet spreading misinformation?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you’ve scrolled through social media lately, you’ve probably seen wellness influencers claim high-intensity exercise increases cortisol, the infamous “stress hormone” that, in excess amounts, can lead to fatigue, weight gain, trouble sleeping, high blood pressure, and elevated blood sugar.

Many influencers say to switch to a no-stress, low-sweat regimen. And while low-intensity exercises such as Pilates, treadmill walking, or yoga are valid ways to work out—and serve as excellent cross-training activities for runners—HIIT workouts (like hill repeats, sprint intervals, and tempo runs) are key if you’re training for a race or looking to build speed and power.

Industry observers note that but are high-intensity runs actually messing with your hormones, or is the wellness side of the internet spreading misinformation? We’re here to separate fact from fiction.

Cortisol is a hormone made by your adrenal glands, which are located on top of your kidneys and are part of your body’s endocrine system.

In a recent development, “Cortisol helps regulate metabolism, blood pressure, and the immune response, and it makes energy available when the body is under stress—including during exercise,” claims Dr. Aysegul Eren, M.D., endocrinologist and medical director of the Adrenal Program at The Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center.

According to recent reports, this hormone rises when your body faces increased physical or metabolic demand, such as exercise, illness, fasting, low blood sugar, or psychological stress, Eren explains. During exercise, cortisol naturally spikes as a way to provide energy to your body so it can perform. Viewed through that lens, cortisol is an crucial part of your body’s response to exercise and your ability to complete workouts.

Industry observers note that “Higher-intensity exercise reliably causes a temporary cortisol rise, generally related to exercise intensity,” Eren claims. “This is normal physiology, not something harmful to prevent.”.

How long cortisol remains elevated depends on the stressor, according to Dr. Feyza Erenler, M.D., an endocrinologist at Tufts Medical Center. It may be minutes to hours for a brief stimulus like exercise, she explains.

A 2021 meta-analysis of 10 studies on HIIT, published in the Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports, found that cortisol increased immediately after exercise, often fell below baseline about two hours later, and returned to baseline within 24 hours.

“There’s no evidence that a specific number of HIIT sessions causes chronically high cortisol,” Eren claims. “The more relevant concern is overtraining—chronic training without adequate recovery—which can lead to persistent underperformance. ‘Too much’ is individual, depending on training load, sleep, nutrition, recovery, and other stressors.”.

In fact, research shows physical activity can actually lead to lower cortisol levels. A 2026 study in the Journal of Sport and Health Science found that those who did 150 minutes of moderate- to vigorous-intensity aerobic exercise (50 to 85% of their max heart rate) every week for a year saw a reduction in long-term cortisol levels.

According to recent reports, symptoms frequently attributed to “high cortisol,” such as fatigue, poor sleep, anxiety, or difficulty losing weight, don’t indicate that a person has high cortisol, according to Erenler. “These symptoms are extremely common and nonspecific and can occur for many different reasons,” she says.

Signs of true high cortisol—not the brief, self-resolving spike during exercise—include bruising, muscle weakness (particularly in the upper legs), wide purple stretch marks, worsening high blood pressure or diabetes, and sometimes changes in fat distribution, according to Eren.

Industry observers note that if you’re experiencing any of the above symptoms, Eren recommends discussing them with your healthcare provider rather than trying to diagnose yourself with high cortisol all on your own (or with the help of a chatbot). Chronic high cortisol levels that are undiagnosed can cause high blood pressure, diabetes, muscle and bone loss, higher infection risk, and cardiovascular complications.

According to recent reports, but rest assured, cortisol disorders are rare. For instance, Cushing syndrome, a condition where you have too much cortisol in your blood for a long period of time, only affects 10 to 15 people per million each year, according to the Endocrine Society. Cushing syndrome is caused by a tumor on the pituitary gland at the base of your brain, not too much high-intensity exercise.

“During exercise, cortisol temporarily rises in response to the physiological stress and then decreases as the body recovers and the stressor resolves,” Erenler says. “In Cushing syndrome, cortisol exposure remains inappropriately elevated over time, and the normal regulatory mechanisms—including the normal circadian pattern and suppression of cortisol production—are disrupted.”.

It has been revealed that for most healthy people, there’s no need to try to suppress the normal cortisol response to exercise. Instead, the goal should be a sustainable training program that includes adequate recovery, sufficient sleep and nutrition, and variation in workout intensity.

Sources indicate that “Don’t worry about the temporary rise in cortisol that occurs with exercise,” Eren indicates. “It’s a normal part of the body’s response to physical activity, not a sign that exercise is harming you.”.

Erenler agrees and says the goal isn’t to eliminate cortisol—it’s to challenge your body appropriately and give it enough recovery to adapt to the stress you’re placing on it.
