Business Class Product Worldwide.

Industry observers note that picture this: you're seated in a private suite at 38,000 feet somewhere over the Atlantic, your door clicked shut behind you, a glass of Dom Pérignon on the side table, and a fully flat bed dressed in Westin Heavenly bedding waiting for you. Your partner is in the suite next to yours — and when you lower the center dividing panel, you're sharing a meal in what Qatar Airways calls the "Double Bed" configuration. This is QSuites, and it is, without exaggeration, the single most celebrated business class product in the world. Now here's the number that stops the ChooseFI community cold: a cash ticket in QSuites from Newly introduced York JFK to Doha DOH typically runs **$5,000 to $10,000 per person**. That's a mortgage payment. That's a family vacation budget. That's real money that compounds in an index fund. With Qatar Avios through the Privilege Club program, that same seat costs **75,000 Avios**. When you do the math against even the conservative cash price of $5,000, you're extracting **6.7 cents per point**. Against the top-end cash price of $10,000, that's **13.3 cents per point** — in a world where most loyalty currencies are "worth" 1 cent each. This is a 6x to 13x multiplier on every point you've earned. Here's what makes this a genuine pricing inefficiency rather than just marketing: Qatar's award chart is fixed and partner-friendly, meaning the number of points required doesn't scale dynamically with cash prices the way most airline programs now do. When demand spikes and cash fares hit $10,000, your award price stays exactly 75,000 Avios. The loyalty program hasn't caught up to the revenue management engine, and that gap is your opportunity. For anyone on the path to financial independence, this is the travel rewards philosophy in its purest form: redirect real spending you're already doing onto the right cards, accumulate points as a byproduct, and convert those points into experiences that would otherwise require liquidating investments. The QSuites redemption is the pinnacle of that system — a **nearly free** business class experience that delivers more luxury per point than almost anything else in the world of travel rewards.

The mechanism behind this sweet spot is elegant once you see it, and once you see it, you'll start recognizing similar patterns everywhere in the loyalty space.

Qatar prices its own flights in its own currency — and that currency is cheap to acquire.

Qatar Airways Privilege Club Avios are the program's native points currency. When Qatar sets award prices for its own operated flights, including QSuites, it prices them in a way that's competitive and fixed — not subject to the dynamic pricing algorithms that have made programs like United MileagePlus or Delta SkyMiles increasingly unpredictable. Seventy-five thousand Avios for a transatlantic or transoceanic business class seat is a published, stable price. Qatar isn't trying to extract maximum value from every award booking; they want to keep the program attractive to drive loyalty.

In a recent development, the critical insight is this: you don't need to earn Qatar Avios through Qatar flights. You can transfer them directly from credit card programs you're probably already using.

Citi ThankYou Points → Qatar Avios at 1:1 — This is the fastest and cleanest route. Transfers from Citi to Qatar are instant, meaning you can search for availability, confirm the seat is bookable, and transfer in the same session without risk. For anyone holding a Citi Premier or Citi Prestige card, this is a direct pipeline to QSuites.

Capital One Miles → Qatar Avios at 1:1 — A strong secondary option. Capital One's transfer to Qatar takes 2–5 days, so you'll want to confirm availability first and ideally put the seat on a 24-hour hold if possible before initiating the transfer. Venture X and Venture card holders have access to this path.

Sources indicate that marriott Bonvoy Points → Qatar Avios at 3:1 — This is the least efficient path. The 3:1 ratio means you're effectively diluting your Bonvoy points, and transfers take 1–5 days. Use this only as a top-off strategy if you're a few thousand Avios short and have Bonvoy points sitting idle.

Industry observers note that this is a huge deal that deserves its own callout. Qatar charges zero fuel surcharges on Qatar-operated award flights. This is not universal — British Airways Avios, for example, can pile on $700+ in carrier-imposed surcharges on longhaul awards. With Qatar Privilege Club, what you see is what you pay: 75,000 Avios plus the government taxes, which are typically modest.

Qatar allows stopovers in Doha and open-jaw routing on award tickets. This means you can build a trip that stops in Doha — giving you access to the Al Mourjan Business Lounge, one of the world's premier airport lounges — before continuing to a final destination. The stopover rule turns a single award redemption into a multi-destination experience, a classic FI travel rewards optimization move.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Here’s what that looks like inside real coaching conversations.
  • When most people picture “accountability,” they picture a drill sergeant.
  • In a recent development, someone standing over you going “What were you thinking?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here’s what that looks like inside real coaching conversations.

When most people picture “accountability,” they picture a drill sergeant.

In a recent development, someone standing over you going “What were you thinking? Why did you skip that? Do you even want this?“.

(And if there’s no drill sergeant handy, we do a pretty good job of beating ourselves up all on our own.).

Here’s the thing: if being hard on yourself worked, it would have worked by now.

Great accountability isn’t built on being a hard-ass.

It’s built on forward momentum and honest feedback.

The drill sergeant questions YOU. Your motivation. How much you want it.

Real accountability helps you try again swiftly.

Then helps you see what you’re doing well and what can improve.

A client of mine had a hectic week. Travel, out of their routine, workouts missed.

The drill sergeant move is “why didn’t you do your workouts?!” at the exact moment they were already struggling.

Sources indicate that “Hey! I know this has been a hectic week. Let’s do some push-ups together. Do a set next chance you get and shoot me a 👍. I’ll do one too.”.

Industry observers note that this got a 👍 and a “Thanks for the encouragement! This week has been so hectic my schedule got away from me.”.

That win got them back on the routine.

Then we build off of that by looking ahead to the next few days.

“How’s the rest of this week looking for strength training? I went ahead and put together a few variations in case you’re short on time.”.

When you’re already struggling, the question isn’t “hey, why didn’t you do that?”.

It’s getting the next available win.

Then looking ahead to what’s coming up after that.

But forward momentum is only the first part of the equation.

The second step is giving honest feedback on both the wins AND the challenges.

To be a neutral observer. To point out what’s going well, what’s not, and suggest how we can improve it moving forward.

Based on the actual human in front of me: their unique goals, motivations, and whatever flavor of chaos they have going on in their own life (work, family, travel, illness, injury, etc.).

Recent findings suggest that “Hey! I reviewed the strength workout on Friday. Solid work all around here. I can see from your form check video that you’re doing a better job staying balanced across your whole foot on the squat. 💪.

Sources indicate that I also noticed that the middle of the week has been tougher to get consistent workouts in. You’ve hit 2 out of the last 4 midweek workouts. I know work has been crazy with the project deadline you have coming up, so my guess is you’re getting buried and it makes it hard to get to the gym. Am I on the right track? I have some ideas for how we tackle that next week that I’ll drop down below in a video for you.”.

In a recent development, this is the honest part. It didn’t go anywhere!

But instead of berating you for missing a workout, the goal is to look at all the evidence and suggest next steps.

Including if the evidence says that something BIG needs to change. It’s all on the table.

Accountability isn’t punishment for what you didn’t do.

It’s helping you decide what you do next.

If your week went haywire, before you beat yourself up, take this approach:.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that this quick yoga flow at home is, as the name promises, a continuously moving, flowy vinyasa practice for full-body flexibility that moves your body in all the ways you need.
  • So if you woke up feeling a little sore or stiff, taking yourself through these movements can bring relief and get you feeling more comfortable in your body.
  • No props are required although you are always welcome to use them anytime you would like more support.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that this quick yoga flow at home is, as the name promises, a continuously moving, flowy vinyasa practice for full-body flexibility that moves your body in all the ways you need. Rather than holding poses for an extended period of time, you’re moving with your breath in a fluid and rhythmic 10-minute yoga routine that will definitely energize you and target your back, hips, and hamstrings.

So if you woke up feeling a little sore or stiff, taking yourself through these movements can bring relief and get you feeling more comfortable in your body. I encourage you to choose a one-word intention for your day that you pause and focus on at the outset and throughout your practice. What is one word that captures how you want to feel today, what you want to focus on, or what matters to you right now?

No props are required although you are always welcome to use them anytime you would like more support.

You’re going to start by targeting the spine. From your hands and knees, your palms go underneath your shoulders, knees underneath your hips. As you inhale, lower your belly, lift your gaze and arch your back in Cow Pose.

As you exhale, reverse that motion. Thinking of pushing into your fingertips and knuckles, pushing the mat away from you, and letting your head release and your neck relax in Cat Pose.

And then go in between these two poses, getting into all parts of the spine, including the neck, upper back, mid back, lower back, all the way to your tailbone, trying to get that full range of motion.

Come back to hands and knees with a neutral spine.

Still on your hands and knees, lift your right leg and trace some circles with it, as big as you can, and then let’s reverse the direction of those circles. You’re simply trying to create movement through your right hip. You don’t need to overthink this one.

Step your right foot straight out to the side and press the outer edge of your foot against the floor. Lift yourself upright and reach your left arm overhead and toward the right in a side body stretch known as Gate Pose.

Sources indicate that come back to your hands and knees, tuck your toes, and hover your knees a little above the mat. You can probably feel your core engage.

In a recent development, walk your feet back to keep your shoulders over your wrists in Plank Pose. Strongly press the mat away from you, drawing your lower belly inward and broadening through your upper back. Think of lengthening your tailbone toward your heels and drawing your lower belly inward and upward.

Industry observers note that let’s find Downward-Facing Dog. Lift your hips up and back, and peddle out your feet by straightening one leg and bending the other to stretch your ankles and calves. Keep your arms straight without locking your elbows. Feel the length through your spine.

Lower your knees to the mat and repeat the poses on your left side, including Hip Circles, Gate Pose, Hovering Tabletop, Plank, and Downward-Facing Dog.

From Downward-Facing Dog, reach your right leg toward the sky, bend your right knee, open your hip, and take one more of those substantial hip circles from your Three-Legged Dog.

From Down Dog, inhale as you step your right foot forward, spin your back foot almost parallel to the short side of the mat as if you were coming into Warrior 2. Exhale as you flow into Extended Side Angle, bringing your right forearm onto your right thigh and reaching your left arm overhead.

As you inhale, straighten your front leg and reach your right arm all the way back in Reverse Triangle.

According to recent reports, then exhale back into Extended Side Angle, sinking your hips a little lower. Repeat that flow twice more like this.

Recent findings suggest that bring both palms to the mat on either side of your right foot and find Pigeon Pose from here. So take your right knee behind your right wrist and reach your left leg straight back. Inhale as you come high onto your fingertips to lift and lengthen, then exhale as you bend forward.

Recent findings suggest that move in between the two shapes twice more as you undulate through the spine. Then the next time you lower yourself close to the mat, stay here for 5 long, slow breaths. Try to release tension through your shoulder blades and arms.

In a recent development, when you’re ready, lift yourself off the mat and find your Downward-Facing Dog. If you like, you can first come forward into Plank and then lower yourself to the mat and take Cobra. Then repeat these poses on your left side, starting with Three-Legged Dog, Dynamic Extended Side Angle, and Dynamic Pigeon.

In a recent development, come back to Downward-Facing Dog. Pause here for several breaths.

Bring your knees to the mat and take a seat. As with most morning practices, I don’t include a Savasana in case you might be tempted to fall back asleep, but you’re always welcome to take it on your own.

Sit tall and roll your shoulders down and away from your ears. Maybe you bring your hands together at the front of your heart. Pause here for as long as you can.

Recent findings suggest that thank you so much for doing this quick vinyasa flow at home with me. May you feel really good and have gotten a boost of energy. Let me know what your intention is for the day ahead in a comment below.

Who’s ready for coaching? 7 GLP-1 clients, from “not yet” to “let’s go!”

📅 11 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 23 min read (4519 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Precisionnutrition

⏱️ ~23 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that reviewed by Brian St.
  • That’s the thought many health and fitness coaches had when GLP-1 medications first hit the mass market.
  • In a recent development, though semaglutide (Ozempic) became available in 2017, it initially felt like a theoretical threat.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that reviewed by Brian St. Pierre, MS, RD.

That’s the thought many health and fitness coaches had when GLP-1 medications first hit the mass market.

In a recent development, though semaglutide (Ozempic) became available in 2017, it initially felt like a theoretical threat. Prescription rates were still very low, and it seemed like no one actually knew anyone who was taking it.

Now, in 2026, over 1 in 10 US adults are taking a GLP-1 medication. Most of us know someone on it (or we’re on it ourselves).

According to recent reports, with wider use, opinions towards the medication have softened too. Most coaches no longer see it as a threat, and instead appreciate it as a valuable tool for certain clients, with coaching as an additive complement.

Many coaches still have concerns though, primarily about their clients’ long term health on the medication. (Among the worries: Loss of muscle mass! Using a “band-aid” solution! Bypassing foundational health habits! And more!).

However, whether you count yourself as a GLP-1 supporter or a GLP-1 skeptic, there’s a framing that might change the way you think about your work in this field:.

As Kate Solovieva, Super Coach and PN’s Director of Community, indicates: “As a coach, you’re not in the GLP-1 world; you’re in the GLP-1 support world.”.

That’s actually good news. Because trying to coach everyone taking a GLP-1 just isn’t possible. And spending time thinking about all the people using GLP-1s “the wrong way” is, bluntly, wasted energy. Some of those people just don’t want, need, or aren’t ready for your help.

Recent findings suggest that meanwhile, there is a subgroup of people on GLP-1s who are ready, willing, and able to receive your support. Honing in on this group is where you can actually make a difference (and where your business can thrive).

In the following article, we’ll cover seven GLP-1 clients you’re likely to meet. Each reflects a different point in the GLP-1 medication journey, and a different level of readiness for coaching. Based on our experience coaching over 175,000 clients (of which an increasing number are on GLP-1s), we’ll offer strategies to work with each.

Before we begin, a reminder: People change, and readiness isn’t fixed.

A person who starts off saying “I’m doing fine on my own” may eventually morph into “I’m flailing and really need someone else in my corner”—and vice versa.

In a recent development, if the person in front of you sounds like one of these clients, that’s where they are right now. So listen carefully to how your client speaks at every session, and respond dynamically.

In general, Coach Kate says someone is usually ready for coaching when they demonstrate two things:.

Keep that in the back of your mind as you interact with client prospects, and as you read about each client, summarized in the table below.

Now, on to the different GLP-1 clients.

This is the person who’s started a GLP-1 medication—and they love it.

They’ve experienced minimal side effects, and have gotten great results on a relatively low dose.

They haven’t changed much about their exercise habits or their diet (except the eating less part, which the medication has taken care of), but they’re seeing what they want to see on the scale, so they don’t feel motivated to change anything.

It might be tempting to “lure” this kind of client in by warning them of the dangers of using a GLP-1 medication without adding in long-term health behaviors (like resistance training and strategic nutrition), but this type of approach can backfire.

In a recent development, at best, you may sound like a downer. At worst, you may sound like an active antagonist.

In a recent development, in Motivational Interviewing, a communication approach commonly used in coaching, this is called the “righting reflex.” It’s the urge that coaches, counselors, and therapists often have to help or “correct course” for their client. You see them doing something “wrong,” and you want to help them “fix” it.

However, following this instinct may actually strengthen a client’s defenses, and prevent change.

If a person is flying high on their current approach, their readiness for coaching is extremely low.

As Coach Kate says, “they’re just not my person yet.”.

Your best move with this client is to genuinely celebrate their current results, then plant the seed for support should they need it in the future.

For example, you could say: “It must feel so good to see all these positive results! If you ever feel like you want to work on another layer, like resistance training or optimizing your nutrition, I’d love to work together.”.

Then, just stay available. (“My door is always open!”).

This is the person who hasn’t started a GLP-1 medication—and might never, despite being a great candidate for one.

Maybe their doctor has already suggested the medication to them and they’ve read everything they can on the topic.

It has been revealed that and yet, they’re frozen with fear at the starting line. They’re afraid of side effects, of being on medication for life, of not holding up their end of the bargain. (“I’ve been trying to start strength training for years. If I take this medication it matters even more… What if I still can’t do it?”).

Toni Bauer, Super Coach and PN’s Director of Coaching and Education Operations also claims that, in some cases, a client’s hesitation isn’t about side effects. “Some of our clients wonder, ‘Am I a good person or a bad person if I start taking a GLP-1 medication? Am I weak? Am I giving up?’” Coach Toni says these concerns aren’t unique to GLP-1 medications, but they seem to be especially common.

She reasons, “If you have high cholesterol, are you weak for taking cholesterol medication? No. But often people don’t view obesity as a disease at a societal level, so the conversation is different here.”.

Regardless of the root cause of this person’s hesitation, the advice below can help them find clarity.

First, let’s be clear: Deciding whether or not to take a medication isn’t a coaching decision, and falls out of your scope of practice. That choice is ultimately up to your client and a medical provider who can assess whether a GLP-1 is appropriate given their medical history.

That mentioned, clients may still come to you wanting to discuss their options.

So the question becomes: How do you support someone through a decision you can’t make for them?

Coach Toni advises: “You can share facts and data. For example, study results and what you’ve seen with other clients. But you can’t say, ‘For you, this is the right choice.’”.

Instead, the biggest coaching opportunity here is to help clients articulate what’s actually driving their hesitation.

This hesitation about whether to do something different or stay the same is called ambivalence, and it’s a normal (albeit uncomfortable) stage of change.

Sources indicate that problem is, without the right tools, a person can stay stuck in ambivalence for months or even years. And, much like being stuck at an airport in between two destinations, it sucks.

In a recent development, but at PN, we have a cool exercise to deal with client ambivalence. It’s called the 4 Crazy Questions. Essentially, you explore:.

In this context, the questions can help a client explore the risk of starting a GLP-1 (which they’ve probably already voiced), but also the risk of not starting, which they may not have considered yet.

Our 4 Crazy Questions worksheet can encourage clients to explore the pros and cons of both choices. With these considerations laid out explicitly, most people feel a lot more clear about their next steps—or at least what questions they need to ask their medical provider before they can move forward.

Industry observers note that importantly, this exercise doesn’t have a “right” outcome. Some people work through it and fill the prescription. Others decide the medication isn’t for them, and that’s fine. (It’s also worth reminding clients that starting isn’t necessarily permanent: With their provider’s input, a trial run on the medication is a perfectly valid way in.).

According to recent reports, either way, there are opportunities to support your client. As Coach Toni puts it: “Whether you go ‘natural’ or whether you go GLP-1, the foundational habits are essentially the same.”.

This is the person who started a GLP-1 with lots of optimism—and now feels like they have a plague that won’t end.

In a cruel twist, this person might actually be seeing great fat loss results. And yet, they’re nauseated, exhausted, dreading their next dose, and wondering whether it’s worth continuing this medication.

In a recent development, adding to their sense of defeat, they may also be comparing themselves to a “Honeymooner” in their life, so they might also be wondering if there’s something wrong with them. (“It worked so well for my friend! I must be broken in some way.”).

First, offer some neutral education to depersonalize their experience.

Namely, they should know that side effects are extremely common: About half of owners report nausea, a third report diarrhea, and a fifth report vomiting.1 So, what this person thinks is exceptional might actually just be a normal adjustment. (This doesn’t make the experience suck less, but it can give them some hope.).

Also, getting GLP-1s right is a process of trial and error: the right medication, the right dose, and the right nutritional strategies to reduce symptoms.

In a recent development, if their symptoms are severe, get them to loop in their doctor. Medication type and dosing is under the purview of a medical professional, so involving them is essential.

After that, your best coaching move is to suggest an experiment.

▶ Ask about dose. To be clear, you’re asking about it, not adjusting it. Says Coach Toni: “Often, when people are experiencing extreme side effects, they’ve ratcheted up their dose too promptly. Sometimes the easiest way to keep somebody on a GLP-1 who’s experiencing high side effects is to lower their dosage.” Coach Toni makes clear that while dosage isn’t a coach’s domain, you can help draw a client’s attention to it.

▶ Start a food journal. It doesn’t need to be every day—just around the meals that precede the worst symptoms. You’re looking for three things:.

▶ Try smaller portions, eaten more often. Coach Toni indicates if you only try one thing, this one is the most reliable strategy. GLP-1 clients may be tempted to cut meals when symptoms are high, but this increases the likelihood of undereating and nutrient deficiencies. The goal, in her words: “Can we get small enough, frequent enough meals that we get nutrients in, but they never feel overwhelmed or super full?”.

To stay within your scope of practice, language matters.

Don’t say: “You’re nauseous, so you should eat smaller meals.”.

Instead, say: “Folks who are nauseous sometimes do better with smaller, more frequent meals. Want to try it this week and see what you notice?”.

In the first example, you’ve offered a “prescription” (which coaches can’t legally do). In the second example, you’ve offered an experiment to consider.

Side effects (such as nausea, vomiting, constipation, and/or diarrhea) are extremely common among GLP-1 users, and typically last one to two weeks after initiating the medication. Some symptoms can last longer (particularly constipation), but most are mild to moderate, and usually improve within a few weeks.

Symptoms can also return each time a dosage is increased, though they’re usually milder and more short-lived. These too tend to improve after the first week or so.

However, you should strongly encourage a client to reach out promptly to their medical provider if they notice:.

According to recent reports, reassure your client they’re not being dramatic by reporting these symptoms. Their medical team needs to hear this kind of information to help them get the best results, while preserving overall health.

According to recent reports, also: Your client will get better care if they show up prepared. So, get them to jot down and bring:.

This is the person whose results look great, but less visible changes are creating longer term risks.

According to recent reports, this person is likely to be quite sedentary, and when you ask what they do for exercise, they might tell you “I walk.” But they’re not the outlier kind of walker who consistently gets 20,000 steps a day. They just… walk a little.

Women are more likely to fall into this category, especially if they come from a generation or culture where strength training simply wasn’t a thing women did (or were welcomed to do).

Additionally, this person might be running on a decades-long plain-toast-and-coffee breakfast habit, with lower protein intake already ingrained before medication further reduced appetite.

The scale is dropping though, so they’re thrilled. It’s just that nobody’s measuring what kind of weight is dropping.

It has been revealed that keep in mind that this description is a starting hypothesis, not a diagnosis. Low activity and low protein raise the risk of muscle loss, but they don’t confirm it. That’s what the measures below are for.

Your job is to bring awareness to the invisible. Because once this person sees what’s at stake, they’ll be more likely to see the value in changing their habits, and in coaching.

However, theoretical warnings about muscle loss are easy to dismiss.

This is one of the reasons why Coach Kate says, “I don’t care if I coach you or not—please just get a DEXA as a baseline.”.

When a person has a quantifiable, objective measure of their muscle composition, it’s often more motivating than any amount of abstract concern.

Ideally, every person who begins a GLP-1 medication should get a DEXA scan before they start, then again at six or twelve months to see how they’re progressing.

It has been revealed that if a client can’t or won’t do a DEXA, assess strength and function in other ways. Ask: “How do the stairs feel compared to a few months ago? What about carrying groceries?” Gather objective data too, recording baselines for squat, deadlift, and bench press (or other accessible exercises) to compare to over time. Declines in any of these areas can reveal potential muscle loss, and can motivate a client to take action.

Without protective strategies, up to 40 percent of weight lost from GLP-1 medications can come from lean mass, with a majority of that being muscle.2.

In order to prevent that from happening, there are two behaviors to prioritize:.

It has been revealed that ▶ Protein at every meal. When appetite is suppressed, every bite has to earn its place. Aim for 25-40 grams of protein at every meal and 15-20 grams for snacks. (On days when appetite is severely suppressed, protein powders can be a more palatable way to reach that target.).

According to recent reports, ▶ Strength training, scaled to what they’d actually do. The term “weight lifting” might overwhelm a person who’s never set foot in a gym, so don’t start there. Start where PN always starts: Ask what they could do twice this week that they’re 9-out-of-10 confident they’d actually do. Sit-to-stands off the couch. A few moves with a resistance band. Bodyweight anything. Scale up from there, one week at a time.

This is the person for whom the medication has worked a little too well.

Their appetite hasn’t just decreased—it’s gone.

Recent findings suggest that they’re not eating enough, and often don’t notice until you ask. “When did you last eat?” you say, and they say, “Ummm… Yesterday afternoon? I think?”.

Their protein and overall calorie intake is plummeting, and soon their energy levels will too.

Plus, something more subtle might also be happening: Food stops being a pleasure and becomes a chore, or even a source of dread.

Recent findings suggest that for some, this might seem like an upside down world. They may have spent their whole life fighting to eat less. The idea of fighting to eat more feels completely absurd—and entirely off their radar.

Before anything else: If there’s an active eating disorder in the picture, this medication likely shouldn’t have been prescribed. A vulnerability to disordered eating can both contribute to or be triggered by the above scenario.

Sources indicate that so, scope of practice first. Ask this person if they’ve ever struggled with disordered eating. If the answer is yes, refer out to a doctor or a dietitian. You can absolutely stay involved as a guide, but not as the only professional in the room. Have your referral network ready before you need it.

Industry observers note that but sometimes, you won’t know. Your client may have been screened and cleared. Or, they may not have disclosed. So your job is to figure out what you’re actually looking at—and that starts with what Coach Toni calls the “show me” approach.

As with every client here, treat this one as something to investigate, not a label. Rather than acting on a hunch, collect something concrete, such as a few days of food logging (in writing or via photos).

From there, it branches two ways.

▶ If they’ll track, do some food math, and the numbers may do the work for you. When some clients see that their calorie intake is hovering around 800 to 1,000 Calories per day, it’s the only wake up call they need. They weren’t intentionally restricting; they genuinely just had no idea.

For this client, establishing an eating routine is the best next action.

According to recent reports, your client may be used to following appetite as a cue to eat, but now that medication has removed it, they need a different cue. That means eating on a schedule, likely every 3–4 hours, including protein at every one of those occasions. Portions can be small if appetite is very low, but they should be nutrient-dense.

▶ If they won’t track—and especially if they resist in a way that feels purposely avoidant—that resistance itself is information.

Coach Toni suggests that if you suspect that disordered eating is in the picture and a client is really resistant about tracking, it might be time for a crucial conversation—an often uncomfortable, but honest and essential conversation between a client and a coach.

It has been revealed that she suggests leading with non-judgement and safety. For example:.

“I want you to know this is a safe space to talk. My goal as a coach is always to prioritize your overall health. However, there have been a couple of things you’ve shared recently that have me wondering whether we’re protecting your body’s basic needs.”.

Then name the specific things you noticed, sticking to facts. (“You’ve mentioned you’ve been losing hair and struggling more during workouts. Those can both be signs of undereating. Would you be open to revisiting food journaling for a short stretch so we can see more clearly what’s happening, or telling your doctor about your symptoms?”).

If this conversation is enough to help a client see the value in tracking, follow the advice after “If they’ll track” above.

If what surfaces is a genuinely troubled relationship with food, refer out, while offering to stay involved for support as needed.

This is the person who got the results they wanted with the medication, and is now choosing to wean off.

They’re not quitting because of crappy results or intolerable side effects, they’ve simply decided they don’t want to be on a GLP-1 forever.

The coaching opportunity here is, in part, about tempering expectations.

Most people imagine coming off as the finish line. Instead though, it’s more like starting a different endurance course: The medication has been managing their appetite, and now they have to.

Recent findings suggest that ideally, you start working with this client while the medication is still doing some of the heavy lifting with appetite regulation. If you can have six months to build the right habits as well as prepare mentally for the tapering off period, your client will be in a much better position.

Make sure the previously mentioned habits—like resistance training and optimizing protein—are already firmly established. If your client is managing those habits consistently (not perfectly, but consistently), even on their busiest, most stressful, most side-effect-disrupted days, then they’re more likely to be able to maintain them when they’re off their medication and food distractions re-enter the picture.

Sources indicate that after that, work on how you’ll continue to define success. This client has been accustomed to measuring it on the scale, but the scale will move—some regain is normal. So, ask them early: What does success look like if the scale ticks up eight pounds but your habits hold?

Sources indicate that be honest about the odds, too. People who changed nothing while on the medication almost universally regain most of the weight—usually within the first year and a half or so3—because the appetite that went down comes right back up.

However, people who integrate and sustain healthier nutrition and exercise behaviors while they’re on medication are four times better at maintaining a ten percent or higher weight loss when they come off the medication.4.

This is the person who was also getting great results on the medication—except instead of choosing to go off it on their own time, they’re forced to quit due to external circumstances.

Maybe their insurance stopped covering it, or they lost the job that came with the benefits, or the one drug they tolerated turned out to cost four times as much as the one they couldn’t tolerate.

It has been revealed that about 50 percent of GLP-1 users stop the medication within the first year of using it.5 Some stop due to side effects, and others stop because they’ve gotten the results they want and they want to see if they can maintain them drug-free. But many are simply priced out. The latter is an especially frustrating scenario because, for this person, a “solution” exists. It’s just that, for them, the solution is out of reach.

Recent findings suggest that understandably, this person may be angry or even ashamed that they can’t afford this medication. Those feelings may or may not show up in your coaching, but it’s good to prepare for them anyway.

First, reassure this person that this is a system failure, not a personal one.

Whether someone can access affordable medication comes down to their insurance initiative, the region they live in, and their socioeconomic status—also known as the social determinants of health. Those forces shape health outcomes far more than willpower does, and none of them are a measure of how hard someone has tried or how “worthy” they are.

Acknowledging that reality isn’t about throwing up your hands and saying, “Well, I’m screwed!” Rather, it’s about accepting some miserable truths about the world, and then shifting from self-blame to problem-solving.

Once they’ve had a chance to process some (very valid) anger and disappointment, it’s time to focus on what they can control.

In a recent development, at PN, we call this the Spheres of Control exercise. The image below shows you how it works.

Access, price, and coverage are not on the list of controllables, and fighting those realities may only compound frustration.

Meanwhile, they can control other influential factors, like their protein intake, their training, their sleep, their food environment, and maybe their next insurance appeal.

Use the image above to begin a conversation with your client about what is within their control, and lean in hard on those factors.

Recent findings suggest that the truth is, you can’t predict how a client will respond to medication. And, some regain after stopping it is expected.

However, diet and lifestyle habits hugely affect what kind of weight clients lose, plus the rate and amount of that regain.

Sources indicate that “I can’t promise anyone they’ll lose a specific amount of weight or that they’ll never regain it—and I’d be suspicious of any coach who did. What I can tell you is that the habits we build while the medication is doing its work are the ones that’ll still stand when it isn’t.”.

According to recent reports, of course, “coming off” isn’t the endpoint for everyone. Many providers now treat obesity as a chronic condition and these medications as long-term therapy—the same way we’d treat cardiac disease. Again, whether someone stays on, tapers, or stops is a conversation for them and their provider.

But for those who do come off, Coach Toni says the people who hold their results share one thing: “They maintain consistency with their behaviors as if they were still on the medication. Like nothing changes.”.

She shares an analogy for why that works:.

It has been revealed that “Think about the Oregon Trail. Wagon wheels made ruts in the trail by hitting the same ground over and over and over. You can still see those ruts today. Habits are the same way: If you lay down those neural pathways and reinforce them enough times while your client is on the medication, they’ll have a better chance of continuing on the same path even when they go off the medication.”.

It’s not: “You’ll keep it off.”.

It’s: “While the medication is doing its work, we’ll cut ruts deep enough that those pathways will still be there after the medication is gone.”.

Practically, that means regular resistance training, rock solid nutrition, appetite awareness, and attending to the parts of health that never show up on a scale—sleep, energy, mood, relationships, and identity, which is where Coach Toni lands:.

“Ideally, your client will have embraced the identity of a ‘newly introduced person.’ As in, ‘I am the person who wakes up at 6 a.m. and walks two miles. I am the person who eats protein at every meal. I am the person who does resistance training because it builds the tissue I need to age well.’ That’s the client who maintains.”.

The seven client examples above help you answer two questions:.

Is this person ready for coaching?

How do I meet them where they are?

Once someone becomes your client, the question changes to:.

And when nausea, fatigue, stalled results, and weakening strength and physical function all show up at once in the same client, that can be tricky to answer.

Knowing where to start is one of the core skills taught in the upcoming GLP Coaching Institute Certification, developed in partnership with Precision Nutrition.

According to recent reports, the certification combines GLP-1-specific science and practical coaching frameworks with PN’s proven coaching methodology. You’ll learn how to use a framework called The Five GLP-1 Types: Strength, Fuel, Fitness, Recovery, and Results.

Unlike the profiles in this article, the Five Types aren’t about how ready clients are. They’re coaching priorities: a way to decide what to work on first, and when to shift focus as a client’s needs change.

To learn more, join the waitlist. You’ll be the first to know when the certification introduces, with early access before enrolment opens to everyone else.

Bored With Your Workout? Try a New Level, Not a New Program

📅 25 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (520 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nerdfitness

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This was the first thing a fresh client said to me.
  • When we dug into it, here’s the pattern that emerged:.
  • Strength training, then running, then a yoga challenge, then back to lifting with a different app.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here’s the client story this comes from.

This was the first thing a fresh client said to me.

When we dug into it, here’s the pattern that emerged:.

-> See something upcoming, give that a try.

Strength training, then running, then a yoga challenge, then back to lifting with a different app.

Nerd Fitness Coaching was the latest in a long line of fresh starts.

And here’s the thing: all of it was GOOD.

She was moving. She was trying upcoming things. She was having fun (at least at first).

But she was frustrated with herself.

She felt like she kept starting over and never getting anywhere.

And she wanted help figuring out what to do.

Let’s be real: trying something new is exciting.

Sources indicate that A newly introduced program, a new class, a new challenge. There’s a buzz to it.

And that buzz isn’t bad. Enjoying it is a massive part of what keeps people moving.

The catch is that most goals need some repetition.

Getting stronger, running farther, learning a skill. You get better at the things you practice again and again.

So the question isn’t “how do I stop getting bored?”.

It’s “how do I keep some of that new-thing fun AND repeat things enough to see progress?” 🧐.

That’s what we worked on together.

When I built her program, I kept its overall shape the same week to week.

But inside it, a few key exercises got a target. Something like:.

“Once you can do 12 reps with 25 pounds, we level up.”.

The targets were far enough away to stretch her, and close enough that she could hit them in 2 to 6 weeks of focused practice.

When she hit one, we leveled up that exercise: new reps or weight, or a new variation. Everything else stayed put.

So something was always changing.

There was always a target she was closing in on and a level she’d recently beaten.

But the frame stayed the same. We were still working on the same overall qualities.

And that’s what let her progress stack up instead of resetting every few weeks.

She was able to stay really consistent with her program.

According to recent reports, she still fell off some. (Life happens.).

But when she came back, she wasn’t looking for something new.

She was excited to pick up her program and keep progressing.

And sure, sometimes her goals would change.

We spent 6 months training for her first half marathon, then switched gears to focus on building muscle.

But that was a choice, not a restart.

If you love bouncing between things and you’re happy doing it, keep bouncing.

This is for when the bouncing starts to feel frustrating.

Before you reach for a new program, try a new level.

✅ Set a target you could reach in 2 to 6 weeks (a rep count or a weight).

✅ When you hit it, level up that one exercise with fresh reps, a new weight, or a new variation. Leave everything else alone.

I’m excited to see what you come up with. 😃.

Here’s the reader email that kicked this off, and your first quests.

I got a lovely email from a reader who was so excited to find Nerd Fitness.

“I’m mainly looking to get healthier, get stronger, and finally build some habits that I can actually stick with long-term. I’m hoping Nerd Fitness can help make the process a little less overwhelming – and maybe a bit more fun, too!”.

She came to the right place! 🙌 We have tons of cool resources to help with exactly those things.

It has been revealed that but you know what? I have an even better idea.

Let me map out the next 30 days for you.

So you know exactly what to do – without the second-guessing.

Each week, for the next 4 weeks, I’ll send you a quest.

Each one will focus on a different aspect of fitness.

According to recent reports, and by the time you complete all of them, you’ll have the foundation for a healthier, stronger, more consistent you. 💪.

(And we’ll make sure we have some fun with it, too.).

One quick thing – I only want to send you these emails if you actually want to get them, so there’s a link down at the bottom to opt in. Make sure you don’t miss it!

OK, with all that out of the way, let’s get started with the quest for this week.

Well, actually, it’s a few quests. But I promise they won’t take long!

Seriously. That’s the first “step” (pun intended 😜).

According to recent reports, any length. Any location. Even if it’s a few laps around your house!

This marks the start of the 30 days, and a shift in momentum.

You’re out there doing the thing.

Recent findings suggest that draw 30 boxes. We’re going to use this to track the next 30 days.

It can look like a standard calendar, or even a treasure map if you want!

Put it somewhere you’ll see it.

Each quest gets its own mark. Whenever you complete one, add it to that day’s box.

Consider this your “Adventure Log.”.

This will be crucial for later.

For this first week, your goal is to get some extra movement in every day.

This isn’t a full blown workout.

This is about making time for movement more “normal”.

Industry observers note that keep it simple. A few bodyweight exercises while the coffee brews. Stretching on the floor while you watch TV at night. A couple of minutes at a time.

It has been revealed that list out 6 different exercises and roll a die to determine what to do. For example, that could look like:.

Industry observers note that each day you do a movement snack, mark an M in that day’s box. The end of your week might look something like this, with some hits and some misses. Totally normal.

That’s the start of our 30-day adventure.

We’ll continue to level up and build from here.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that magnus Ditlev of Denmark wins the 2026 IRONMAN Florida in a World Record Time of 7:19:17 on November 7, 2026 in Panama City, Florida.
  • It has been revealed that one month after a heartbreaking DNF in Kona, Magnus Ditlev (DEN) rode away from the field at Ironman Florida and never looked back.
  • It has been revealed that florida was a chance at redemption for Ditlev, who had come agonizingly close to winning the Ironman World Championship in Kona.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that magnus Ditlev of Denmark wins the 2026 IRONMAN Florida in a World Record Time of 7:19:17 on November 7, 2026 in Panama City, Florida. (Photo by Donald Miralle/Getty Images for IRONMAN) (Photo: Getty Images for IRONMAN).

It has been revealed that one month after a heartbreaking DNF in Kona, Magnus Ditlev (DEN) rode away from the field at Ironman Florida and never looked back. His 7:19:17 took 1:47 off the previous men’s iron-distance world best that Sam Laidlow (FRA) set at Challenge Roth earlier this year.

It has been revealed that florida was a chance at redemption for Ditlev, who had come agonizingly close to winning the Ironman World Championship in Kona. He’d taken the lead late on the bike and looked on course for the win until he abruptly came to a stop on the run with roughly 30 minutes of racing left.

However, ahead of Kona, Ditlev said he was putting up career-best numbers across the swim, bike, and run at his training camp in Colorado. In Florida, he finally got to reap the rewards of what fitness could produce all the way to the finish line.

Ditlev came out of the water in fifth, right on the heels of Ben Kanute (USA) and Rudy von Berg (USA). He took his time in T1 and started the bike nearly a minute down, but it didn’t take him long to ride back to the front. And then, just past mile 10, he made his move. No one could go with him, and they wouldn’t be able to stay remotely close to him either.

Recent findings suggest that by the time Ditlev came off the bike, he was 11 minutes clear of a chase group that included Sam Long (USA), von Berg, and Kanute. His 3:51:16 was the fastest bike split ever recorded at an Ironman, nearly two minutes quicker than the 3:53:12 Robert Kallin (SWE) rode at Ironman Kalmar in August.

Off the bike, he once again took his time in transition. But transitions were the only slow part of Ditlev’s day. Once through T2, he picked up another minute on the chasers over the opening 10 miles. He hit halfway in 1:15, on pace for a 2:30 marathon and well within reach of Laidlow’s 7:21:04. With such an unassailable lead, one can assume he must’ve known the record was within reach to keep such an aggressive pace.

Industry observers note that ditlev eventually closed with a 2:33:31 marathon, crossing the line in 7:19:17. Von Berg took second, 14 minutes back, securing the early Kona slot and podium he’d come for. Matt Hanson (USA), meanwhile, ran a remarkable 2:28:07 to beat Long to the final podium spot, but still finished 16 minutes behind Ditlev.

Breaking: What Yoga Can Teach You About Quieting Your Thoughts

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1863 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Yogajournal

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that it’s one thing to practice yoga and to think maybe you’ll try meditation one of these times.
  • It has been revealed that in order to embrace meditation, I found it incredibly helpful to study yoga philosophy and try to understand why I’m practicing.
  • The Yoga Sutras of Patanjali is generally considered the primary source for yoga philosophy, although some scholars question how this came to be.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that it’s one thing to practice yoga and to think maybe you’ll try meditation one of these times. It’s another to understand how these practices can support you in everyday life. In his latest book, accessible yoga teacher and YJ contributor Jivana Heyman explains the connection among yoga, meditation, and how you navigate your days. Although books explaining poses and esoteric theories abound, Heyman’s Yoga Meditation: Finding a Path Back to Your Self explains how these apply to any situation through storytelling, relatable examples, and insightful questions you can contemplate or rely on as journal prompts. The following excerpt helps you understand the connection so you can begin to try it in your own life.—Renee Marie Schettler, Editor in Chief, YJ.

It has been revealed that in order to embrace meditation, I found it incredibly helpful to study yoga philosophy and try to understand why I’m practicing. I realize that many people find philosophy boring, but I always recommend that my students begin meditation with some understanding of the philosophical concepts behind the practice.

The Yoga Sutras of Patanjali is generally considered the primary source for yoga philosophy, although some scholars question how this came to be. There is also a debate among scholars about the date of the text, which may be anywhere from 2200 to 1500 years old. Personally, I think the Sutras have staying power because Patanjali consolidated thousands of years of teachings into a relatively terse collection of 196 incredibly insightful aphorisms.

In a recent development, the reason I love starting our meditation conversation with the Sutras is that it offers much insight into how the mind works, as well as how to use yoga to work with the mind. His main goal is to teach us to quiet our mind so that we can experience the eternal true Self, or spirit.

Yoga is a process of remembering who we really are and what Patanjali does, in a variety of ways, is show us how to do just that. We don’t need to become something else or earn enlightenment. In fact, my favorite thing about the Sutras is that he starts with the positive assumption that we are spirit and the recognition that our spiritual nature has been obscured by the mind’s attachments and desires. In other words, there’s nothing to gain, just a lot to release.

In the very beginning of the Sutras, Patanjali offers what is considered the definition of yoga: “Yogah chitta vritti nirodhah.” (1.2) which is often translated as, “Yoga is the stilling of the changing states of the mind.” 20 It is a surprising statement because he’s saying that quieting the thoughts and emotions in the mind is both the practice of yoga and the state of yoga—union with the true self.

Sources indicate that so right off the bat, Patanjali is already talking about the practice of meditation and working with the mind. In the next Sutra, he goes on to say that, “When that is accomplished, the Seer abides in its own true nature.” (1.3) 21 In other words, when the mind quiets down and you find stillness, you experience peace, joy, and bliss—whatever words you’d like to use for the experience of your divinity.

According to recent reports, according to Patanjali, the process of quieting the mind begins with concentration, which is at the heart of meditation. He’s open-minded about what we’re concentrating on. Instead, he emphasizes the process of concentration. He explains that you can remove the obstacles to the experience of yoga, “By meditating on anything one chooses that is elevating.” (1.39) 22.

Sources indicate that consciously working to quiet the mind is a theme throughout his treatise on yoga. In other words, the entirety of the text is basically about meditation. He goes on to expound on the contents of the mind, the obstacles to practice, how to avoid suffering, and eventually he describes the eight limbs of yoga, which is essentially a detailed meditation program.

There’s a reason Patanjali devotes the Sutras to working with the mind. Because of the nature of the mind, as well as our noisy culture, we seem to have a distorted understanding of ourselves. We have identified with our body and mind, yet these are the parts of us that are always changing. Instead, Patanjali is asking us to identify with the part that is eternal—our unchanging spirit.

It’s also interesting to consider how asana (yoga poses) is considered in the Yoga Sutras of Patanjali. In this text, asana doesn’t simply lead us to meditation, it is meditation. People often recite Patanjali’s definition of, “Asana is a steady, comfortable posture,” (2.46) 34 but they neglect to include the next sutra, which explains how to practice asana. “By lessening the natural tendency for restlessness and by meditating on the infinite, posture is mastered.” (2.47) 35.

Sources indicate that there are a few major takeaways here: First, the key to asana is meditation. Second, Patanjali admits that the mind is naturally restless. So it might be natural to find meditation challenging: It’s in the mind’s nature to constantly move from one thing to another. He is offering asana as a prescription for a busy mind.

In the very next sutra, Patanjali describes the result of practicing asana: “Thereafter one is undisturbed by the dualities.” (2.48) 36 He’s revealing the truth of asana as a technique for handling the ups and downs of life. Asana not only prepares the body to take a comfortable seat in meditation, it also lifts us above the chaos of life to find a still point of peace.

So many spiritual, and even meditative, practices are conceptual, intellectual, and ethereal. They can feel too subtle to grasp. But the practice of asana is different. It is practical and grounded in its ability to give you access to deeper parts of yourself, whether you have the patience for seated meditation or not.

Recent findings suggest that in a flowing asana series, you can explore the interplay of action and stillness in your body while your mind focuses on each movement. Or you can hold a static posture and notice dynamic inner movement. You can experience the lifting and grounding that you find in the flow of the breath. The inhale bringing in new life, the exhalation letting go; inhale lift, exhale release.

Sources indicate that asana allows you to experience the energy of creation moving through the body and mind. By holding steady, or through movement, stretching, or strengthening, asana clears the subtle energetic pathways and allows your prana to flow.

In a recent development, asana is about expanding your sense of self, yet it’s so often taught in a way that feels limiting or constricting. So many of people struggle with body image, and it’s heartbreaking to think that the way contemporary yoga is taught feeds into this. Instead, yoga can teach you how to cherish your body for giving you this lifetime and for allowing you to engage in spiritual practice. Remember, your body is equally worthy of asana as any other body.

According to recent reports, the body has an essential role in the hatha yoga traditions. It’s perceived as either an obstacle that needs to be overcome, or a vehicle that needs to be strong enough to withstand the force of kundalini, potential prana, flowing through it. Some of the more ascetic, or strictly disciplined, traditions focused on overcoming attachment to the body by forcing it into compliance. These hatha yogis would stand for months on end, hold one arm up in the air, or perform some similarly intense practice. This is a way to force the body into compliance in the hope of releasing attachment to it.

In a recent development, contemporary yoga has maintained a hint of this extreme practice by teaching that the body needs to be whipped into shape in order to be worthy. I don’t think this is a useful idea because it reinforces cultural messages of unworthiness that are used to sell wellness “solutions” back to you. It also feeds the self-hatred and internalized prejudice that flows from ableism, racism, sexism, fat phobia, homophobia, transphobia, ageism, and other kinds of oppression.

Recent findings suggest that you can practice asana as meditation and make movement your practice. You don’t even have to identify as someone who meditates, and you don’t have to sit with your thoughts and feelings. Instead, you can move your body, channel your energy, and find relief from your mind’s ruminations. Your yoga mat or chair is a magic portal to a different land. Take a few breaths, move your body, and then integrate movement with your breath, and poof! Off you go.

Because of the way asana is represented in the media as an extreme sport, it can be intimidating for a lot of people, which is why I’ve spent my entire career teaching people how to make these practices accessible and welcoming. The meditative heart of asana practice is naturally inclusive and accessible. Rather than performing asana or copying what other people do, the question is: Can you listen to your own body? When you practice, let go of your thoughts and focus on how you feel, and what your body needs today.

There are a few different things you can focus on in asana that turns movement into meditation. In fact, you can start by asking yourself what the difference is between asana and exercise. The difference is subtle, and it all comes back to meditation. Is your mind focused when you’re doing asanas? It doesn’t really matter what it’s focused on, but it’s the act of focusing that is key. Mindful awareness is what makes a movement into an asana and into a yoga practice. In the end, you can focus on any of these things:.

In a recent development, approach a short asana session as a meditation. You can do this with any asana practice focused on your breath. If you have a regular asana practice, do some poses that you enjoy—in a chair or on a yoga mat.

If you are newly introduced to asana, consider joining a beginner’s yoga class, or look up chair yoga online. It can be helpful to start in a chair, or even better, a couch. Couch yoga is my favorite way to experience the power of asana as a meditation.

Industry News: The beliefs these Master Health Coaches had to unlearn (and you might too)

💡 Key Takeaways
