Less Cars, More Money: My Visit to the City of the Future

📅 07 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1933 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mrmoneymustache

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Money Mustache, I do my best to be your one-stop-shop for Lifestyle Guru ideas.
  • But there’s one single area of life where all of these factors come together with an almost Nuclear Fusion level of synergy and effectiveness.
  • That we immediately switch to building our cities and countries around people, instead of cars.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In my role as Mr. Money Mustache, I do my best to be your one-stop-shop for Lifestyle Guru ideas. So over the years we’ve covered not just the Money side of life, but also the even more important stuff like health and fitness and the psychology of better, happier living.

But there’s one single area of life where all of these factors come together with an almost Nuclear Fusion level of synergy and effectiveness. And because of that, if I could have one single wish in the world, this is what I would wish for. It’s a change so massive that it would make every person on the planet better off and fix most of our problems in one grand sweep. And it’s probably not what you’d expect:.

That we immediately switch to building our cities and countries around people, instead of cars.

(and then fix all of our existing ones too, so that our entire world is built around person-friendly living.).

Recent findings suggest that the benefits of this are way bigger than almost anyone can imagine. We’re not just talking about eliminating a bit of pollution or a few traffic jams or car crashes. No. This is about far richer, healthier, and most importantly more fun living for everyone.

To put even conservative numbers to this, we’re talking about a life boost of over $20,000 per person per year, which compounds into well over two million dollars per adult lifetime.

On a nationwide scale, this would boost the wealth of the United States by about seven trillion dollars per year, which would compound into about 770 trillion over the next five decades.

Which happens to be more than the current total amount of human wealth on the entire planet.

You will have a house that is both cheaper and more beautiful and spacious. Your body and brain will be healthier and stronger and sexier and cost a lot less time and healthcare dollars to maintain.

And all of our wallets and investment accounts, both public and private will be absolutely overflowing with surplus income, reduced expenses, and fuel an investment and prosperity boom like the world has never seen.

“Isn’t city planning just a stuffy thing that your city council does in the background while we’re all off living our lives?”.

Recent findings suggest that well, yes it is right now. And that’s the whole problem: cities are built by people whose primary job is to maintain the status quo and prevent disruptions. And those committes are elected and encouraged by crusty old companies and organizations, and plain old grumpy neighbors who just don’t have the vision to see what they are missing.

I’m convinced that if everyone could see through the smoggy haze of the status quo, we would all agree that this idea of a radical change is not only the best idea, but the only reasonable idea to even consider.

So our job is to learn and explain just how big and how easy this is. And what it boils down to is pretty damned simple.

Whoa, that’s a bit of a surprise.

So for the same amount of space you can have an entire pretty nice two bedroom apartment, or you can have just enough space for two (small) cars to park and pull out. But it gets even crazier than this. Check out this random intersection here in my own city:.

Recent findings suggest that WHAT?! So every time you have two big car roads intersect, which happens hundreds of times in every big city, you are wasting enough space to build a luxurious, resort-like living area with about one hundred two-bedroom apartments and still have room for a pool, a dog park, a grocery store, a couple of restaurants, and so on.

This is just the beginning of the insanity, because I have only shown you two parking spaces and one intersection. The reality is that our entire cities are made almost entirely of stupid, expensive wasted space like this.

And the problem is so extreme that the only reason we think we need cars to get around, is because we have wasted most of our space on accommodating cars, which spread everything out so far (and made everything so loud and dangerous) that nobody feels like walking or biking!

Whenever you propose any great latest idea, you’ll always get a bunch of smartasses who like to complain and resist change, without even bothering to think it through.

“But how are we going to keep driving our cars just as much as we do now?”.

Which is ridiculous – because the whole point is that as soon as you cut out all the huge wasted spaces we create to accommodate cars, you are suddenly FREE from needing cars so much!

Instead, you can just weave a brand latest city, with a bunch of variations of this beautiful resort which also include offices, grocery stores, climbing gyms and every other amenity.

And yes, you’d still have some roads between them, but they would be mostly for deliveries, emergency vehicles and people who need mobility assistance.

I hope you’re not going to make me ride the bus?

It has been revealed that I am all for public transit in theory, but to be honest I don’t usually have the patience for it. I don’t do lineups, and I don’t like to stand around waiting passively for my transportation to arrive – when it’s time to go somewhere, I just want to go, and go now, and get there fast. So my own personal choice is to take a bike for short distances (under 2 miles) or an e-bike for larger ones (up to about 15 miles).

Although this is often news to car drivers, bikes are much faster than cars for urban transport, plus they give me exercise and thrill, which is way better than being stuck at the red light with the cars.

If you take this already-superior method of urban transport and cut out the 90% of the land that we waste on accommodating the inferior cars, then you end up with a revolution: everybody gets where they are going ten times faster, at much lower cost, and has much more fun doing it.

Industry observers note that and sure, there will also be light rail and faster buses. And sure, you can still hop in an Uber or even bring your own car into a city like this.But the point is that it will just happen much much less often.

Okay I’m convinced, but how can we actually accomplish this?

Mr. Money Mustache can talk a significant game with all these fancy words and pictures, but the truth is that I’m way too impatient to put up with all the bureaucracy and complaints that arise when you try to actually change a city. I’ve been doing my best here in Longmont, and I have gotten just about nowhere. We’re still just stacking on more and more layers of ridiculous car shit where I live.

Sources indicate that thankfully, other people are much more patient and effective than I am at affecting change, and one group has made such incredible progress that you can now go LIVE in their first creation: a 1000-person car-free neighborhood called Culdesac Tempe. And as I write this, I am staying in a hotel right nearby, having spent the past two days touring and visiting and interviewing the founders*.

While we were at it, my Phoenix-area-house-fixing friend Tracy Royce and I also hosted a meetup for an enthusiastic group of our readers/viewers right there in Culdesac’s emerging central plaza.

Culdesac is Awesome and Could Change Everything.

If you only look at the financial spreadsheet, you would think this first Culdesac project is just going to be a highly profitable 1000-person cluster of apartment buildings, spread out across 17 acres of land. And while financial sustainability is indeed a key reason why this model will succeed, the money is the least exciting part.

When you look at these pictures compared to a normal housing complex, the main thing you will notice is that all the space that would normally be wasted on parking lots, is instead used for beautiful walking and gathering areas.

The next major upgrade is that they mixed in the amenities for daily life right into the neighborhood, rather than forcing all the future residents to get into their cars to drive out to find them:.

I was also impressed with just the feel of walking the Mediterranean-vibed spaces between the buildings, even at this early stage when everything is still under construction.

Due to the hot desert climate of the region, everything is built around providing shade, breeze, and reflecting heat during the summer, while also maximizing the joyful fact that there is no winter there (the coldest month of the year still has an average daily high of 65F/18C, which means palm trees, leafy gardens and fruits and flowers forever.).

With a setup like this, and 999 new neighbors to meet, I would rarely feel the need to leave the place. Which really cuts down on my desire to use a car. But on top of that, Culdesac has strategically placed itself in Tempe, a city right in the center of the Phoenix metro area, within walking distance of the main university and right on a light rail stop which allows you to reach almost everything (including the airport) for FREE, since an annual pass to the transit system is included with your rent.

But of course, you can also get around on foot, bike, e-bike, scooter, or hop into one of Culdesac’s fleet of rideshare electric cars for a trip to the mountains or whatever else you might want to do that’s outside of bike and transit range.

It has been revealed that it’s insane. In fact it’s so good that I am going to attempt to move there myself at the end of 2023, enjoying my first escape from Colorado winter and celebrating the fact that my boy will be a legal adult at that time.

But even this is just a pilot project because Culdesac has much bigger intends.

From my conversations with the founders, I think they want to do this:.

So How Can We Benefit From This, and Support it?

And Then What Will Be Our Payback?

This whole change is exciting, and it is immense.

Understanding these ideas around city planning is the economic and social equivalent to being a doctor, and finding a 35-year-old patient in a hospital who is suffering from every chronic disease, but then discovering that they have been following a diet of Coke and Donuts for their whole lives and never been out on a walk, once.

In other words, the changes are so obvious, and the amount of win/win synergy so great, that every step we take towards making our cities better, and every car trip we eliminate, will absolutely explode our personal and national wealth upwards for generations to come.

The stakes just couldn’t be higher.

In a recent development, another collaborator in the overall effort for car free cities is a bank-founding multi entrepreneur local friend named Kevin Dahlstrom. His recent Twitter rant on building car-free cities from the scratch gathered a shocking amount of very positive feedback and interesting comments.

* Despite my positive raving about this neighborhood, I have no financial or business connection with the project or any of the team members. I am just really excited about their work and want them to succeed!

#22026. I Got Shingles Training for a Marathon. I’m Not the Only One.

I Got Shingles Training for a Marathon. I’m Not the Only One.

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1530 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Triathlete

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, shingles typically appears as a band of blistering, painful rash on one side of the body.
  • According to recent reports, I had just finished the last hard training run of my marathon build, 19 miles with 15 at race pace.
  • “You’ll have two weeks to taper, and you’ll be ready to run that BQ (Boston Marathon Qualifying time) on race day.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, shingles typically appears as a band of blistering, painful rash on one side of the body. (Photo: Getty Images).

According to recent reports, I had just finished the last hard training run of my marathon build, 19 miles with 15 at race pace. I nailed it, but couldn’t help thinking it felt harder than it should have.

“It’s just nerves,” I told myself. “You’ll have two weeks to taper, and you’ll be ready to run that BQ (Boston Marathon Qualifying time) on race day.”.

The next day, I felt exhausted, and my ribs were sore and tender to the touch. I started to wonder if I’d pulled a muscle in my rib cage while breathing heavily during my training run. I, of course, turned to Google. “Ribs sore from running.” “Ribs hurt after running.” Most of the posts advised that I’d feel better in a day.

Sources indicate that but I didn’t feel better the next day. Instead, I noticed a small pink mark on my stomach, and now my ribs felt both sore and tingly. My Google searches grew more alarming: I could have shingles.

I scheduled an appointment for that same day, and my doctor confirmed it. She took one look at me and said, “I’m so sorry, you have shingles.”.

Shingles is a painful viral infection that looks like a terrible rash and usually involves nerve pain that can last for months. The virus comes from dormant chickenpox in your body that can reappear when you’re stressed.

Industry observers note that my doctor asked about stressors in my life. “I haven’t really been that stressed,” I promised, saying my family life and my career were extremely smooth. “But I have been training for a marathon,” I noted.

In a recent development, “That could do it,” she told me. “Your body is clearly telling you that you were pushing too hard.”.

I’m 43, younger than the typical shingles patient, but I’m part of an unfortunate trend. Shingles cases are on the rise and the biggest increase is among people in their 30s and 40s. One study found overall shingles cases nearly doubled between 2005 and 2021. Another found cases in Americans under 50 quadrupled from the late 1940s to 2000, and are still going up, according to data from the CDC.

A massive reason for the increase among millennials is that we fall into a gap: 50 and up, and you can get the shingles vaccine; 30 and under, and you’ve had the chickenpox vaccine, which will make getting shingles way less likely.

According to recent reports, that age range is also most common among marathoners, so my big question was whether running, especially hard training, can give you shingles. Unfortunately, that specific question hasn’t been extensively studied, so there’s no clear-cut answer. But doctors are drawing correlations between heavy training and whether it decreases the body’s immunity overall.

In a recent development, there’s research that shows immunity dips after heavy training, says David Nieman, DrPH, FACSM, director of the Human Performance Laboratory at Appalachian State University. He pointed to a study involving mice and the herpes virus.

Recent findings suggest that “When you infected the mice and then forced them to run to exhaustion, there was a higher mortality rate in those mice than mice that just did moderate activity and rested,” he states. “Moderate activity actually helped a little bit, but by far the really bad response was in the mice that ran to exhaustion.”.

In another study, researchers gave horses the flu and then ran them really hard. Those horses developed a longer-lasting, more intense bout of the flu compared to the horses who were infected but didn’t run hard, he remarked.

In a recent development, but Nieman and other researchers agree that moderate exercise can actually boost your immunity. James Turner, a professor at the Sport, Exercise and Rehabilitation Sciences school at the University of Birmingham, claims it’s far more common that inadequate sleep, diet and psychological stress suppress immunity than exercise, even really hard training.

“Research on both prolonged exercise and marathon running shows that antibody responses are not suppressed and might actually be higher,” he says.

Recent findings suggest that meanwhile, Dr. William Schaffner, MD, a professor of infectious diseases at Vanderbilt Health who’s an expert in shingles, says it’s too soon to say definitely that lots of stress leads to the virus. He points out there’s no evidence that soldiers in combat or police and firefighters have an increased risk of shingles.

It has been revealed that “When people get a shingles episode, there is a tendency to look back in their lives to see if there might be some sort of inciting event or stressful event and there’s a tendency to link the two,” he states. “But the question is, is that just coincidence because there’s a lot of stress in life, or was it a causal relationship? I think we’ll still have to say that hasn’t been definitively settled.”.

Sources indicate that instead, for Schaffner, the likeliest explanation for the increase in shingles is because the chickenpox vaccine is decreasing our exposure to chickenpox. We used to all get chickenpox as children, and so the virus was more common in the wild. That gave our immune systems a boost. Now that there’s a vaccine, that isn’t happening, which means we may be more likely to get shingles, he said.

Whether my running caused my shingles or not, as soon as I had my diagnosis, my next questions were about my marathon. My doctor mentioned my symptoms would likely peak in four days to a week, and so it still seemed possible I would be ready for race day. I rushed out to get a seven-day course of Valtrex—if you start an antiviral treatment promptly enough, it can stop the spread of the shingles rash.

But as the week passed and the rash grew along my rib cage to my back, it only continued to feel worse. I was achy everywhere, and my ribs felt like they were constantly being stabbed with tiny needles. A week later, I called it and canceled my marathon plans, harboring a hope that within a few weeks I would be better and could rebound to run my BQ.

What I did next probably hurt my cause rather than helped it. As soon as I felt a bit better, I would go out and do a race-pace run, which would give me a painful setback that lasted for several days. This likely was making my bout with the virus longer, Nieman says.

In a recent development, he reminded me of the mice who were running to exhaustion and not getting well. The mice really needed to keep it low-key to get an immune boost, not drain.

“If they did 30 minutes of something like a brisk walk equivalent, that would help a little bit,” he notes.

My conversation with him sounded like a negotiation.

“I’m mostly feeling better, but I still sometimes have sensations in my ribs, so do I still need to take it easy?” I asked.

According to recent reports, “I have a lot of empathy. I know you don’t want to hear it,” he said gently. Nieman has run 58 marathons himself, so he knows the feeling. “You don’t want anybody telling you not to run, but this is where you’ve got to be really, really careful and just bide your time and slowly get back into it once you feel better.”.

It has been revealed that his advice to runners: listen to your body and don’t push yourself. That’s not an easy metric for marathoners who are used to pushing beyond what feels comfortable, but Nieman says exhaustion can exacerbate the nerve pain and make it all last much longer.

Other things to keep in mind: it’s possible that sunburns can impede your immune system, so cover up once you’re back out and running, states Jennifer Moffat, a SUNY microbiology and immunology professor and expert on chickenpox and shingles.

And, Moffat indicates, while you still have a rash, you’re contagious and can spread the virus to others through contact. If you’re at the gym or anywhere you might touch other people, you should have the rash fully covered.

She also advises keeping an eye on the other stresses around marathons, like not eating enough, not sleeping enough, and the mental stress around races.

“The anticipation, logistics, travel hassles, changes in environment and food, rivalries with other competitors, jet lag, time away from family, the cost can become overwhelming,” she claims. “Getting to the starting line of a marathon is much more than showing up with your shoes tied.”.

In fact, she indicates, it’s common for people to come down with other viral infections right before a race (the dreaded taper cold).

Recent findings suggest that as for me, two months after my rash first appeared, I finally truly threw in the towel. I couldn’t keep up any kind of marathon training without making myself feel worse, so I switched to low-effort maintenance running and decided my BQ would have to come next year.

I Used to Buy Cycling Kit for How It Looked. Now I Buy It for How It Gets Me Through the Ride—My Three Rules for Cycling Kit

📅 30 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1068 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • According to recent reports, after spending almost two decades riding and years running bike shops, I have narrowed down my priorities for key criteria when buying cycling apparel.
  • Apparel falls into different categories depending on the rider.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

According to recent reports, after spending almost two decades riding and years running bike shops, I have narrowed down my priorities for key criteria when buying cycling apparel. I’m looking for a product that is durable, performs well in varying conditions, and is comfortable over miles on the bike.

Apparel falls into different categories depending on the rider. For some, it falls into a category of fashion. Those riders want their choice of apparel to tell a story about who they are on the bike.

Industry observers note that for other riders, safety is the biggest driving factor. This group is intentionally easy to see by their bright colors riding by. While other riders solely look for a great deal, digging through clearance racks at bike shops as the seasons change.

It has been revealed that finding kit that performs the way we want our bike to perform can give us a better experience on our ride compared to getting whatever the cool kids are wearing—just for fashion’s sake. Here I’m going to dive deeper into each of the priorities I have for my jerseys and bibs to shed some light on why there’s value in this shift—especially this time of year.

What I look for in a jersey, especially for fall, is one that will vent well on the way up, but keep me comfortable on the way back down. I love a good gilet, especially leaving it open on the way down a road. If my jersey can do what the gilet does then that’s one less piece of kit I have to buy and bring. Lately I’ve been using the Dottore Hybrid Long Sleeve jersey from Q36.5 and it checks off all those boxes.

I tried this jersey out on a recent trip to Italy where we had a roughly 2,500-foot climb followed immediately by an equal descent. The temperature was hovering around the mid-fifties and usually, I would bring a vest for a ride like this. However, I was told this jersey should be perfect for these conditions, so I wanted to give it a proper test. On the way up I didn’t feel a need to unzip the jersey at all and on the screaming descent I never felt cold. Somehow Q36.5 figured out how to give the best of both worlds in one jersey.

Recent findings suggest that many of us think of a good pair of bibs being the key component to comfort on the bike—and in some ways that’s not wrong. Comfort on your sit bones can be greatly improved by getting the right saddle and sometimes a bike fit to determine what that saddle is and how the saddle should be positioned. But a good pair of bibs can still greatly improve comfort on the bike even after you get a fit and get the right saddle.

Recent findings suggest that not all chamois pads are created equal, and not all bibs hold the chamois in the place you need after miles of pedaling. Part of the challenge with bibs is you don’t really know until you get on the bike to ride—and good bibs aren’t exactly an inexpensive purchase.

It has been revealed that “An unlined full length bib like the Velocio Luxe Tights offers a more comfortable go to bib for when you need to cover you legs but don't need to have fleece warmth,” states Trevor Raab, our resident bike racer and photographer at Bicycling. What I typically look for in bibs is a pair with minimal seams, has a chamois pad that offers both padding and ventilation, and good support and structure from the overalls to help hold the bib in place.

Sources indicate that the final piece of my puzzle for gear and apparel is durability. Part of the reality is that just like bikes, apparel has pieces that are more consumable than others and will need to be replaced over time.

It has been revealed that I’m someone who tends to stress test both bikes and apparel from hitting the ground. I haven’t found any apparel that holds up to a good impact to the pavement or gravel— as can be seen by many of my bibs having a tear on one of the hips. However, not all material holds up the same over time.

It has been revealed that from the bibs that I have tried I either haven’t put enough miles in them or I have put over a year of miles on them and there is a noticeable impact to the comfort of the chamois. But something to note: more padding isn’t inherently better in a chamois. From a durability perspective and my experience, the thicker pads compress over time and aren’t necessarily more comfortable on the bike. The pair I’ve gotten the most miles on this year are the Q36.5 Dottore Bib Shorts. I’ve put a few hundred miles in them and they are still as comfortable as the first ride. Every rider I talk to that has tried this pair of bibs has experienced the same thing.

According to recent reports, it’s vital to acknowledge the pricing of some of this high-end kit is not a small investment. Shifting your perspective of apparel as just clothes to looking at apparel as gear can make it easier to understand. Too many times when I worked in a shop someone would spend thousands of dollars on a bike only to buy low-priced apparel. There’s nothing wrong with buying entry-level kit to get started. But if you are someone who spends thousands on your bike, then it’s likely ride quality matters to you regardless of the price. If you start to think about your apparel as gear, it’s easier to see that great apparel can impact your ride just like riding on a great bike.

Jason Griffin is Bicycling's Senior Health and Fitness Editor, bringing more than a decade of fitness experience and years in the cycling industry to every story. A former personal trainer and bike shop manager, he's lined up for crits, tackled enduros, but prefers getting lost on multi-day bikepacking adventures. Lately though, his toughest balancing act has been fitting trainer rides between family life and the next adventure.

#22021. Breaking: Our 30 Unwritten Rules of Triathlon

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1090 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Triathlete ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Our 30 Unwritten Rules of Triathlon

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1090 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Triathlete

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that tim Heming outlines the comical 30 unwritten rules of triathlon that every athlete should know.
  • Like a lot of sports, triathlon is full of rules.
  • However, and particularly helpful for beginners, there are plenty more unwritten rules that we need to be aware of.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that tim Heming outlines the comical 30 unwritten rules of triathlon that every athlete should know. (Photo: Challenge Family).

Like a lot of sports, triathlon is full of rules. For example, you’re not allowed to cut the course, have a motor on your bike, curse at officials, punch a rival, or, most craven of all, have fewer than three safety pins on your race number in France.

However, and particularly helpful for beginners, there are plenty more unwritten rules that we need to be aware of. Some of them, we’ve helpfully outlined below:.

Industry observers note that 2. Forever Alone — The training paradox. The more you do triathlons, the more all your friends are triathletes, and the more you will train alone.

According to recent reports, 3. You Are Not Kristian — The Norwegian Method is to train more hours in a day than you do not train. For more training methods, see YouTube.

4. The Devil’s in the Details — Dedicate 20 hours a week to training for three months in the lead up to your A race. Spend zero minutes working on transition.

According to recent reports, 5. Shelve Twitter Hate — Write a mantra on your water bottle and start an Instagram account for reels, stories, and collabs. Don’t be an angry person on Twitter. That’s not cool.

6. Match at All Costs — Never sacrifice style for performance. Color-coded kit and equipment are essential, unless you’re going for garish retro, which is an acceptable look for 2026 only.

According to recent reports, 7. Weather or Not? — Check the weather forecast and water temperature before checking the weather forecast and water temperature, and then solicit opinions on what the weather and water temperature are likely to be on race day.

Recent findings suggest that 8. Wetsuit Your Worries Away — Convince yourself you can’t swim without a wetsuit/won’t be able to get your wetsuit off if it’s a wetsuit swim.

Industry observers note that 9. Experience Equals Complacency — The athlete guide must be studied with a focus that inversely correlates to how many races the athlete has done.

It has been revealed that 10. Selfie First, Reality Later — Take a selfie with the giant M-Dot “Ironman Is In Town” sign. Post this to social media as soon as you land, feigning a smile because although you’ve arrived, your bike hasn’t yet followed.

Industry observers note that 11. Hell’s Bells — Set three alarms minimum and then wonder why the first of them is going off as you force-feed yourself rice because you couldn’t sleep anyway.

Recent findings suggest that 12. Nothing Matters as Much as Everything — Take time to stare at your race tattoo, realize the transfer has only half stuck, and have a mild panic by convincing yourself you’ll be disqualified before the start.

It has been revealed that 13. Apply Liberally — Use sunscreen, making sure you miss a key patch of skin. It will show more of your suffering.

14. Pay it Forward — In the name of karma, offer to: a) Zip up someone’s wetsuit; b) Lend them a bike pump (even if it’s not yours); c) Thank everyone you see profusely and wish them all a great day.

In a recent development, 15. Ride the Intake Earthquake — Increase your volume of carbohydrates per hour exponentially with the same dedication you had when you raced 15 years ago and were insistent on using only your 5% body fat as a fuel source.

Sources indicate that 16. Be a Bathroom Banterer — Talk with bravado about your trained ability to both pee in the swim and on the bike while you stand for an hour in a revolving porta potty line.

17. What’s Good for the Goose is Good for the Gander — Oops! You punched someone in the eye in the swim completely by accident. Also, the breaststroker you got stuck behind at the first buoy deliberately kicked you in the face.

In a recent development, 18. Meditate on Aquatic Paradoxes — During the swim, reflect on: a) Whoever learned to swim as a kid is basically a cheater. Or b) “Why do triathletes swim so freaking slowly?”.

Industry observers note that 19. Style Reigns — Replace existing drink bottles on the bike with those from the on-course sponsor. Call bottles bidons if you’ve ever watched a clip of the Tour de France.

Recent findings suggest that 20. The Refs Need You (Really) — Become militant about drafting and shout obscenities at a pack who: a). Aren’t in the race anyway; b) Are out for a gentle social weekend ride; c) Are still moving faster than you.

Sources indicate that 21. Ride the Highs and Lows — When you are riding downhill, you think you will win. When you are riding uphill, you think you will come last.

Industry observers note that 22. Roll the Dice — Breathe a sigh of relief when you complete the bike leg without puncturing because you haven’t practiced changing tires for five years.

23. Don’t be Patronizing Pat — If you pass someone on the run, resist the urge to tap them encouragingly on the back. One athlete’s chirpy come-on is another athlete’s patronizing pat. And if you must do it, always avoid the backside.

24. Leave Self-Awareness Back at the Hotel — Do something in the finish chute that in any other walk of life you would find cringey. This includes sweaty mess marriage proposals to a long-suffering partner who has a cooked neck from staring at a race tracker for the past 14 hours.

25. Be Congratulating Carl — Always congratulate the first person you see at the finish. However hollow-eyed your expression or soiled your tri suit. It’s your duty to have that mutual moment with a complete stranger.

Sources indicate that 26. The Rules of Race Photography are Unbending — Acknowledge that official race photographs only ever capture: 1. Grotesque faces. 2: When you “briefly” sat up out of aero. 3. Ugly heel strikes.

Recent findings suggest that 27. You’re the Best — Use multiple filters of the race results, including but not limited to age-groups, disciplines (including transitions), and nationalities to claim a top-10 position at some aspect of your race. If you rode a road bike, you can also disqualify everyone who rode a TT/tri bike.

In a recent development, 28. Brutality Reigns — Include the word “brutal” at least three times during any social media race report.

Skip the Gimmicky Bike Gifts. Our Editors Recommend These 20 Useful Picks Under $50

📅 24 Apr 2018 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1648 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • As a lifelong cyclist, I’ve received well-intentioned bicycle-themed presents that sit around unused, get forgotten in my closet, or are regifted or donated years later.
  • In a recent development, admittedly, buying gifts for cyclists isn’t always easy, and every bicycle rider is different.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

As a lifelong cyclist, I’ve received well-intentioned bicycle-themed presents that sit around unused, get forgotten in my closet, or are regifted or donated years later. If you’re shopping for a Christmas or birthday gift for a bike rider, buy something they will truly appreciate and actually use.

In a recent development, admittedly, buying gifts for cyclists isn’t always easy, and every bicycle rider is different. Cycling is often an expensive, gear-heavy activity with many niches and sub-categories, each with particular equipment needs. Resist the temptation to buy a T-shirt with a poorly drawn bike, AI-generated artwork, or a novelty cycling jersey. Instead, choose something they will love. You can find great gifts that show you put in the extra effort, won’t break your budget, or take weeks to arrive.

Here’s a list of 20 of the most helpful, beautiful, fun, and affordable gifts for cyclists under $50; items we’ve tested, loved, and rely on. Want even more great deals on cycling gear and accessories? Bookmark our Best Bike Gear Deals page for sales and discounts from top cycling retailers.

According to recent reports, bells are handy on the bike path, around town, and on the trail. Aussie brand Knog’s Oi bell is discreet, looks good on everything from a commuter to a race bike, and weighs only about 25 grams. Pick up the Oi Classic with a glass-fiber lever or step up to the Oi Luxe with a metal hammer for about $20 more.

Lezyne makes some of our favorite cycling lights for commuting, road, gravel, and mountain biking. However, while super bright and durable, the brand’s lights can be a bit costly. The KTV Drive combo is a lightweight set of front and rear lights to keep riders visible on commutes and in urban environments. They’re rechargeable, have up to 40 hours of runtime, and fit most bikes.

It has been revealed that electric mini inflators have taken the cycling world by storm. These devices let you promptly and precisely air up any bike tire. However, most inflators are a bit too large and heavy to carry in a jersey pocket or seat bag. Although the Pocket SE doesn’t have a pressure gauge, this pint-sized inflator weighs only 90 grams and fills up to four tires per charge.

Industry observers note that the Duraglove ETs from Defeet are an awesome addition to any rider’s fall and winter cycling wardrobe. They’re perfect for rides where temperatures are still above freezing but not warm enough to go without gloves. These gloves have rubber grippers (for holding your handlebar in wet conditions) and are touchscreen-compatible with your smartphone or head unit. They’re an excellent value for under $25.

Sometimes the best gifts are high-end versions of normal things you wouldn’t buy for yourself. While only 33 grams and the size of an Allen key, Daysaver’s Essential8 has the same wrenches as your regular multitool. The design uses nested and flippable magnetic bits made from high-quality stainless steel. As a bonus gift, the Essential8 pairs perfectly with the Coworking5 extension.

Industry observers note that what started as a homemade, low-sugar, all-natural sports drink is now a player in cycling nutrition. Skratch Labs offers a palatable solution that keeps you hydrated and energized without causing tummy aches. The brand’s formula is designed to replace exactly what you lose through heavy sweating, whether riding outdoors or on the indoor trainer. Skratch offers several flavors (like lemon-lime, orange, pineapple, and more) and seasonal ones (like apple cider).

Want to save weight in your tires or space in your seat bag? TPU tubes are lighter than traditional butyl rubber tubes and roll faster. They also pack down to about half the size of traditional inner tubes, so they’re the perfect spare tube for your flat kit. They’re available in sizes that fit most road, gravel, and mountain bikes.

We were skeptical that $40 shorts could be this good. However, the Black Bibs consistently outperform shorts that cost six times as much. They’re very simple—no fancy fabrics or creative cuts—and that’s why we love them. Made entirely of plain black Lycra with mesh straps and large leg grippers at the cuffs, they don’t look like anything special. However, even after logging over a year in the Black Bibs, one tester consistently reaches for them first.

It has been revealed that toe covers are perfect for days when it’s not quite cold enough for full booties, but you want to keep your toes warm on the ride. Pearl Izumi’s Amfib model is a solid pick; plus, they are reflective for rides after dark. They provide enough stretch to fit over most road shoes (with cleats) and are easy to put on and take off.

In a recent development, the small but mighty Mattone is a great choice for sleek, waterproof, and secure storage. Thanks to its elastic material, you can pack it to the gills or keep a minimal setup and cinch it tight with the Boa dial.

Industry observers note that we look for two traits in a good seat bag: Carrying essentials securely without rattling, and mounting under the saddle without moving around. The Speedsleev Ranger 2.0 Small checks those boxes admirably. It has slots for repair items including CO2 and tire plugs, and a larger compartment for spare tubes and multitools. We’ve loaded it with two TPU tubes, a full-size multitool, CO2, and a plug kit, and still have room to spare.

The Wolf Tooth 6-bit hex wrench multitool is a great gift for any maintenance-minded cyclist. With an optional key ring and a sleek profile, the tool is easy to carry on rides (or when asked to fix your nephew’s bike after holiday dinner). It has everything you need for most basic repairs. Plus, it’s made in America, with replacement parts available.

In a recent development, dynaplug makes the best (and lightest) tubeless tire plugging tools on the market. The Carbon Racer comes pre-loaded with plugs and takes the guesswork out of fixing a tubeless puncture when sealant isn’t working. The Carbon Racer works like the brand's aluminum Racer Pro plug tool but uses lighter (and more cost-effective) nylon and glass-fiber construction.

Stan’s NoTubes is the original tubeless sealant brand and still one of our top overall picks. Most tubeless sealant was designed for mountain bike and gravel tires that run lower pressures. However, road tires typically need more air pressure, which makes punctures and cuts harder to seal. Stan’s latest introduction is optimized for road bikes with 50+ psi and claims to repair holes up to 7.8mm in size.

A foam roller is a must-have accessory for recovery, preventing injury, and staying fresh. “I’ve been using this foam roller for years, and it's still going strong,” said Senior Health & Fitness Editor Jason Griffin. You can use it to work out tension throughout your body, especially on the glutes, quads, and IT band. Griffin also describes a dual purpose for this foam roller: “I even use this as a balance-board base with an old skateboard deck for cross-training days.”.

Industry observers note that multitools are incredibly convenient, but can be hard to manipulate in tight spaces or when you need extra torque to loosen a stubborn fastener. This micro ratchet is a smart alternative that can speed up repairs and adjustments. It includes hex sizes: 2-, 2.5-, 3-, 4-, 5-, 6-, and 8mm, plus T10 and T25 Torx bits, a Phillips screwdriver, and two tire levers. Plus, it’s still small enough to stash in a hip pack or hydration pack.

The machined aluminum Sport Mount is a great gift because it has everything we love about K-Edge’s products—it’s functional, looks great, and is priced right. The Sport Mount fits 31.8mm round bars and holds your head unit sleekly out front and aligned with the stem. Unlike cheap mounts, the Sport’s insert is replaceable if damaged.

Recent findings suggest that socks are always a go-to gift choice when you don’t know what to give someone. Luckily, almost every cyclist needs more riding socks—and Swiftwick makes some of our favorites. The Merino wool Pursuit crew socks keep your feet dry and warm in winter while providing cushioning and compression.

Industry observers note that if your giftee doesn’t already have a Buff in their closet to wear as a scarf, headband, or helmet liner, now is a great time to get one—it also works as a face covering when the temperature dips. The stretchy Merino wool fabric is easy to pull up over the mouth and nose as needed, and it wicks moisture to keep you dry.

Do you have a young reader in your life who likes bikes? “The Ragtag Best Friends Bicycle Club” by Marley Blonsky, a cycling advocate and co-founder of All Bodies on Bikes, tells children about Maisel, her sister Zoe, and upcoming friends as she learns that riding her own way makes cycling great.

Sources indicate that as Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and Upcoming England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

Wiz Khalifa has never been particularly shy about his love of smoking weed, but lately, he's been chasing a different kind of high. On Sunday, November 8, the "Black and Yellow" rapper made his 5K debut at Diplo's Run Club in Los Angeles, clocking 22:55 at an average pace of 7:23 per mile. He finished 95th among 10,991 participants, which is quite the racing debut for someone who only started getting serious about the sport a few months ago.

And to think his whole running obsession started with what was supposed to be a simple walk.

In an October interview with Hypebeast, Khalifa explained that he’d gone out to a trail one day, decided to pick up the pace, and eventually checked his watch to discover he’d gone four miles. And to his surprise, he also realized he’d accidentally discovered a new hobby.

"Oh sh*t! I kind of liked that," he recalled.

Sources indicate that apparently, that was enough to get him investing in proper shoes and gear, and by July, he was documenting his workouts on social media, telling his Instagram followers how much he enjoyed getting out there with increasingly ambitious mileage goals (and even catching Strava's attention when the platform offered to help verify his account). More recently, he challenged himself to cover 30 miles in a week, telling fans, "You can join in or watch me be great.".

Of course, given Khalifa's well-documented relationship with marijuana, there's an obvious question about how all this cardio is treating him. He certainly doesn't seem too concerned.

It has been revealed that "My lungs are holding up great. I'm getting faster," he told Hypebeast, crediting his years of Muay Thai training and performing onstage for his endurance.

Whatever his routine, Khalifa certainly had plenty of energy left after Sunday's 5K. In a post-race Instagram video, he's seen enjoying every second of his latest racing career, bouncing around, dancing, and proudly showing off his Strava results.

And as for his post-race celebration? He wound up in Diplo's DJ booth, of course.

Sean Abrams was the Senior Editor, Growth and Engagement at Men’s Health. He’s a former hip hop dancer who likes long walks on the beach and large glasses of tequila. You can find his previous work at Maxim, Elite Daily, and AskMen.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that we earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Tracking your heart rate with a heart rate monitor (HRM) during your runs is one of the most powerful ways to optimize your training, whether you’re a dedicated marathoner, power triathlete, or just aiming to move more intentionally. As a runner, I understand that my heart rate is notable, but I don’t necessarily understand using it as a training device. That’s why I reached out to an expert to find out why it’s important and how to use that data.

As exercise physiologist and run coach Alyssa Lombardi tells Runner’s World, “Monitoring your heart rate while training can be a great tool to help you understand how hard your body is working. It’s notable for a balanced training program to have lots of easy recovery days where your heart rate is low, balanced by some harder intensity workouts where your heart rate is high.” Understanding and utilizing heart-rate zones—ranging from zone 1 (very light) to zone 5 (maximum effort)—can help you tailor your training for performance, endurance, and recovery.

In a recent development, while zone 2 running gets loads of buzz as the golden ticket for endurance building and recovery, Lombardi emphasizes that “all zones have their place in a training program.” She also notes an important caveat: “As an exercise physiologist I can understand the benefits of heart rate training but when I am coaching my athletes I do not have them follow heart rate based training to a T because your heart rate can vary so much day to day.” Lombardi lists how factors like heat, hydration, location, and medications can change your heart rate. “It is a great tool to have but I never have my athletes follow that 100 percent.”.

According to recent reports, this nuanced approach is critical—HRMs are invaluable tools, but their data should be viewed in context. Each athlete responds differently, and some exceptionally fit runners may see higher heart rates at lower intensity simply because their bodies have adapted to efficiently sustain greater workloads.

As a side note, these are largely HSA/FSA eligible, so you might not be out-of-pocket for the cost. Just check your eligibility, and keep those receipts.

Recent findings suggest that alyssa Lombardi is a certified personal trainer, run coach, and clinical exercise physiologist with more than six years of experience. A former collegiate runner with a master’s in exercise science, she coaches athletes of all levels through her business, Run Fit With Me. Lombardi emphasizes individualized training, injury prevention, and strength work, blending evidence-based science with real-world experience to help runners get faster, stay healthy, and achieve their goals.

The Polar H10 stands out as the best overall heart rate monitor for its unmatched accuracy and comfort. Its ECG technology delivers precise data, making it a favorite among serious athletes. The soft, non-slip strap comes in multiple sizes, but women should note it can be a tricky fit with some supportive sports bras—though it works comfortably under lower-line running tank bras. Men with chest hair have mentioned a slight pulling sensation, but most find it secure once adjusted. With long battery life, waterproofing up to 30 meters, dual Bluetooth connectivity, and onboard memory, it’s a reliable companion for any training style.

The Powr Labs Chest Heart Rate Monitor offers solid performance for a fraction of the price of premium brands, making it a great budget-friendly option. I found the strap to be comfortable and adjustable, though the sensor is a bit bulky. Its dual ANT+ and Bluetooth connectivity worked seamlessly with my Garmin and smartphone apps.

Industry observers note that while it’s water-resistant, I’d avoid prolonged swimming sessions. It tracks heart rate reliably across different workouts, from running to CrossFit. The strap fits well on me, but it might feel a bit tight or loose for some depending on body shape. Overall, it’s a dependable, no-frills monitor that gets the job done without breaking the bank, especially if this is your first foray into HR training.

Sources indicate that if you have a Forerunner 570 or above, you’ll know that some of the more advanced metrics like cadence and step speed loss require a heart rate monitor for measurement. This HRM is not only the best for that application but also one of the best we tested—period. It’s unbelievably comfy, it’s incredibly accurate, and it syncs seamlessly with whatever Garmin watch you use, and it’s not limited to only Garmin devices. You love your Apple Watch? Fab. Use it. You don’t run with a watch? First of all, how dare you. Second of all, it still works. You just need to link it to your phone instead. (You’re a rebel. I don’t get it, but I appreciate it.).

It has been revealed that I do wish that it came in more and extended sizes. And honestly, if you’re stacked through the lats and pecs, it might not work, which is unfortunately pretty much true for the majority of chest straps. But for the majority of runners, this is an economical, comfortable, feature-packed choice that gets you into Garmin’s system. Welcome to the cult.

It has been revealed that the Coros Heart Rate Monitor is my favorite pick when I want accurate tracking without the chest strap drama. The soft, stretchy fabric band hugs my upper arm comfortably—no digging, no slipping—and works well for a wide range of arm sizes. I barely feel it on long runs, and it never tangles with my tops. The optical sensor stays steady most of the time, though it can lag a bit on sudden sprints. It’s a bit more laggy than other HRMs I tested, by a few seconds. This is not a unique problem to Coros, but it is more noticeable here.

It has been revealed that battery life is solid at up to 38 hours, and Bluetooth syncing is quick, but the connection range isn’t amazing—you’ll want to keep your watch or phone fairly close. I’ve also noticed it can get a little itchy once I start sweating hard, so a quick postrun rinse is a must. Still, for comfort, simplicity, and ditching the chest strap, it’s a win in my book.

The Whoop Peak is a heckuva fun wearable device for deep health and fitness insights—tracking not just your heart rate, but also recovery, sleep quality, strain, and more. I love how all that data comes together to show me exactly when to push harder and when to rest. I am notorious for doing all the things, all at once, like training for a marathon while also working on a deadline for my book and keeping my demanding day job. This is great for my AuDHD brain, but can be hard on my body. The Whoop dials into that and lets me know I’ve been going too hard and my recovery metrics are showing that. The only real trade-off with this wearable? You have to look at your phone for every stat, since the band has no face or display.

According to recent reports, and while you do pay for a monthly membership to access the full suite of features, the first year is included, which makes it easier to justify. It doesn’t warn you as often as the Oura ring or a Garmin device about your habits, but features a lighter touch in the “you’re overdoing it” shame department.

Sources indicate that the Garmin HRM-Fit has totally changed how I think about heart rate straps. Instead of wrapping around my chest like the usual band (and fighting with my sports bra every run), it clips right onto the underband of a medium- or high-support bra. No chafing, no slipping—just accurate tracking that feels almost invisible once I get going.

It did take a minute to learn how to get the clips sitting just right, but now it’s second nature. My heart rate data is spot-on, and I love that it pairs instantly with my Garmin watch and other devices via Bluetooth or ANT+. The chunky clips do show under tight tops, so it’s not exactly stealthy, but the yearlong battery life makes up for it. For me, it’s comfort, accuracy, and freedom—all in one.

I am a massive fan of the upgrades on the Oura Ring 5. First of all, it’s a lot slimmer and lighter than previous models, and it also doesn’t scratch as easily. On top of that, the battery life is much improved. But what really matters is what the ring does.

It’s an accurate HRM that picks up activities easily, sometimes too easily, as it can occasionally register things like vacuuming as “dancing” or cleaning the bathroom as “HIIT.” Though that might speak more to the vigor with which I scrub the bathroom than any mistake of the ring itself.

Industry observers note that when I’m on my run, it tracks my heart rate, oxygen, and effort and gives me insights on where I can improve and what I can do to achieve that, and it’s easy to understand and well thought out. But what I really love is how it looks at my cycle, and helps me understand how that might be affecting my workouts. As it turns out, perimenopause is messing with my life hard-core, and now my previously unpredictable cycle has become even more unpredictable, and it’s making my runs around my period so much worse.

But there’s help in the app for that, as well. In the app, you can connect with health practitioners or link to your own healthcare provider, upload your labs, food diary, and more, and get advice based on your current goals and situation. I recently linked to my primary care doctor and my hematologist to determine just how my cycle, training, diet, and anemia were affecting each other, and we came up with a plan for treatment. To the infusion clinic I go! Before I had this ability, the process was a lot longer and a much bigger pain in the butt. Now, my doctors and I can make concrete plans far more easily, and it’s been a big blessing.

Accuracy is paramount for heart rate monitors. A reliable HRM provides consistent, precise heart rate readings during various activities, from cardio to strength training. Inaccurate readings can undermine workout effectiveness and hinder fitness progress, making you wonder if your heart is even trying.

Industry observers note that when it comes to heart rate tracking, it’s all about what feels right for you, especially when you’re really pushing it. Chest straps give you accurate readings but can be a bit annoying, while wrist monitors and rings are convenient but might glitch out during intense workouts. So, the real MVP here is whatever you’ll actually wear and trust for your grind—try ’em both if you can.

Industry observers note that say goodbye to connection woes. Thanks to Bluetooth and ANT+, gadgets play nice with all your beloved external devices and go-to fitness apps. Some even have the ability to send the readings right to your doctor.

No one likes a dead heart rate monitor in the middle of a workout, so think about how often you’ll need to swap out those batteries. Make sure you have a good stash of fresh ones on hand, or consider rechargeable options to keep the fun going. That way, your entertainment won’t be interrupted by a sudden power outage.

It has been revealed that A durable HRM needs to keep up with your lifestyle, whether you’re breaking a sweat or just enjoying a brisk walk. Chest bands are generally very durable, while smartwatches and wristbands offer good longevity but may be a bit more precious, and smart health tracking rings are designed for continuous wear and can withstand daily activities but may scratch.

In a recent development, running dynamics, on-device memory, and water resistance can enhance utility for diverse athletes. Additionally, some advanced watches and rings offer features like period and ovulation prediction, providing valuable health insights for users. These capabilities make them more than just fitness trackers, transforming them into comprehensive personal health companions.

According to recent reports, these can get pricey. Select a monitor that fits your budget and needs, and don’t forget that some, like the Whoop and Oura ring, have additional membership fees.

Sources indicate that many standard heart rate monitors—especially chest straps and armbands—pose real and annoying challenges for size inclusivity. Limited strap size ranges often make them too small for bigger runners and too large or bulky for petite athletes, affecting comfort, fit, and even accuracy.

It has been revealed that for women with large breasts who require more supportive bras, chest straps can be particularly tricky. Supportive or high-compression bras may push the strap down, create pressure points, or cause shifting, which can lead to discomfort, chafing, or inconsistent readings. When shopping for a heart rate monitor, it’s crucial to consider not only strap length and adjustability but also how well the design works with your body type and workout apparel to ensure both comfort and reliable data.

How accurate are wrist-based HRMs compared to chest straps?Wrist-based optical sensors are good these days—accurate enough for most people—but chest straps still win during activities with sudden heart rate spikes or lots of wrist movement.

In a recent development, do I need a subscription for my HRM?Most HRMs don’t require one, but some, like Whoop or Oura, do charge a monthly membership for access to their full analytics and insights. That subscription cost is worth factoring into your budget.

Can heart rate monitors detect health issues?HRMs aren’t medical devices, but trends in your heart rate, recovery, or heart rhythm can signal changes worth discussing with your healthcare provider. Some devices, like the Apple Watch, even have FDA-cleared ECG apps to record heart rhythm data.

#22014. Herniated Discs Are a Common Cycling Injury—Here’s Everything You Need to Know

📅 03 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2315 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Bicycling ↗ Open Full Page

Herniated Discs Are a Common Cycling Injury—Here’s Everything You Need to Know

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2315 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, sometimes it happens with a bang, like when former Tour de France pro Marty Jemison was racing Tour of Flanders in the late 1990s.
  • Recent findings suggest that jemison finished the race and the others that followed until he retired about 18 months later, though he had pain off the bike and for the first 30 or 60 minutes of riding, and knew something was wrong.
  • Industry observers note that other times, it’s the proverbial straw that breaks the camel’s (or the cyclist’s) back, as was the case with avid long-distance cyclist Mark Elsasser of Philadelphia who developed some sciatica in 2018.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, sometimes it happens with a bang, like when former Tour de France pro Marty Jemison was racing Tour of Flanders in the late 1990s. His saddle slipped to be nose up. He thought “no big deal” until one of the steep cobbled climbs, where he was in the saddle cranking out maximum wattage.“And my back just popped,” he says.

Recent findings suggest that jemison finished the race and the others that followed until he retired about 18 months later, though he had pain off the bike and for the first 30 or 60 minutes of riding, and knew something was wrong. That something was a herniated disc that became nearly debilitating after retirement, eventually required two procedures, and still flares up to this day if he’s not meticulous about his bike position and on top of his core work.

Industry observers note that other times, it’s the proverbial straw that breaks the camel’s (or the cyclist’s) back, as was the case with avid long-distance cyclist Mark Elsasser of Philadelphia who developed some sciatica in 2018. He was able to ride through it just fine, but couldn’t sit for any length of time before the pain was unbearable. The diagnosis: a herniated disc in his low back, which he resolved with physical therapy and has kept at bay by changing his position on the bike, going from a 0-rise to 5-degree stem. “My spine is less compromised being a bit more upright rather than nose down on top of the stem,” he states.

It has been revealed that herniated discs are fairly common in the general population, occurring most frequently among 30- to 50-year-old adults, and men more often than women. Interestingly, you may have one right now and not even know it. “We know from radiographical studies that 50 percent of those aged 40 may have some form of disc herniation. We might consider it normal, age-related changes, and many of those won’t be symptomatic,” says bike fitter and sports physiotherapist Bianca Broadbent, co-owner of The Cycling Physios based in the United Kingdom.

In fact, one research review published in the American Journal of Neuroradiology found that degenerative changes in the discs, which include herniated discs, are present in nearly 90 percent of adults 60 and older and often require no intervention. A herniated disc only causes pain if it’s pressing or otherwise irritating a nerve root in the spine.

Join Bicycling All Access for more injury-prevention tips and training advice!

Your spine is comprised of 24 vertebrae. Between those vertebrae are fluid-filled cushions known as discs, which act as shock absorbers for your spinal bones.

“Imagine your spinal discs as jelly-filled doughnuts,” states Andrew Pruitt, Ed.D., the founder of the Boulder Center for Sports Medicine and CU Sports Medicine and Performance Center. “A herniation happens when the jelly inside pops out.”.

Recent findings suggest that you may hear people using other terms like “bulging disc,” “ruptured disc,” or “slipped disc.” Technically, a bulging disc is just that: It’s when the jelly inside the donut is pushing against the side enough to bulge out from the vertebrae but isn’t leaking out. A ruptured or slipped disc refers to an actual herniation, where the doughnut cracks, allowing the gel-filled center to squeeze out.

A bulging and/or herniated disc can cause pain by creating pressure on the nearby nerves. There’s some evidence that the leaked fluid from herniated discs also can cause chemical irritation and inflammation of the spinal nerve roots.

Again, it’s possible to have an asymptomatic herniated disc where you feel no pain. When you do have pain from a herniated disc, however, you’ll know it.

Pain from the herniated discs is sharp and radiating. Most cyclists experience herniated discs in the lower, lumbar back (we’ll get to why in a bit). So you may feel burning pain often known as sciatica that radiates from your lower back into your glutes and down one or both legs, sometimes even into your feet. You may feel pain similar to an electric shock when you stand or sit or walk. You may also feel radiating numbness, tingling, and/or weakness in your lower extremities.

So how does the jelly get out of the doughnut and start wreaking havoc on your spinal nerves? In a word: pressure. It can be extreme and sudden, like Jemison cranking on the cobbles. Or, in many instances, it can happen gradually over time, as was the case with Elsasser.

When your spine is in its generally straight, neutral position, the pressure from the top down is uniform on your discs, so the jelly inside those cushions is evenly distributed, Pruitt explains.

“When you bend forward, the jelly is pushed back, stressing the skin of that doughnut,” he says. “If you’re sitting all day, that jelly is pressing back there for eight hours. Now jump on a bike, and you add another two hours in an even more extreme position, pressing that jelly further and further, until—pop—it comes out.”.

Though herniation can happen anywhere in the spine, in cyclists it happens most frequently in the lumbar (low back) region close to the base of the spine, or the L5-S1, the bottom-most disc that sits right on top of your tailbone, because that’s where we bend the most, says Menachem Brodie, C.S.C.S., head coach at Human Vortex Training and USA Cycling expert coach.

It has been revealed that “For many cyclists, the L5-S1 is where they’re getting their flexion, and the lumbar spine has about six degrees of movement,” Brodie says. So if you’re not hinging from the hips and keeping your spine within its safe, natural range, you’re pushing those limits. Keeping your spine under that kind of stress for prolonged periods of time pushes you closer to the failure point.

Along those lines, research indicates that riders with a lower handlebar position and greater flexion in that key lower back region were more likely to have low back pain. Though, importantly, the research also suggests that poor core strength and endurance could contribute to the spinal stress and low back pain in cyclists.

Of course, the bike isn’t the only place you can stress your spine. The gym can be another place riders put their spine under unhealthy stress, states Dane DeLozier, D.P.T., the biomechanics lab director at and co-founder of Revo Physiotherapy and Sports Performance. Maintaining a stable, neutral spine is very crucial when resistance training, especially when doing substantial lifts like deadlifts and squats as well as under velocity like with kettlebell swings, DeLozier says.

“When you have your spine under load, you want it to be neutral and very stabilized. You want to be hinging through your hips, not bending and extending your spine under load,” he says.

If you’re unsure of if you’re maintaining a neutral spine, DeLozier recommends setting up your phone and recording yourself (or having a friend video record you) so you can see if you are breaking or flexing under load.

The good news is a 2020 scientific paper, “Slipped disc: Overview,” reports that about 90 percent of people will get relief from their pain and restricted movement within six weeks even if they receive no medical treatment. That’s because the body gets rid of part of the prolapsed tissue or it shifts position so that the nerves aren’t irritated anymore, according to the overview.

According to recent reports, you can help that process along with physical therapy, DeLozier claims. “The vast majority of folks feel better and have a great outcome by doing mobility exercises for the hip and low back and decompression exercises for the spine.”.

The exercises you do depends on your individual situation, but your physical therapist may recommend mobility, stability, and core strengthening exercises such as:.

Press Up: Lie facedown with your feet together, toes pointed, and your forearms on the floor palms. Pull your shoulder blades down and in towards your spine and press into forearms to lift your chest off of the floor, keeping your neck long and hips on the floor. If mobility allows, you can press up further by placing hands below your shoulders to come into an up-dog position. Hold for 3 to 5 seconds. Repeat about 15 times.

Recent findings suggest that hip Flexor Stretch: Kneel with the affected knee on the floor, tighten your glutes, and brace your abdominal muscles while keeping your back straight. Pressing hips forward. Hold this stretch for 30 seconds. Do 3 times.

Bird Dog: Get on your hands and knees with your palms flat on the floor, shoulder-width apart. Slowly raise and straighten your right leg and left arm at the same time. Keep your hips aligned with the torso and not tilted to one side. Hold for 10 seconds. Return to start. Repeat on the other side.

It has been revealed that cycling itself, when done with a healthy riding posture, can also be a great rehab tool to strengthen the discs and surrounding structures, Broadbent says. In fact, a study done on high-volume road cyclists who rode nearly 100 miles a week for five or more years had beneficial adaptations to their discs and psoas (the biggest hip flexor muscle), which were beneficial for spinal health.

If you’re riding through your rehab, Brodie recommends “crocodile breathing” when you get off the bike. To do it, lie facedown with your forehead resting on the back of your hands and let your chest and hips sink into the floor. Inhale deeply into your belly, expanding your diaphragm for four slow counts. Pause for two seconds, then exhale for six slow counts.

Finally, while many herniated discs can be treated conservatively with physical therapy, some require injection therapy like nerve blocks, if the symptoms are severe, Broadbent notes. In rare cases, spinal disc herniation can cause extreme pressure and swelling of the nerves at the end of the spinal cord causing a medical emergency known as cauda equina syndrome.

“If your bladder and bowels aren’t working properly, you have saddle numbness (off the bike as well), or you have sexual dysfunction such as unable to get an erection then you should seek urgent medical investigation,” Broadbent says.

Again, cycling can actually improve spinal strength and the health and hydration of your discs, claims Broadbent.

According to recent reports, having a good bike position and the right saddle is key. “You want your spine in a healthy position that doesn’t strain those discs in your lower back,” Pruitt indicates. If you ride a gravel or a mountain bike, you’re likely already in a slightly more upright, more neutral spine position, he says.

According to recent reports, an anatomical saddle will also allow you to put your weight on your perineum without putting harmful pressure on those sensitive tissues, so you’re able to reach the bars without bending too far and putting your spine in an unhealthy position. “Saddle technology improvements have really helped reduce degenerative disc disease,” he says.

Industry observers note that you also can protect your spine by doing core-strengthening exercises several times a week. Brodie recommends what are known as the “massive three” exercises for spinal stability, developed by renowned back pain expert, Stuart McGill, Ph.D., Professor Emeritus of Spine Biomechanics at the University of Waterloo. These exercises stiffen the musculature throughout the core in a way that enhances stability in the spine.

How to do these exercises: The American Council of Exercise recommends performing three sets for each using a reverse pyramid rep/set scheme. Start with a higher number of repetitions for the first set, then decrease by 2 to 6 reps, then decrease by another 2 to 4 reps on the last set. So you might start with 8-6-4 reps and work your way up to 12-10-8 reps as you get stronger and build endurance. Hold each exercise for no more than 8 to 10 seconds.

Sources indicate that mcGill Curl-up: Lie on your back with one leg extended and the other leg bent, foot flat on the floor. Put your hands under your low back to maintain your natural arch. In one move, lift your head, shoulders, and chest off the floor, keeping your neck and back in the neutral position. Hold. Then slowly return to start. Do half a set. Then switch legs and complete the set.

Sources indicate that side Bridge: Lie on your right side, with your forearm on the floor and elbow underneath your shoulder. Bend your knees at a 90-degree angle. Place your left hand on the opposite shoulder for stability. Lift your hips off the floor so your body forms a straight line from your head to your knees. Hold. Then lower to the starting position and repeat to the other side. Work up to doing the move with your legs straight.

The Bird Dog: (As explained in the previous section).

You can make these exercises part of your warm-up, along with dynamic mobility moves before you get into your bigger lifts.

Off the bike, Brodie recommends practicing good spine hygiene by avoiding hunching forward when you sit and not sitting in a static position for prolonged periods of time, but rather shifting positions in your chair every 15 minutes and getting up, moving around, and doing a little standing stretch, extending your arms, reaching overhead and taking a deep breath every 60 to 90 minutes.

In a recent development, finally, don’t overlook your mattress. A firm mattress with a pillow top will help support your spine while you sleep, Brodie notes. “A lot of people overlook this and it can make a major difference in your back health.”.

#22013. Breaking: Inspired by Fall Marathon Season? Here’s What You Need to Do to Prepare for 26.2

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1174 w)
