📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Sources indicate that as a cyclist for over three decades, I’ve crashed many times.
  • Sources indicate that when shopping for fresh road and gravel helmets, cyclists often base their choices almost entirely on looks, price, and overall comfort.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Sources indicate that as a cyclist for over three decades, I’ve crashed many times. Unfortunately, I’ve also had a few concussions. Because of this, safety is key to me when I choose a new helmet. Over the last few seasons, I’ve tested dozens of great helmets, from budget picks under $50 to go-fast aero lids and lightweight models for over $500. Plus, I also test trail helmets, commuter lids, and everything in between.

Sources indicate that when shopping for fresh road and gravel helmets, cyclists often base their choices almost entirely on looks, price, and overall comfort. Depending on our riding goals and budget, we also balance weight, aerodynamics, and style. We want safety features, but many riders assume most helmets do a decent job of protecting our noggin—they’re all certified, right?

Sources indicate that helmet safety isn’t as straightforward as it may seem. Current Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) standards—as well as more rigorous, voluntary requirements, such as those from ASTM—account for straight-line impacts and G-forces from a collision. These standards don’t address the rotational forces from a crash that contribute significantly to concussions and traumatic brain injuries. Plus, the CPSC’s standards took effect on March 10, 1999—advancements in technology, design, materials, and manufacturing over the last 27 years have changed bike helmets.

So, what standards and certifications cover rotational forces? Currently, none. To better protect against rotational forces and reduce concussions, many brands incorporate Mips liners (and similar anti-rotational designs) into their helmets. Brands also test their helmets internally to their own, generally unpublished, criteria. The Virginia Tech helmet lab’s STAR score provides the best independent testing and ranking for helmets across most cycling disciplines.

Industry observers note that virginia Tech tests helmets for safety; it doesn’t evaluate fit, comfort, weight, price, or overall practicality. Bicycling’s test team collectively rides tens of thousands of miles each year on tarmac, gravel roads, singletrack, and commuting. That means we have a lot of time to ride-test lids—including more than half of Virginia Tech’s 5-STAR-rated road helmets.

For 15 years, Virginia Tech has tested helmets through a battery of 24 impact tests that analyse safety performance and assign an overall STAR (Summation of Tests for the Analysis of Risk) score.

“The overall score estimates the number of concussions the average person would see if they experienced identical impacts at rates matching their weightings while cycling,” says Virginia Tech’s lab. The lower the STAR score, the better a helmet performed in testing.

Then, to each helmet it tests, Virginia Tech awards an overall STAR rating (one through five); helmets with four- and five-STARs are “recommended.” The lab does not recommend helmets scoring three STARs or fewer.

Virginia Tech has tested and published results on more than 300 bicycle helmets. To date, the lab has awarded 56 helmets its coveted 5-STAR rating, and another 104 received 4 STARs. To make researching and choosing a new helmet easier, it also sorts the helmets it tests into mountain, road, urban, multi-sport, full-face, and E-bike categories. Of the 5-STAR helmets, 21 of them are road lids.

Industry observers note that editor’s Note: These helmets are the top 5-rated road bike helmets in Virginia Tech’s bicycle helmet rankings as of November 9, 2026. The Virginia Tech helmet lab regularly tests helmets and updates the overall rankings; the top 5 can change at any time. Please consult Virginia Tech’s bicycle helmet ranking list for up-to-date rankings.

“Who is Pikio?” and “What is a Si Oblik?” Those were the questions our editors all asked when we saw this helmet rocket to the top of Virginia Tech’s STAR ratings. The Pikio isn’t only the top-rated road helmet; it’s also Virginia Tech’s best-performing helmet, period. It beats the others by a considerable margin, logging an unbelievably low 4.61 STAR score. For context, the difference between the Pikio and the second-place overall Canyon Deflectr RLS mountain bike helmet is 2.21 points; that’s the same gap between the 2nd and 28th positions in current rankings.

It has been revealed that all of that safety comes at a relatively steep $379 cost. While the Si Oblik’s price aligns with other range-topping helmets from Giro, POC, Specialized, and MET, Pikio’s looks and finish feel comparable to mid-tier models from more well-known brands. For example, Pikio’s color options are somewhat conservative choices, and the rear strap anchor point is through-shell.

It has been revealed that the Si Oblik fits well and has a broad range of adjustment for my medium-sized head. The rear adjusts up and down (to account for head shape and hairstyles) and features a dial to microadjust fit. The straps, however, are not as cleanly executed as expected for the price, especially compared to POC or Specialized, and I found them slightly tedious to adjust. On road and gravel rides, the Si Oblik’s airflow doesn’t feel bad, but I didn’t test this lid in peak summer heat. And while the Pikio weighs about the same as Giro and MET helmets in this test, it feels physically bigger, though not as mushroomy as the POC Cytal.

Recent findings suggest that for a new brand, Pikio Labs made a solid first effort. Unlike its competitors, Pikio doesn’t have decades of trial and error or a flashy WorldTour team. Hopefully, as the firm grows, it can dial in details, sharpen pricing, and spice up the aesthetic, because the Si Oblik already sets a very high bar for safety.

The POC Cytal’s unique shape and bold look make it easy to spot in a peloton. Another reason the Cytal stands out is due to its overall size—it’s a physically massive lid. But despite its dimensions and slightly heavy weight, it doesn’t feel that large on your head while riding and ventilates surprisingly well.

The Cytal’s great ventilation comes from its massive vents and internal air channels that funnel air directly over your forehead while riding. I found out how well it vents while riding over the summer in France during “la canicule” (the heatwave). I could still feel the Cytal pushing air in 100-degree temps, even if it was roasting hot.

Sources indicate that in our recent review of P2R’s $100 aero-helmet, ride tester Tom Messina said it “has no business being this good.” And with its lower price and STAR score, we say the same thing about P2R’s $60 A20 Mips. With its excellent safety rating, great adjustability, and budget-friendly price, the A20 Mips outperforms many helmets that cost three, four, or even five times its price.

Sources indicate that P2R somehow hits the A20’s low price without cutting corners on features. It has nice straps with adjustable quick clamps that offer plenty of adjustment. P2R also includes a USB-rechargeable light that magnetically clips into the rear vent for commuting or extra visibility on the road.

Industry observers note that the one downside we found with the A20 Mips is that it feels optimized for rounder head shapes. While it fits me well, a couple of others who tried it on said it was a little snug near their temples.

Industry observers note that given the Trenta 3K Carbon’s pedigree, it’s hard not to name it “Best for Racing.” UAE Team Emirates’ official sponsor is MET, and the Trenta is one of the helmets it supplies to the squad—including Tour de France champion Tadej Pogačar and World Champion Brandon McNulty. While UAE riders often race the Italian brand’s Manta aero helmet, they sometimes pick the lightweight, well-ventilated Trenta 3K Carbon for climbing stages and training.

Industry observers note that unlike some modern helmets with similarly strong protection, the Trenta feels light and racey on your head, and almost disappears when you’re riding. The straps offer good adjustability, and the Mips Air Node liner protects without feeling bulky. However, the Trenta’s biggest drawback is its price tag. At over $500, this is an expensive piece of kit.

Ranked 14th overall and 5th in road helmets, Giro’s Aries Spherical stands out in our testing for its overall comfort, adjustability, low weight, and great looks. While its STAR score is much higher than the first-place Pikio, the Aries is a very safe helmet and received Virginia Tech’s 5-STAR rating. Having crashed on the road while wearing an Aries Spherical, I also know this helmet works.

Industry observers note that of the approximately one dozen road and gravel helmets in my rotation at any given time, I reach for the Aries Spherical most often. The Aries fits my head perfectly, and the Roc Loc dial system offers plenty of adjustability for hair length or if I’m wearing a cap underneath in rain or cold weather. Giro makes the Aries in a wide range of colors and graphics to fit almost any rider’s personality or fashion.

It has been revealed that as Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and Upcoming England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

In a recent development, we earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Editor’s Note, November 11, 2026: The long-awaited Alphafly 4 is out now—and selling out fast. You can find more options at sites like Fleet Feet.

Brownie points if you knew the waffle iron and Swoosh go a long way back. It was the early 1960s when University of Oregon track coach Bill Bowerman cofounded Blue Ribbon Sports (BRS) with one of his runners, Phil Knight. BRS was a proprietor of Onitsuka Tiger’s athletic shoes before manufacturing its own product. Depending on who you believe, Bowerman customized running shoes using a waffle iron either in the early 1960s, when he gave pairs to his athletes to compete in, or in 1971, the same year BRS was renamed Nike, after the Greek goddess of victory. And that’s how legends are born (and shoe awards are given).

Sources indicate that you can read Knight’s side of the story by reading Shoe Dog, or watch Prefontaine or Without Limits for a more dramatic tale about one of the University of Oregon’s star athletes with Nike’s origin story in the background (the 1997 movie is the superior of the two, IMHO). Since the dawn of the Swoosh, the brand has rocked the running industry boat with its innovations. In the past 10 years, for instance, the Vaporfly 4% appeared on the scene, creating mass ripples of fresh World Athletics guidelines, academic studies on super shoes and running economy, and world records such as the late Kelvin Kiptum’s superhuman 2:00:35 at the 2023 Chicago Marathon.

Back in my early days at Runner’s World in 2018, the first Nike shoe I tested—and ran in—was the inimitable Vaporfly. The shoe left an impression, causing me to never turn back from racing marathons in carbon-fiber-plated trainers. But one thing that made me move on to other brands’ super shoe iterations was the narrow fit and unstable ride of Nike’s racers. All the more to show the brand’s ever-continuing evolution into being the best as well as more inclusive.

Battle of the Brands: The Best Brooks Running Shoes ● The Best Adidas Running Shoes ● The Best Mizuno Running Shoes.

Sources indicate that I’ve run and raced in several of the shoes on this list. As a Nike newb when I was hired at RW, I was schooled in the Swoosh’s indelible influence on the running industry—our magazine’s first matter came out six years after Nike’s renaming—and witnessed the dawn of the super shoe. All of the shoes on this list were tested by members of our 300-and-counting test team of local runners. They come from all walks of life, varying by gait pattern, arch height, and footstrike.

The Vomero 18 is the first Nike shoe I ran in that didn’t initially feel like a Nike trainer. The shoes fit wide. Its midfoot is broader than the narrow lasts I associate with the Swoosh. Running in the Vomero 18 for the first time, I noticed two things: this shoe is über-soft and doesn’t cause my ankles to turn inward.

It has been revealed that this Vomero is the starting point of the brand’s other cushioned shoes, which also include this list’s Vomero Plus and soon-to-be-released Vomero Premium. The story behind this new fit is that Nike shoe development listened to women, applying their fit preferences to both the women’s and men’s versions. Turns out men like the new last too, according to a Nike rep I spoke with recently on the phone.

The Vomero 18 serves as a long-run trainer, daily trainer, and recovery shoe. The cushioning reminds me of Brooks’s Glycerin Max; it’s marshmallowy but responsive. The energy return is still there instead of being zapped like a sponge turning your runs into a slog.

Industry observers note that “Hands down these are the best shoes I’ve tested!” noted shoe tester Casey Green, a 7:00 pacer who previously tested the Pegasus Plus. “Despite all the extra cushioning the ride was incredibly smooth, responsive, and the shoe never felt weighed down despite the added padding. Every mile I ran in them felt great and slight accelerations or faster average paces were no problem.”.

Shop Men’s at nike.com | Shop Women’s at nike.com.

Sources indicate that the Winflo has always been a solid pick for beginners and high school runners. The price is an absolute steal well below the now-standard $170. But the shoe doesn’t feel cheap. Its plush cushioning, which Nike revved up with the twelfth iteration by adding even more Cushlon 3.0 foam underfoot, is fantastic for base building, long runs, or those jobs that require hours of standing.

It has been revealed that A small knock is that Nike fit. Unlike the updated Vomero 18 and Structure 26, the Winflo 12 still has that classic Nike foot shape that’s too narrow for some. Sizing up will help alleviate the constriction. It’s worth it for the price and bouncy ride.

Shop Men’s nike.com | Shop Women’s nike.com.

Sources indicate that the Structure 26 has a few key updates that make it the stability shoe you shouldn’t sleep on. It’s me: I’m the one who slept on it. This is because Nike isn’t at the forefront of my mind when I recommend stability trainers. Lesson learned: the Structure 26 isn’t a shoe to forget. It provides reliable but subtle support for overpronators and neutral runners looking for more guidance, as well as a responsive ride. And it’s relatively cheap for a premium trainer.

In a recent development, the shoe now has ReactX foam, the same foam in the Pegasus 41 and Vomero 18. The foam delivers more rebound compared to the Structure 25’s Cushlon 3.0. An internal midfoot fit band—the triangular structure you can see on either side of the shoe—along with overlays brushed on the sides provide support. The Air Zoom bag was removed in the forefoot and replaced with blown rubber on the outsole to encourage smoother heel-toe transitions. Finally, the upper is cozier too. Nike padded up the collar and tongue for more cushioned touch points and a more secure fit.

Sources indicate that testers liked the shoe for its versatility and used it as their daily trainer for all kinds of workouts. “The shoe is an absolute do-it-all workhorse,” noted tester Justin Brown. “I wore it for easy runs, and even progressed up to tempo paces and used it for some strides where I was close to sprinting and I feel like the shoe stood up to all of these really well. At the same time the stability nature of the shoe was honestly nailed, and I felt very secure in the shoe at all times even on wet pavement. The ride was smooth and felt cushioned, but there was enough energy return that I didn’t feel like I couldn’t go faster in it.”.

In a recent development, tester Rich Maier also highlighted the shoe’s support. “I was really impressed by the stability that I felt in both my feet and my legs,” he noted. “I usually only experience that level of comfort and support with heavier shoes, but these managed to combine stability with a lighter weight shoe.”.

Shop Men’s at nike.com | Shop Women’s at nike.com.

Even though the ACG Peg Trail isn’t intended for technical trails—that’s what the ACG Zegama Trail is for—our testers still praised the shoe for its capabilities on the unbeaten path.

Recent findings suggest that “What I liked most about the shoe was its low-profile design that really hugged your foot on all the twists and turns out on the trail,” stated tester Jeff Kilian. “Traction was exceptional as well. I feel this shoe is in a league all of its own. I would say the closest thing I can compare this Pegasus to is the Altra Timp, they’re both a lightweight shoe with not much cushioning in the sole.”.

The lack of cushioning was a low point for some testers who wanted more support in the forefoot.

Despite the desire for more cushioning, they did appreciate the wider fit in the forefoot and toebox, which helped with stability on the trail.

Industry observers note that “The fit has vastly improved,” said shoe tester Jessica Huber. “The width is perfect. There is plenty of space in the toes without feeling bulky.”.

Shop Men’s at nike.com | Shop Women’s at nike.com.

Recent findings suggest that the Nike shoe team wanted to make sure the next Pegasus was snappier and springier than the 41. The team added a full-length Air Zoom unit in the midsole, instead of separate units in previous models. This provides better compression throughout the shoe and improved energy return.

“What I like most is that it feels smooth, with a great rolling ride, but also supportive underfoot,” stated tester Molly Sunderlin. “It feels easy to run promptly in, but also like I can do a two-hour long run without getting sore underfoot. I am not sure if this has to do with the shape of the heel which has sort of a ‘roll’ feature. It also wraps my foot so well, almost sock-like with cushion in the right spots. I like putting them on.”.

Industry observers note that sunderlin is referring to the slightly curved toe of the shoe, which encourages smooth turnover. The shoe has a slightly modified foot shape to create a more accommodating fit in the midfoot and toe area. Still too tight for you? Not to worry; the Pegasus 42 is also available in extra wide.

Shop Men’s at nike.com | Shop Women’s at nike.com.

Industry observers note that if you miss the Peg Turbo, get a load of the Peg Plus. The second iteration of the shoe is speedier and snappier thanks to an exposed Air unit, which we know signals “fast” in a Nike shoe. The unit functions as a carbon plate; it provides propulsion by compressing during forefoot impact. Its exposure gives it room to breathe; Nike reports this Peg Plus has 18 percent more energy return than the previous version.

Nike wanted to make sure this sensation was consistent with all sizes. The bigger the shoe size, the bigger the Air unit. Runner-in-Chief Jeff Dengate liked the high rebound, but noted the shoe felt slightly heavy compared to other trainers in the speed category.

Recent findings suggest that “That Air unit pushes back against you quickly, letting you feel snappy with your stride,” wrote Dengate in his review. “Sure, it’s heavy, but in that instance it doesn’t feel slow.”.

Shop Men’s at nike.com | Shop Women’s at nike.com.

In a recent development, nike’s mission with the Structure Plus was to change our perception of the stability trainer. Instead of a rigid, firm shoe, the brand wanted to make stability more palatable for all. The Structure Plus is lighter than its cousin, the Structure 26, and is more dynamic; instead of a full ReactX midsole, the Plus is dual-foamed with ReactX on the bottom and soft, energetic ZoomX PEBA foam on the top.

All this is housed in a 42mm stack height, which is 4mm taller than the Structure 26. Such a tall height would cause some to doubt the shoe’s support, but Nike widened the platform and implemented a convex flat sidewall with dense cushioning underneath the arch. The result: support for overpronators and neutral runners who want a little more pep in their stability trainer.

It has been revealed that “What I liked most about the Nike Structure Plus was the strong sense of support it delivered on every run,” mentioned tester Julian Caiazzo, an overpronator who averages 7:45 training pace. “The shoe felt stable and dependable without ever coming across as stiff or restrictive. It gave me the confidence to settle into my stride, and even with all that structure, the ride still felt smooth and enjoyable. It struck a great balance between guidance and comfort, which is exactly what I look for in a daily trainer.”.

According to recent reports, I wore the Structure Plus on a couple of long runs, including my 20-miler during my marathon buildup. Unlike the Vomero Plus, which had my feet roll inward on an 18-miler, the Structure Plus kept my form stable despite the growing fatigue in my weary, long-run legs.

Alternatively, runners who want a more grounded feel—and want to save—can opt for the Structure 26 ($145).

Shop Men’s at nike.com | Shop Women’s at nike.com.

This super trainer has next-level softness, from its thick—but breathable—cozy upper to its 43mm (heel) of plush, responsive foam underfoot. Its older sibling, the Vomero 18, has a dual-foam midsole with a top layer of ZoomX and bottom layer of ReactX. With the Vomero Plus, Nike went full PEBA, with the midsole using 100 percent ZoomX.

Recent findings suggest that the shoe is lighter than the Vomero 18 and a smidge shorter (the heel on the Vomero 18 hits 44mm), but I honestly couldn’t detect a major difference in the ride. The Vomero Plus is bouncier, yet if you want to save $25, you could stick with the Vomero 18 (your legs will be none the wiser). But if you want to experience the powers of PEBA and can drop some extra cash, just listen to our testers who gave the Vomero Plus top marks. Our very own editorial assistant Michael McDonough will convince you that of the two Vomeros the Plus is the superior.

Sources indicate that “The Nike Vomero Plus is one of, if not my favorite shoe that I’ve tested so far,” noted McDonough. “The shoe lives up to the ‘plus’ in its name—I tested the Vomero 18s over the winter, and while I thought those were great as well, the Vomero Plus is an upgrade in several ways. Although they have the exact same amount of cushion, the switch from a mix of ReactX and ZoomX foam to purely ZoomX foam is an absolute game changer. The shoes feel lighter, cushier, and faster—and the fact that the shoe was able to improve all three factors at the same time was pretty remarkable.”.

Shop Men’s at nike.com | Shop Women’s at nike.com.

How do you update a shoe that broke the marathon world record back in 2023? The Nike team kept the substantial changes we loved from the Alphafly 3 and transferred them into the Alphafly 4—with minor tweaks. The scooped, spoon-shaped carbon plate is slightly wider to provide more stability. The thin, almost see-through knit upper, Atomknit 2.0, is similar to the previous version’s with the exception of vertical banding to provide a more secure fit in the midfoot area.

In a recent development, the biggest change is in the forefoot. The Air unit is softer and lighter. In his testing, Dengate noted how the unit visibly squishes when you push down. This gives the shoe pop and makes the heel-toe transition smoother as it works with the rocker profile.

Is it quieter than past Alphaflys? According to Dengate... quieter. But comparatively louder than other super shoes he’s tested, and squeaky too. We’ll find out more once tester feedback comes in.

Shop Men’s at fleetfeet.com | Shop Women’s at nike.com.

Industry observers note that nike’s All Conditions Gear (ACG) has been around since 1989. This year, the brand introduced a upcoming era of trail shoes under the ACG name. One of them is the ACG Zegama Trail, a shoe meant for tough all-terrain.

The shoe’s exterior makes it look unquestionably built for technical terrain. The ACG Zegama Trail has a durable cool mesh upper and an ankle cuff that functions as a gaiter, keeping debris out of your shoes. It was a favorite feature for our tester, Chris Fisher, who tested the ACG Zegama Trail last winter.

“Best thing about the Nike Zegama’s was getting into them,” he said. “They’ve got a modified gaiter collar design with a more traditional tongue that allows for easily slipping your feet in. The stretch collar does well at keeping debris out of the shoe which was nice with all the snow I was running in.”.

A secure lacing system helps with stability on uneven, twisty trails, as does a broader base. The shoe has a wide forefoot and toebox to allow your toes to splay and lend support.

Shop Men’s at nike.com | Shop Women’s at nike.com.

To help runners pick and choose the soft ride they’re looking for, Nike has reworked its cushioning into three main categories:.

Responsive Cushioning: Pegasus line, providing energy return for all-day wear.

Maximum Cushioning: Vomero line, offering ultimate plush comfort for longer runs.

Supportive Cushioning: Structure line, designed for stability and a supportive ride.

Cushlon: A descendent of Phylon foam, Cushlon is a proprietary EVA foam. It’s lighter than standard EVA midsoles, and provides support and springiness underfoot.

ReactX: Created using an injection process, this foam has more rebound than React foam.

ZoomX: Nike lightest and bounciest foam, it is primarily composed of PEBA.

According to recent reports, working in tandem with midsole foam, Zoom Air units are pouches on the shoe filled with air that help with propulsion. Upon landing, the units compress and absorb impact, then spring back to their original shape.

Should I race in the Alphafly or Vaporfly?

According to recent reports, nike’s premium marathon racing shoe is the Alphafly. It has all the bells and whistles, including PEBA, a Flyplate, and Zoom Air units. This means it’s made to withstand that high-mileage. While the Vaporfly can also be your shoe of choice for marathoning, it’s leaner, Zoom Air unit-free, and is built for racing distances as short as the mile.

Are Nike’s shoes women-specific?

During Vomero 18 development, the brand used women’s feedback to create “a better shoe for everyone.” Using these findings, the Nike team applied this to both the women’s and men’s models. According to a Nike rep RW spoke with, turns out men liked the adjustments inferred from women’s feedback too.

Industry observers note that amanda Furrer, Editor, Running Reviews, studied journalism at NYU and writing at Emerson College. She has reviewed gear and covered other topics in the running space for almost 10 years. Since 2013, she has consecutively run the Boston Marathon. She also has a master’s degree in gastronomy from Boston University and was formerly a professional baker for two years before hanging up her apron.

#21979. Is Your Cycling Computer Lying to You?

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1310 w)

Is Your Cycling Computer Lying to You?

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1310 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, spend enough time comparing power meters, and you’ll quickly learn that they don’t always agree.
  • According to recent reports, if you use a power meter for training, what matters most is that the numbers you’re seeing today are comparable to the ones you saw last week or last month.
  • According to recent reports, but what if your power meter isn’t the only thing affecting those numbers?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, spend enough time comparing power meters, and you’ll quickly learn that they don’t always agree. Put a power meter on your crank and another on your pedals, and the numbers may not match exactly. That can be frustrating when you’re trying to figure out which one is right, but for most riders, a small, consistent difference isn’t necessarily a problem.

According to recent reports, if you use a power meter for training, what matters most is that the numbers you’re seeing today are comparable to the ones you saw last week or last month. Whether your threshold is actually 250 watts or 255 watts matters less than knowing that an interval at that power represents the same effort from one ride to the next.

According to recent reports, but what if your power meter isn’t the only thing affecting those numbers? What if the bike computer recording your ride is changing the data before you ever upload it to Strava or TrainingPeaks?

Sources indicate that I recently noticed something odd while testing a cycling computer. At first, I was doing this to compare GPS track accuracy, but since I was testing, I also paired all the devices to my heart rate strap and Quarq power meter. When I compared the ride files afterward, what stood out was that their power numbers didn’t match. Initially, the differences were small enough. But when I looked more closely, I noticed it immediately. Every time I stopped pedaling, one computer still recorded power.

Before I get into what the heck sticky watts are, I should say I first learned about the issue in 2025 when I saw a video from Shane Miller, who goes by GPLama on YouTube. The video is called “Power Meter Data Recording: The Wild West?”, and it’s worth watching. Shane was the first person I saw digging into this particular recording issue with cycling computers.

So what the heck is it? Sticky watts happen when a cycling computer keeps recording a power value for a few seconds after you’ve stopped pedaling. Instead of dropping to zero, the last power number gets “stuck” in your ride file until the computer finally catches up.

It has been revealed that let’s say you’re riding along at 250 watts and stop pedaling as you approach a corner. Your computer might continue recording 250 watts for a few seconds while you’re coasting. On a graph, that can look like a flat line extending beyond the point where the power should have dropped.

Industry observers note that A few seconds might not sound like much, but think about how often you stop pedaling on a typical ride. Every corner, descent, stop sign, or moment spent coasting in the group is another opportunity for those extra watts to show up in your file. And if you stop pedaling after a hard effort, the computer could be holding a much higher number than 250 watts, which can skew your data.

It has been revealed that it’s also worth distinguishing this from the setting on some computers that lets you exclude zeroes when calculating average power. That setting changes how an average is calculated. Sticky watts affect the power values recorded in the ride file itself, so those extra values can still be there when you upload the ride for analysis.

In a recent development, on one ride, I compared the DURA 2 with a Garmin Edge 850 and an Edge 1060. The two Garmins recorded almost identical power numbers, but the DURA 2 consistently came out higher. When I looked more closely at the files, I found repeated instances where the COROS continued recording the last power value after both Garmins had dropped to zero.

The difference was especially noticeable during a series of short, hard efforts. After one effort, the DURA 2 recorded 565 watts for four seconds while both Garmins recorded zero. After another, it held 656 watts for three seconds. Across a roughly three-minute section containing several of these efforts, the Garmins averaged about 260 watts, while the COROS recorded nearly 307 watts.

In a recent development, those short efforts make the problem easy to see, but the difference showed up across the ride, too. In the roughly 98 minutes of matched power data I compared, the DURA 2 averaged about 186 watts, while both Garmins averaged about 179 watts.

Recent findings suggest that on a second ride, I compared the DURA 2 with a Hammerhead Karoo, Wahoo ELEMNT ACE, and Garmin Edge 850. Again, the COROS recorded higher power through a section with several hard efforts followed by coasting. The Garmin recorded lower numbers than the Karoo and Wahoo in that section, which reminds us that differences can go both ways when computers record the same power meter.

I was honestly surprised to see this on the DURA 2. The original DURA had similar issues early on, but its power recording improved with subsequent updates, and it performed well in GPLama’s 2025 video presenting the matter. I don’t want to turn this into a story about picking on COROS. The firm has a good history of updating and improving its products, and I expect it can address this issue on the DURA 2 as well. For now, these files show why it’s worth paying attention to what your cycling computer records, even when you trust your power meter.

If you mostly ride for fun and don’t pay much attention to your power data afterward, a few extra watts in your ride file probably won’t change your life. But if you use that data to track your training, compare rides, and work with a coach, those differences can matter.

Recent findings suggest that the big problem is that sticky watts don’t necessarily add the same amount to every ride. A steady climb with little coasting might show no difference. But a ride with lots of corners, stop signs, descents, or short, hard efforts followed by coasting could produce a much larger one. That makes it harder to compare rides or judge how much work you actually did.

In a recent development, the easiest way to check is to record the same ride on two cycling computers paired to the same power meter. You don’t necessarily need to buy a second computer. If a friend has one you can borrow, pair both to your power meter and record a ride with a few clear transitions from pedaling to coasting.

Sources indicate that alternatively, you can look closely at the power files your head unit generates. Do a couple of hard efforts, like sprints, where you stop pedaling at the end, then zoom in on those sections. Look for a flat section where one computer continues recording the same power value for several seconds after the other has dropped to zero.

And yes, I know that I’m definitely in some deep weeds over here, and it can be tough to argue that a cycling computer recording a few extra watts is a huge problem worth tackling. For many riders, it might not matter at all. But the current crop of cycling computers is also the most expensive we’ve ever seen. These devices are marketed and sold as precision training tools, and accurate data recording is central to that. These devices should do that, and riders shouldn’t have to question it.

Sources indicate that test Editor Dan Chabanov got his start in cycling as a New York City bike messenger but swiftly found his way into road and cyclocross racing, competing in professional cyclocross races from 2009 to 2019 and winning a Master’s National Championship title in 2018. Prior to joining Bicycling in 2021, Dan worked as part of the race organization for the Red Hook Crit, as a coach with EnduranceWERX, as well as a freelance writer and photographer.

#21977. The Comfort Crisis

The Comfort Crisis

📅 23 Jul 2023 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2594 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mrmoneymustache

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As with many things in life these days, it all started with an episode of the Peter Attia podcast.
  • In a recent development, in this edition, our nation’s most Badass Doctor was interviewing a guest I initially dismissed as not overly applicable to my own lifestyle.
  • Wow, what an amazing turn of phrase, and what a concise summary of the core of this whole Mustachianism thing I’ve been trying to express for the past dozen years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As with many things in life these days, it all started with an episode of the Peter Attia podcast.

In a recent development, in this edition, our nation’s most Badass Doctor was interviewing a guest I initially dismissed as not overly applicable to my own lifestyle. A young,excessively handsome dude who happened to be a writer with a new book out. But the headline of the episode was just intriguing enough to get me to click.

Wow, what an amazing turn of phrase, and what a concise summary of the core of this whole Mustachianism thing I’ve been trying to express for the past dozen years.

While the news headlines cry constantly about our nationwide personal debt crisis or health crisis or any other number of things that suggest that life is so hard these days, I have always seen the opposite: on average, we Americans seem to have a problem of ridiculous overindulgence and easiness in our lives, and our main problem is not recognizing it, and the damage it does to us.

So of course I had to click, and then listen to the whole two hour episode, and then buy the book, and then spend the past month reading and digesting it in small, meaningful chunks like the modern-day chunk of scripture-like wisdom that it is. And wow, am I glad I did so.

The author is Michael Easter, a former writer for Men’s Health magazine was also once catastrophically addicted to alcohol – and descended from a long family line of ancestors with the same affliction.

Industry observers note that he was lucky to catch himself from that fall in time to save his own life, and that story alone makes the book worth reading as someone who has stood by helplessly as loved ones battled with addiction. But I think his history with overindulgence in the hollow comforts of alcohol also gives him an edge on writing about the battle between comfort and hardship on the bigger stage of life in general.

So what is The Comfort Crisis about, and how can it make all of our lives better?

In a recent development, the best part about this book is just what a damned good writer this Easter guy is. Like many of the most fun popular science books*, it follows a split narrative which jumps back and forth to interweave the story of an insanely difficult caribou hunting trip he joined in a remote pocket of Alaska, with the appropriate bits of science, psychology and cultural commentary that help us explain and learn from each chapter of the epic shit he had just endured. This allows us to process and apply the lessons in our own lives.

For example, have you ever wondered why the type of bored, rich suburbanites who populate the board of your local Homeowner Association and whine about unacceptably tall weeds or unauthorized skateboarding on Nextdoor are so insufferable?

Why can’t they do something better with their time?

It turns out that there’s a scientific explanation for these unfortunate people, along with most of our other problems:.

The tendency of humans to always scan our environment for problems, regardless of how safe and perfect that environment is.

The book cited a study in which researchers told people to look for danger, in an environment which gradually became safer and safer:.

“When they ran out of stuff to find they would start looking for a wider range of stuff, even if this was not conscious or intentional, because their job was to look for threats.”.

“With that in mind, Levari recently conducted a series of studies to find out if the human brain searches for problems even when problems become infrequent or don’t exist.“.

According to recent reports, “As we experience fewer problems, we don’t become more satisfied. We just lower our threshold for what we consider a problem.“.

In other words, even when our lives are virtually problem free, instead of appreciating our good fortune we just start making up shit that we can complain about instead.

And then our politicians cock their greasy, finely-tuned ears in our direction and make up policies to appease our mostly-insubstantial concerns. And they invent their own trivial “wedge” problems to get us to all bicker about our different cultures and religions, suddenly caring about things that would not have even been problems if nobody told us they were.

And there’s America’s weakness in a nutshell, and meanwhile our strength comes entirely from the times we choose not to waste our time stooping to this level.

Meanwhile, the opposite effect holds true: people who survive in rougher environments than us end up more resilient and less prone to complaining.

In a series of recent interviews, Ukrainian people living in the war zones of their occupied country were asked “is it safe to live where you live?” and a strangely high percentage still mentioned “Yes” – not all that different from the responses of US residents when asked the same question about their own cities.

In a recent development, this adaptation principle also explains why some first generation immigrants tend to build businesses and wealth while their own offspring in second and third generations are more likely to become complacent and spend it down. As an immigrant myself, I can see why this is: conditions were just slightly more harsh and less comfortable and wealthy where I grew up, so I adapted to those conditions as “normal” which made the United States seem posh and easy by comparison. Which made it easier to spend less money and accumulate more.

The trap of pointless worry is just one of the many revelations of The Comfort Crisis. It also gives insightful explanations for why spending time in Nature boosts our mental and physical health, while cubicles and car driving grind us down.

There’s something in our biological wiring that responds instantly and powerfully to everything natural, in ways that you can’t get anywhere else.

Recent findings suggest that even placing a single plant into a hospital room will measurably improve the recovery of almost all patients from almost all ailments. So can you imagine the power of the medicine you are inhaling if you step into a real, living forest? And what if you spent several hours there, or even several days?

Later, we get lessons on our human adaptation towards the ratio of effort to reward:.

And our bizarre natural aversion to physical exertion:.

Which is remarkable, given the absolutely insane cost this tendency imposes upon us.

Moving your body, even a bit, has enormous benefits – again to almost all people towards reducing the probability and severity of almost all diseases. So can you imagine the benefit of moving your body for several hours per day in a natural environment, and including heavy load bearing and bits of extreme exertion?

Industry observers note that these things are not speculative pieces of alternative medicine. They are known, easily and reproducibly tested, and proven to be the most effective things we can possibly do with our time.

So why, the actual fuck, are people still sitting inside, watching Netflix, driving to work, and then driving to the doctor’s office to get deeper and deeper analysis of a neverending series of exotic and mysterious and unsolvable problems with their physical and mental health?

It has been revealed that we should at least start with the stuff we know is essential – maximum outdoor time every day, heavy exertion including with weights, minimal time spent sitting and driving, and minimum junk food, sugar, and alcohol. You definitely don’t have to be perfect, but just understand that these are the substantial levers for physical and mental health.

Only then, once you reach these minimum basic things for human survival, should you expect that more exotic and niche medicines and treatments are the only course of action.

Industry observers note that by all means, follow your doctor’s orders and don’t just dump all of your medications down the sink because of this MMM rant. But at the same time, realize that the stuff that is hard and uncomfortable is very likely to be the stuff that improves your life the most.

It’s all the stuff that Mr. Money Mustache has been telling you since 2012, but with more detail and less distraction. This book is a concentrated packet of advice for solid living.

Real Life Inspiration from the Good Book.

In a happy coincidence, I happened to be in the middle of some hard stuff** of my own as I worked my way through The Comfort Crisis and I found the perspective quite useful and transformative to apply hot off the press.

It has been revealed that normally somewhat of a homebody, I had embarked on a solo journey for some Carpentourism deep in the mountains of Southwestern Colorado. I had my whole life shrunk down into the newly introduced Model Y including food, bed, and the necessary tools and materials to tackle a pretty long laundry list of tasks on two different construction projects (fixing up a mini-resort property in Salida, and starting construction on a small cabin in Durango).

The trip immediately took a turn towards the dramatic as I climbed into the mountains and drove straight into the most torrential rainstorm I have ever seen, then accidentally broke a traffic law in a remote mountain town right in front of both of the local police officers ($115 fine and two points off my license), then five minutes after that had a small pebble hit my brand-new windshield which instantly spread into a crack that spans the whole thing, all before finally limping into Salida to unpack and get started on the work.

“Significant deal”, I can already hear you saying, “Retired man experiences two minor incidents while taking a vacation in his luxury car.”.

And you’re right, and that is exactly my point.

My life is so stable and comfortable that even these two miniature challenges threw me off balance, and I arrived in a slightly bummed and stressed-out state. But I still knew that in the bigger picture, they are good for me if I accept them as the lessons they are rather than choosing to continue to worry about them.

Industry observers note that as the trip went on, more things happened, almost as if The Comfort Crisis book were trying to prove a point. I drove three hours deeper into the mountains and up the steep dirt road to arrive at my second friend’s piece of land – a plot of forest in the mountains just outside of Durango.

According to recent reports, my work days in that high desert environment in the peak of summer were hot and physically demanding. It was hard to keep my tools, and my food supply in the cooler, and myself protected from the scorching sun (and a strange neverending blizzard of tree pollen) while still getting the job done. There was no indoor plumbing and we had to be very careful with our limited water supply. And then at the end of each day I had to reshuffle everything and set my car back up as a bedroom and crawl in for the night. Alone and far from home.

Recent findings suggest that but instead of feeling depressed as I experienced this constant hardship, the opposite thing was happening: I felt more alive and more badass with each passing day. I got better at being a feral forest man.

One day, my co-builder and I decided to take the afternoon off and head to the wild, remote Lemon Reservoir for some paddleboarding. We didn’t bring our phones or any other conveniences or amenities – just two boards and the minimal clothing required for swimming. And we headed out into a stiff headwind and little whitecap waves, laughing at the freedom of the experience.

It was hard, and slightly scary, as we got further and further from the shore. Progress was slow even with serious paddling, and we didn’t have any particular proposal beyond the spirit of “let’s GO!”.

But again Michael Easter was there whispering in my ear, saying,.

“Is this difficult, Mustache? GOOOOoood! Then you’d better keep going!”.

So we did. And we got way out into that lake, to a point where the water was shielded from the wind by the mountains on the other side. And it was awesome.

We cruised over to the shore to explore a particularly scenic meadow, coated with the softest green mossy grass and exuberantly colored wildflowers, and set at an impossibly steep angle. And damn I wished that I could have taken pictures, but in a strange way this forced me to burn that spot more thoroughly into my memories using my own senses instead.

In a recent development, then we headed back out into the center of the lake, set down the paddles, and just laid down on our boards to let the wind and the waves take us back towards the far end of the lake where we had started. And what a strange, serene feeling it was, floating on just a tube of air over two hundred feet of cold blue water, feeling like a jungle man with no cares and no plans and no material possessions. It could have been scary, but instead it was one of the best and most relaxed moments of my life.

Eventually, this week of forest living and exertion had to come to an end so I could get back to my own town to be a Dad again. But it ended with a final reminder of the principles of the Comfort Crisis – after so many days relatively extreme work and a relatively sparse food supply, I had grown used to a healthy background hunger. Which is yet another thing that we are meant to experience as humans – being satisfied and free from hunger all the time is neither normal nor healthy.

But when my hosts took me out on the town for a final night thank you dinner at the Mexican restaurant, the immense Burrito platter I consumed turned out to be the most delicious meal of my life.

It has been revealed that purposeful Hardship vs. Purposeful Spending.

There has been a lot of talk directed at the FIRE community recently about how bad we are at spending our money, and how we all need to loosen up. And there’s a small amount of truth to it, as my local friends Carl and Mindy recently admitted during a grilling on the Ramit Sethi podcast.

But we also need to keep this whole idea of excessive comfort in mind, and the damage it does to the natural human condition.

It’s great to spend money on adventures and improving yourself, being generous to others, and making the world a better place.

But it’s also way too easy to fool yourself into thinking you “want” things that just make your life easier and easier.

So your job is to catch yourself before this happens, and learn to keep things challenging, even as you upgrade the rest of your life experience.

In other words: buy yourself better tools, not softer chairs.

* Another great book that follows this style is Wired for Love by neruroscientist Stephanie Cacioppo – highly recommended for reading in parallel with a lover, whether upcoming or old.

** not actually hard by reasonable human standards, but it seemed hard by my comfort addicted first world standards.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

In a recent development, I review a ton of running watches, cycling through all of the various features and idiosyncrasies to find which watch would suit which runner best, which watches deserve a place on our lists, and which don’t measure up. Sometimes, there are watches that are really cool, and do a lot of work, but they offer more than what the average runner needs to log their daily miles and monitor their fitness. But for backwoods adventure runners, ultrarunners, or runners who put a lot of demand on their machines, advanced GPS running watches like the ones on this list offer a bit more of everything—from cellular and satellite connectivity to off-road trail mapping to sturdier cases, more multisport functionality, and all around just more.

In a recent development, as an ultrarunner, I am frequently testing watches for 50, 75, or even 100 miles at a stretch. Often these miles are spent deep in the woods in Upstate Latest York on trails that are poorly marked and pretty treacherous. Sometimes, there simply isn’t cell service to be had—anywhere. On top of that, I routinely test them during Hyrox, kayaking, paddle boarding, weight training, hiking, and even skiing—when there’s actually snow on the ground. My daily runs tend toward miles spent in New York City, which you wouldn’t think is an concern, but the tall buildings can thwart GPS pretty hard.

Sources indicate that looking for more running tech? Read our reviews of the best wireless headphones for running, headlamps for runners, and basic running watches.

The Fenix 9 is not flawless, but dang, it is as close to it as I’ve ever tested.I’ve put over 300 miles on the Pro Solar, so I’ll get my little nitpicks out of the way first. Annoyingly, there’s a lag of about half a second to a second when you start a workout, and again when you switch between laps that the 8 did not have. It’s not the most annoying thing in the world, but alas. Also, the app is still the Garmin Connect app. (I will beat this drum until they fix it.).

It has been revealed that now? My happy place, the good stuff. The solar ring on the Pro Solar model puts this watch so far ahead of every other run watch on the market that it can’t even see the others from the rearview. The 51mm is rated for up to 57 days in smartwatch mode with solar, and the 47mm gets up to 34. In the 51mm’s max battery GPS mode, that stretches to 186 hours, or up to 1,000 with solar. I took this out in the backwoodsiest of backwoods Adirondack trails, where I forced it to rely wholly on satellite, and I ran it for 12 solid hours, and it barely ticked the battery.

And that multiband GPS with SatIQ? It’s the best in class, and it locks you down in a hurry. The inReach satellite connectivity lets me run those backwoods and feel safe about doing so. (Though, I still bring a SatCom.).

In a recent development, it’s built like a beast without feeling like one. This is the first Fenix with a titanium case, plus a sapphire lens and a 10 ATM water rating, so rain, sweat, and my early morning postrun ocean swims don’t screw it up.

Industry observers note that it’s chockablock with performance and training metrics, and with Epic, their new multiday activity tracker, it’s better than ever. It’s light on the wrist, and it’s easy to use even with sweaty or sea salty fingers.

My favorite little bonus is the flashlight. It’s dimmable and comes in white, red, or green, so it’s great for visibility on early morning runs and also for finding crap at the bottom of my purse.

According to recent reports, the base Fenix 9 is a solid watch too, but the Pro Solar is the one I’d get. It’s simply a very fine watch.

You might not be familiar with this brand, but when I tell you, they are punching so far above their weight class with this watch that you would think a 10-year-old just knocked out Floyd Mayweather, I’m not kidding.

Sources indicate that the Amazfit Balance Ultra costs $599.99. For that you get a Grade 5 titanium case, a sapphire lens, and a 10 ATM rating that also covers freediving and recreational scuba. It weighs 57 grams without the strap, which is a lot of watch for so little weight. It’s a bit on the thicker side, but not so high profile it’s going to get caught on doors.

Battery is where things start to get unbelievable. The 780 mAh cell battery is rated for up to 30 days of typical use and 10 with the always-on display. In accurate GPS mode you get 50 hours, and power-saving GPS stretches to about 90 in our testing. Unless you’re running through the weekend, you’ll hit your limit before the watch does.

For tracking, it uses dual-band GPS across six satellite systems that ends up acting just like a typical multiband GPS on par with a Coros or a Suunto. That is clutch when you run between tall buildings or under tree cover and your watch would otherwise decide you swam across the Hudson. The 1.5-inch AMOLED screen is bright enough that it can be read in direct sun for the most part.

I will say that the dang buttons on the side are far too easy to depress, leading to accidentally starting activities, but overall, it’s incredible.

In a recent development, the Garmin Enduro 4 is a light upgrade from the 3. It has increased storage, an upgraded band, and introduces some more in-built activities like rucking and rowing alongside Garmin’s multiday training tool Epic. The Enduro line is built for multi-day trekking. Everything about it is engineered for endurance—the rugged design, precise tracking, and especially the solar-powered battery that seems to last forever. You don’t even think about charging most days; it just handles your training, races, and long trail days without missing a beat. The safety and satellite coverage give you extra peace of mind when you’re out alone, far from cell service or the nearest trailhead.

Two features stand out on every serious run. The Pack Weight tool adjusts your effort estimates based on how heavy your gear is, which makes your performance data feel more real—especially on long mountain efforts. And the Next Fork guide keeps you on track, showing how far it is to the next junction so that you don’t have to stop and fumble through maps. Add Garmin’s multiband GPS with SatiQ tech that automatically switches between the best systems into the mix, and logs routes that are spot-on, no matter how deep into the woods you go.

For ultrarunners or anyone training big, the Enduro 4 is reliability wrapped around your wrist—with battery life that feels almost unfair.

Sources indicate that I’ve been using the Suunto Vertical 2 off and on for a while now, and I’ve come to see it as a true multisport powerhouse rather than an everyday watch. It’s the one I pull out when training or adventures get serious—long runs, big mountain weekends, or backcountry routes where accuracy and endurance matter more than aesthetics. What sets it apart immediately are its maps—they’re crisp, easy to read, and fully offline, which makes navigation seamless even in the most remote terrain.

Battery life is another standout feature. The Vertical 2 easily lasts up to 60 days in smartwatch mode and delivers exceptional runtime with dual-band GNSS tracking, something that still amazes me every time I scroll through my recorded routes after multihour training blocks. The titanium and sapphire glass construction give it a premium, expedition-ready feel, and the watch itself feels built to handle harsh conditions without flinching.

It’s definitely not what I’d wear every day—it’s large, rugged, and purpose-built—but that’s exactly the point. For athletes who bounce between cycling, running, skiing, hiking, and more, the Vertical 2 is a multisport dream, offering a level of mapping, tracking, and battery endurance suited for endless exploration.

Recent findings suggest that the Garmin Forerunner 970 has been my daily watch for months, and it feels like the perfect blend of lifestyle usability and serious athletic performance. It’s light, comfortable, and sleek enough to wear all day—but underneath that understated design is a fully loaded training tool built for racing, coaching, and multidiscipline endurance work. Whether I’m tracking an interval session, planning an ultra-block, or guiding athletes through structured workouts, the 970 handles it all seamlessly.

Sources indicate that GPS precision is exceptional thanks to its multiband GNSS system, locking on quickly and maintaining accuracy even through tree cover and narrow streets. The built-in coaching and training readiness tools have become part of my daily routine—providing recovery insights, suggested sessions, and race forecasts that actually feel tailored. For multisport training, it transitions modes smoothly, syncing effortlessly with sensors and Garmin Connect data.

As someone who loves to spend their hard-earned money on running in a pack of fellow weirdos at races, the pace predictor and race features are a significant draw for the Garmin Forerunner 970. I sync my races from Garmin Connect, and the watch spits out predicted times for 5K up to marathons based on my VO2 max, training load, and recent runs, updating as I log more miles. What seals it for me are the race markers overlaid on the course profile, showing projected splits and elevation-adjusted pacing so I can visualize where to surge or conserve energy without second-guessing midrace. It's like having a personal coach whispering realistic goal times right before the gun goes off, turning pricey pack running into a heart-thumping hunt for a PR.

According to recent reports, battery life remains solid, though not as extreme as Garmin’s solar or expedition-focused models, lasting up to 20 days in smartwatch mode. Add in smart notifications, music storage, contactless payments, and wrist-based navigation, and it becomes a rare hybrid—a true performance watch that fits effortlessly into everyday life.

The Apple Watch Ultra 4 is a vast improvement over the Ultra 3, which is a polite way of saying the Ultra 3 had room to grow.

GPS now locks on fast. Apple notes there’s no change here, but other members of my team and I noticed a difference. It might be in the software updates, but it’s better. I'm no longer starting runs before the watch has made up its mind. Once it has locked on, though, it commits to a story that isn’t quite true. Distance runs consistently one to one and a half percent long. During a marathon, that’s a few tenths of a mile I didn't earn.

Sources indicate that battery, thankfully, is finally impressing me. It’s leaps and bounds better, and it charges absurdly fast. I top it up while the coffee brews and I take my shower, and by the time I’m done, it’s fully loaded and ready to go.

Industry observers note that heart rate is the big jump. Against a Holter monitor, it stayed within two to three bpm on steady efforts. Run hard and it drifts to five to seven. I do wish it sampled my heart rate every second of every day instead of every five, but overall I don’t think the difference is huge, and when you combine that with the beauty of their apps, it’s hardly a thing.

According to recent reports, what’s missing for me is lactate threshold. I can live without many advanced run metrics, but I like knowing my threshold for training runs.

In a recent development, in their new and improved health app, the ECG and hypertension alerts are useful, the cycle insights are spot on, and the morning report doesn’t make me feel graded. Transit pay, apps, and phone integration are unmatched. Satellite calling is extremely easy compared to any other watch I’ve tried. It’s a freaking great watch, overall.

When you step into the world of high-end GPS running watches, the sheer number of options can feel overwhelming—until you see the immense power packed into these bad boys. The essentials are non-negotiable: rock-solid multiband GPS precision, exceptional battery life (no one wants to lose tracking on a 50K run), accurate heart rate and recovery metrics, and seamless integration with your training plans. Every watch on this list delivers on those core requirements.

Where they start to spread their wings is everything layered on top. The bells and whistles are kinda wild. Things like dual-frequency GPS for navigating deep woods (or mountaintops), topo and trail maps that actually make sense when you’re lost, and multisport modes that keep up whether you’re running, swimming, skiing, triathlon training, or rolling through a Hyrox circuit. Barometric altitude readings, pulse ox sensors, and training readiness scores just round out the “how cooked am I?” data we’ve all come to both love and loathe in equal measure.

In a recent development, some watches, though, don’t just tell you about your fitness—they could save your butt in a sticky situation. The Garmin Fenix 8 Pro works with Garmin’s inReach satellite system, letting you text or send an SOS nowhere near cell service. The Apple Watch Ultra takes a slightly different route with built-in satellite SOS and cellular, so if you’re off-grid and something goes sideways, you’re not shouting into the void. These are the kinds of features that make the difference between just tracking a run and actually trusting your gear if things go sideways.

It has been revealed that let’s be honest—most runners don’t need a watch this powerful. But if you’re out there chasing hours instead of miles, exploring trail networks that don’t even show up on Google Maps, or toggling between swim intervals, mountain climbs, and winter ski sessions, these make a world of difference. Basically, if you’re a runner like me with electricity in your veins and the ADHD that drives you toward multisport or off-the-beaten-trail running, these watches are for you.

Sources indicate that one of the quietest but most important reasons these watches shine is safety. With incident detection, live tracking, fall alerts, and SOS tools that actually connect you to help, they turn your wrist into a mini rescue hub. The Garmins can ping your emergency contacts automatically or connect through inReach. The Apple Watch Ultra fires off emergency signals via satellite if you end up out of range. And even the Suunto Vertical and Coros Vertix 2S earn their stripes here with detailed offline maps and batteries that cruise through multi-day efforts.

According to recent reports, basically, these aren’t just training tools—they’re peace of mind on your wrist. When you’re 10 miles deep in a trail system and the forest gets quiet, it’s nice knowing your watch is smarter about directions and safety than your phone or maybe even you.

In a recent development, cat Bowen, senior editor of commerce; reviews, is a seasoned runner with more than 20 years of distance running experience, including dozens of marathons, half marathons, and even a few ultra marathons. For over a decade, she has tested parenting, fitness, home, and running gear and written in-depth guides to help readers with their next purchase. Holding multiple advanced degrees and at the moment studying kinesiology, Cat Bowen brings research-backed insight to all of her guides. Passionate about women’s health and neurodivergent inclusion, she advocates for closing research gaps and helping others—especially AudHD people—find joy in running and fitness.

Sources indicate that jeff is Runner-in-Chief for Runner’s World and the director of product testing. He has tested and reviewed running shoes, GPS watches, headphones, apparel, and more for nearly two decades. He regularly tests more than 100 pairs of shoes each year, and once had a 257-day streak running in different models. Jeff can usually be found on the roads, racing anything from the mile to a marathon, but he also enjoys racing up mountains and on snowshoes. When he’s not running, you’ll probably find him hanging from a ladder making repairs and renovations to his house (he’s also director of product testing for Popular Mechanics).

Latest Update: Our Editors Found the Best Early Black Friday E-Bike Deals, Including 45% Off a Cannondale and $499 Budget Picks.

📅 02 Feb 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2112 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling
